Lie symmetry group methods for differential equations

F. Güngör Thanks: gungorf@itu.edu.tr Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Science and Letters, Istanbul Technical University, 34469 Istanbul, Turkey
August 11, 2026
Abstract

Fundamentals on Lie group methods and applications to differential equations are surveyed. Numerous examples are included to elucidate their extensive applicability for analytically solving both ordinary and partial differential equations.

Introduction

This paper reviews a treatment of differential equations using methods from Lie group theory. Symmetry group methods are amongst the most powerful universal tools for the study of differential equations. There has been rapid progress on these methods over the last few decades. Methods and algorithms for classifying subalgebras of Lie algebras, new results on the structure and classification of abstract finite and infinite dimensional Lie algebras [48] and methods for solving group classification problems for differential equations greatly facilitated to systematically obtain exact analytic solutions by quadratures to ordinary differential equations and group-invariant solutions to partial differential equations and to identify equivalent equations. The application of Lie groups to differential equations has a long history. In the second half of the nineteenth century, Norwegian mathematician Sophus Lie (1842-1899) introduced continuous groups of transformations [26, 28] to give a unified and systematic theory for the study of properties of solutions of differential equations just like Evariste Galois’s (1811-1831) dream to solve algebraic equations by radicals, which led to the theory of Galois. In his memoir of 1831, he considered the group of admissible permutations. The theory of Lie groups and algebras originated precisely in the context of differential equations. Over the years, these transformations evolved into the modern theory of abstract Lie groups and algebras.

As far as differential equations are concerned, the main observation was that much of the known solutions methods were actually specific cases of a general solution (general or particular solution) method based on the invariance of a system of differential equations under a continuous group of transformations (called symmetry group of the system).

Symmetry group of a partial differential equation (PDE) can be used to reduce the number of independent variables, to transform known simple solutions to new solutions. For an ordinary differential equation (ODE), even reduction in order can be made. Under some special structure of the symmetry group, reduction can even go all the way down to an algebraic equation, from which general solution can be obtained.

The computation of the symmetry group of a system of differential equations can be computationally complicated, but nevertheless completely algorithmic. Computer algebra systems can automate most of the steps of the Lie symmetry algorithm.

It should be emphasized that applications of Lie group methods using classical group of point transformations are not only restricted to differential equations. They, and when applicable, their generalizations to higher order symmetries can also be carried over to conservation laws, Hamiltonian systems, difference and differential-difference equations, integro-differential equations, delay differential equations, fractional differential equations.

Basic ideas, definitions, theorems and results needed to be able to apply Lie group methods for solving differential equations are presented. Many examples with mathematical and physical applications are considered to illustrate applications to integration of ODEs by the method of reduction of order, construction of group-invariant solutions to PDEs, identification of equivalent equations based on the existence of isomorphic symmetry groups, generating new solutions from known ones, group-classification problem and construction of invariant differential equations.

There exists a vast literature on the methods and applications of Lie groups and algebras to differential equations and other fields of mathematics and physics. For more detailed treatments of the subject, the readers are referred to the books [35, 38, 19, 4, 18, 36, 51, 40, 17] and the handbooks [20, 21, 22]. A basic knowledge of Lie groups and algebras will be assumed. The reader is directed to, for example, a recent book [48] for a good account of basic definitions, theorems and applications of Lie algebras.

1 Vector fields and integral curves

We begin with a brief review of some essential objects that will be employed throughout. Let MM be a differentiable manifold of dimension nn. A curve γ\gamma at a point xx of MM is a differentiable map γ:I→M\gamma:I\to M, where II is a subinterval of ℝ\mathbb{R}, such that γ⁡(0)=x\gamma(0)=x, 0∈I0\in I.

A vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} of the manifold MM is a C∞C^{\infty}-section of T​MTM, in other words a C∞C^{\infty} mapping from MM to T​MTM that assigns to each point xx of M a vector in Tx​MT_{x}M. In the local coordinate system x=(x1,…,xn)∈Mx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in M, 𝐯\mathbf{v} can be expressed as

𝐯|x=∑i=1nξi(x)∂xi,\mathbf{v}|_{x}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}}, (1)

where ξi​(x)∈C∞​(M)\xi_{i}(x)\in C^{\infty}(M), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

An integral curve of the vector field at the point xx is the curve γ\gamma at xx whose tangent vector γ˙​(t)\dot{\gamma}(t) coincides with 𝐯\mathbf{v} at the point x=γ⁡(t)x=\gamma(t) such that γ˙​(t)=𝐯|γ⁡(t)\dot{\gamma}(t)=\mathbf{v}|_{\gamma(t)} for each t∈It\in I. In the local representation of the curve γ\gamma it amounts to saying that the curve satisfies an autonomous system of first order ordinary differential equations

d​γi​(t)d​t=ξi(γ(t)),i=1,…,n.\frac{d\gamma_{i}(t)}{dt}=\xi_{i}(\gamma(t)),\quad i=1,\ldots,n. (2)

The existence and uniqueness theorem for systems of ODES ensures that there is a unique solution to the system with the initial data γ⁡(0)=x0\gamma(0)=x_{0} (the Cauchy problem). This gives rise to the existence of a unique maximal integral curve γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) passing through the point x0=γ⁡(0)∈Mx_{0}=\gamma(0)\in M. We call such a maximal integral curve the flow of 𝐯\mathbf{v} at x=γ⁡(t)x=\gamma(t) and denote Φ⁡(t,x)\Phi(t,x) with the basic properties

Φ⁡(0,x)=x,Φ⁡(s,Φ⁡(t,x))=Φ⁡(t+s,x),dd​t​Φ​(t,x)=𝐯|Φ⁡(t,x),x∈M,\Phi(0,x)=x,\quad\Phi(s,\Phi(t,x))=\Phi(t+s,x),\quad\frac{d}{dt}\Phi(t,x)=\mathbf{v}\big|_{\Phi(t,x)},\quad x\in M, (3)

for all sufficiently small t,s∈ℝt,s\in\mathbb{R}. A more suggestive notation for the flow is Φ⁡(t,x)=exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x\Phi(t,x)=\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}x. The reason is simply that it satisfies the ordinary exponential rules. The second property implies that Φ⁡(−t,x)=Φ−1​(t,x)\Phi(-t,x)=\Phi^{-1}(t,x) or exp⁡(t​𝐯)−1​x=exp⁡(−t​𝐯)​x\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}^{-1}x=\exp{(-t\mathbf{v})}x. One can infinitesimally express the flow

exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x=x+t​𝐯|x+𝒪⁡(t2).\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}x=x+t\mathbf{v}|_{x}+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}). (4)

The flow exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}x generated by the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} is sometimes called a one-parameter group of transformations as it arises as the action of the Lie group ℝ\mathbb{R} on the manifold MM.

Conversely, given a flow with the first two properties of (3), we can reconstruct its generating vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} by differentiating the flow:

𝐯|x=dd​t​exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x|t=0,x∈M.\mathbf{v}|_{x}=\frac{d}{dt}\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}x\big|_{t=0},\quad x\in M.

The inverse process of constructing the flow is usually called exponentiation (or integration) of 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Rectification of a vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} in a neighborhood of a regular point (a point xx at which 𝐯|x\mathbf{v}|_{x} does not vanish) is always possible.

Theorem 1.1.

If x0x_{0} is a regular point of 𝐯\mathbf{v}, then there exist local rectifying (or straightening out) coordinates y=(y1,…,yn)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) near x0x_{0} such that y=∂y1y=\partial_{y_{1}} generates the translational flow exp⁡(t​𝐯)​y=(y1+t,y2,…,yn)\exp{(t\mathbf{v})}y=(y_{1}+t,y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}).

Let 𝐯\mathbf{v} be a vector field in the local coordinates

𝐯=∑i=1nξi(x)∂xi.\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}}. (5)

Application of a vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} to a smooth function f:M→ℝf:M\to\mathbb{R}, also referred to the Lie derivative of ff with respect to the vector field, determines the infinitesimal rate of change in ff as the parameter tt of the induced flow exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x\exp{(t\mathbf{v})x} of 𝐯\mathbf{v} varies:

𝐯⁡(f⁡(x))=∑i=1nξi​(x)​∂f∂xi=dd​t|t=0​f​(exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x).\mathbf{v}(f(x))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}f(\exp{(t\mathbf{v})x}). (6)

It is observed that vector fields act on functions as derivations in the sense that they are linear and satisfy the Leibnitz rule

𝐯⁡(f+g)=𝐯⁡(f)+𝐯⁡(g),𝐯⁡(f​g)=f​𝐯​(g)+g​𝐯​(f).\mathbf{v}(f+g)=\mathbf{v}(f)+\mathbf{v}(g),\quad\mathbf{v}(fg)=f\mathbf{v}(g)+g\mathbf{v}(f). (7)

The action of the flow generated by 𝐯\mathbf{v} on a function can be obtained from the following Lie series (assuming its convergence)

f⁡(exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x)=∑j=0∞εjj!​𝐯j​(f⁡(x)).f(\exp{(t\mathbf{v})x})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{\varepsilon^{j}}{j!}\mathbf{v}^{j}(f(x)). (8)

The Lie series is derived by expanding f⁡(exp⁡(t​𝐯)​x)f(\exp{(t\mathbf{v})x}) into the Taylor’s series in ε\varepsilon. For the special choice f⁡(x)=xf(x)=x, we recover the flow (4).

If y=ψ⁡(x)y=\psi(x) is a change of coordinates, then by the chain rule, the vector field (5) in the new coordinates yy is expressed as

𝐯=∑j=1n∑i=1nξi​(ψ−1​(y))​∂ψj∂xi​(ψ−1​(y))​∂∂yj=∑j=1n𝐯⁡(ψj​(x))|x=ψ−1​(y)​∂∂yj.\mathbf{v}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(\psi^{-1}(y))\frac{\partial\psi_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}(\psi^{-1}(y))\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{j}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}(\psi_{j}(x))\big|_{x=\psi^{-1}(y)}\frac{\partial}{\partial y_{j}}. (9)

The commutator or Lie bracket of two vector fields 𝐯\mathbf{v} and 𝐰\mathbf{w} is defined as the unique vector field satisfying

[𝐯,𝐰]​f=𝐯⁡(𝐰⁡(f))−𝐰⁡(𝐯⁡(f))[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}]f=\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{w}(f))-\mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}(f)) (10)

for all smooth functions f:M→ℝf:M\to\mathbb{R}. If, in local coordinates,

𝐯=∑i=1nξi(x)∂xi,𝐰=∑i=1nηi(x)∂xi,\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}},\quad\mathbf{w}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\eta_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}},

then

[𝐯,𝐰]=∑i=1n{𝐯(ηi)−𝐰(ξi)}∂xi.[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\mathbf{v}(\eta_{i})-\mathbf{w}(\xi_{i})\right\}\partial_{x_{i}}.

The coefficients 𝐯⁡(ηi)\mathbf{v}(\eta_{i}) and 𝐰⁡(ξi)\mathbf{w}(\xi_{i}) are the actions of the vector fields 𝐯\mathbf{v} and 𝐰\mathbf{w} as derivations on the functions ηi\eta_{i} and ξi\xi_{i}, respectively as defined in (6).

2 Differential equations and their symmetry group

We consider a system of nn-th order differential equations ℰ\mathcal{E}

ℰ:𝖤ν(x,u(n))=𝖤ν(x,u,u(1),…,u(n))=0,ν=1,2,…,N,\mathcal{E}:\quad\mathsf{E}_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)})=\mathsf{E}_{\nu}(x,u,u^{(1)},\ldots,u^{(n)})=0,\quad\nu=1,2,\ldots,N, (11)

where x=(x1,…,xp)∈ℝpx=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, u=(u1,…,uq)∈ℝqu=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{q} (p,q∈ℤ+p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}) are the independent and dependent variables, which form local coordinates on the space of independent and dependent variables E=X×U≃ℝp×ℝqE=X\times U\simeq\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}. The derivatives of uu are denoted by uα,J=∂Juα/∂xJu_{\alpha,J}=\partial^{J}u_{\alpha}/\partial x_{J}, where J=(j1,…,jk)J=(j_{1},\ldots,j_{k}), 1≤jν≤p1\leq j_{\nu}\leq p, k=j1+…+jkk=j_{1}+\ldots+j_{k}, is a symmetric multi-index of order k=#​Jk=\#J. u(k)u^{(k)} denotes all partial derivatives of order ≤k\leq k of the components uαu_{\alpha} of uu, which provide coordinates on the jet space Jn​(x,u(n))=Jn​EJ^{n}(x,u^{(n)})=J^{n}E . If there is a single independent and dependent variable, namely p=1p=1 and q=1q=1, then the system becomes a scalar ordinary differential equation. In that case, we simply write

𝖤⁡(x,u,u1,u2,…,un)=0,\mathsf{E}(x,u,u_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{n})=0,

where u1=uxu_{1}=u_{x}, u2=ux​xu_{2}=u_{xx}, …\ldots, un=u(n)u_{n}=u^{(n)}.

The system 𝖤ν=0\mathsf{E}_{\nu}=0 defined by a collection of smooth functions 𝖤=(𝖤1,…,𝖤N)\mathsf{E}=(\mathsf{E}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{E}_{N}) can be identified with a variety 𝒮𝖤={(x,u(n)):𝖤=0}\mathcal{S}_{\mathsf{E}}=\left\{(x,u^{(n)}):\mathsf{E}=0\right\} contained in the nn-th order jet space JnJ^{n} with local coordinates (x,u(n))(x,u^{(n)}).

The functions 𝖤ν​(x,u(n))\mathsf{E}_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)}) will be assumed to be regular, meaning that the Jacobian matrix of 𝖤ν\mathsf{E}_{\nu} with respect to the jet coordinates (x,u(n))(x,u^{(n)}) has maximal rank

rank⁡(∂𝖤ν∂xi,∂𝖤ν∂uα,J)=N,\rank\left(\frac{\partial\mathsf{E}_{\nu}}{\partial x_{i}},\frac{\partial\mathsf{E}_{\nu}}{\partial u_{\alpha,J}}\right)=N,

at each (x,u(n))(x,u^{(n)}) satisfying the system.

A classical symmetry group of (11) is a local group GG of point transformations Φ:E→E\Phi:E\to E, a locally defined invertible map on the space of independent and dependent variables, mapping solutions of the system to solutions

Φ:(x~,u~)=g.(x,u)=(Φ1​(x,u),Φ2​(x,u)CLOSE.\Phi:\quad(\tilde{x},\tilde{u})=g.(x,u)=(\Phi_{1}(x,u),\Phi_{2}(x,u).

Such transformations act on solutions u=f⁡(x)u=f(x) by mapping pointwise their graphs. More precisely, if Γf={(x,f(x)}\Gamma_{f}=\left\{(x,f(x)\right\} is the graph of f⁡(x)f(x), then the mapped graph will have the graph Γf~={(x~,f~(x~)}=g.Γf≡{g.(x,f(x))}\Gamma_{\tilde{f}}=\{(\tilde{x},\tilde{f}(\tilde{x})\}=g.\Gamma_{f}\equiv\left\{g.(x,f(x))\right\}.

Contact or generalized transformations where Φ\Phi depends on higher order derivatives will not be treated here.

Definition 2.1.

A local Lie group of point transformations GG is called a symmetry group of the system of partial differential equations (11) if f~=g.f\tilde{f}=g.f is a solution whenever ff is.

To find the symmetry group, the prolonged transformation pr(n)​Φ:Jn→Jn{\rm pr}^{(n)}\Phi:J^{n}\to J^{n} is required to preserve the differential structure of the equation manifold 𝒮𝖤\mathcal{S}_{\mathsf{E}}. In order to find the symmetry group Lie’s infinitesimal approach will be used. We need to use the prolongation tool for the group transformation and the vector field generating it. Let Φε=exp⁡(ε​𝐯)\Phi_{\varepsilon}=\exp(\varepsilon\mathbf{v}) be a one-parameter subgroup of the connected group GG and let

𝐯=∑i=1pξi(x,u)∂xi+∑α=1qφα(x,u)∂uα\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}(x,u)\partial_{x_{i}}+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}\varphi_{\alpha}(x,u)\partial_{u_{\alpha}} (12)

be the infinitesimal generator of Φε\Phi_{\varepsilon}. The infinitesimal generator of the prolonged one-parameter subgroup pr(n)​Φε{\rm pr}^{(n)}\Phi_{\varepsilon} is defined to be the prolongation of the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Definition 2.2.

The nn-th prolongation pr(n)​𝐯{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v} of 𝐯\mathbf{v} is a vector field on the nn-th jet space JnJ^{n} defined by

pr(n)​𝐯|(x,u(n))=dd​ε|ε=0​pr(n)​Φε​(x,u(n)){\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}\big|_{(x,u^{(n)})}=\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}{\rm pr}^{(n)}\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,u^{(n)}) (13)

for every (x,u(n))∈Jn(x,u^{(n)})\in J^{n}.

If we integrate pr(n)​𝐯{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v} we find the prolongation of the group action pr(n)​Φε{\rm pr}^{(n)}\Phi_{\varepsilon} on the space JnJ^{n}. The prolonged vector field pr(n)​𝐯{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v} has the form

pr(n)𝐯=∑i=1pξi∂xi+∑α=1q∑#​J≤nφαJ∂uα,J,{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}\partial_{x_{i}}+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}\sum_{\#J\leq n}\varphi_{\alpha}^{J}\partial_{u_{\alpha,J}}, (14)

where the coefficients φαJ\varphi_{\alpha}^{J} are given by the formula

φαJ=DJ​(φα−∑i=1pξi​uα,i)+∑i=1pξi​uα,J,i,\varphi_{\alpha}^{J}=D_{J}\left(\varphi_{\alpha}-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}u_{\alpha,i}\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}u_{\alpha,J,i}, (15)

where uα,i=∂uα/∂xiu_{\alpha,i}=\partial u_{\alpha}/\partial x_{i}, uα,J,i=∂uα,J/∂xiu_{\alpha,J,i}=\partial u_{\alpha,J}/\partial x_{i} and DJ=Dj1​…​DjkD_{J}=D_{j_{1}}\ldots D_{j_{k}}, 1≤jν≤p1\leq j_{\nu}\leq p is the JJ-th total derivative operator [35]. Here DiD_{i} is the total differentiation operator defined by

Di=∂∂xi+∑α=1q∑Juα,J,i​∂∂uα,J.D_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}\sum_{J}u_{\alpha,J,i}\frac{\partial}{\partial u_{\alpha,J}}.

DiD_{i} involves infinite summation, but its application to a particular differential function will only require finitely many terms of order 0≤#​J≤n0\leq\#J\leq n, where nn is the highest order derivative in the differential function on which DiD_{i} acts.

There is a useful recursive formula for the coefficients of the prolonged vector field in (14)

φαJ,i=Di​φαJ−∑k=1p(Di​ξk)​uα,J,k.\varphi_{\alpha}^{J,i}=D_{i}\varphi_{\alpha}^{J}-\sum_{k=1}^{p}(D_{i}\xi_{k})u_{\alpha,J,k}. (16)

If nn-th prolongation is known, the (n+1)(n+1)-th prolongation can be calculated by the formula (16). In particular, the coefficients of the first order derivatives uxju_{x_{j}} in (14) are then given by

φαj=Dj​φα−∑k=1p(Dj​ξk)​uα,k.\varphi_{\alpha}^{j}=D_{j}\varphi_{\alpha}-\sum_{k=1}^{p}(D_{j}\xi_{k})u_{\alpha,k}. (17)

In the special case p=q=1p=q=1, the recursion formula (16) simplifies to

φj=Dxφj−1−(Dxξ)u(j),j=1,2,….\varphi^{j}=D_{x}\varphi^{j-1}-(D_{x}\xi)u^{(j)},\quad j=1,2,\ldots. (18)

The coefficients of the second prolongation of the vector field 𝐯=ξ(x,u)∂x+φ(x,u)∂u\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,u)\partial_{x}+\varphi(x,u)\partial_{u} corresponds to j=1,2j=1,2 with the convention φ0=φ\varphi^{0}=\varphi

φx=Dx​φ−(Dx​ξ)​ux,φx​x=Dx​φx−(Dx​ξ)​ux​x,Q=φ−ξ​ux.\varphi^{x}=D_{x}\varphi-(D_{x}\xi)u_{x},\quad\varphi^{xx}=D_{x}\varphi^{x}-(D_{x}\xi)u_{xx},\quad Q=\varphi-\xi u_{x}.

The prolongations of vector fields satisfy the linearity

pr(n)​(a​𝐯+b​𝐰)=a​pr(n)​𝐯+b​pr(n)​𝐰,{\rm pr}^{(n)}(a\mathbf{v}+b\mathbf{w})=a\;{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}+b\;{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{w}, (19)

for constants aa, bb and the Lie algebra property

pr(n)​[𝐯,𝐰]=[pr(n)​𝐯,pr(n)​𝐰].{\rm pr}^{(n)}[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}]=[{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v},{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{w}]. (20)

Hence, the prolongation process defines a Lie algebra homomorphism from the space of vector fields on J0J^{0} to the space of vector fields on JnJ^{n}. If the vector fields 𝐯\mathbf{v} form a Lie algebra, then their prolongations realize an isomorphic Lie algebra of vector fields on JnJ^{n}.

Example 2.3.

Let us consider the smooth projective vector field

𝐯=x2∂x+xu∂u\mathbf{v}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xu\partial_{u} (21)

generating the one-parameter local projective group

Φε​(x,u):x~​(x,u,ε)=x1−ε​x,u~​(x,u,ε)=u1−ε​x,\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,u):\quad\tilde{x}(x,u;\varepsilon)=\frac{x}{1-\varepsilon x},\quad\tilde{u}(x,u;\varepsilon)=\frac{u}{1-\varepsilon x}, (22)

whenever 1−ε​x≠01-\varepsilon x\neq 0. The vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} can be recovered by differentiating Φε​(x,u)\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,u) at ε=0\varepsilon=0.

The first and second prolonged group transformations are derived by the usual chain rule for the ordinary derivatives:

pr(1)​Φε​(x,u,u1)=(x~,u~,u~1),u~1=u1+ε⁡(u−x​u1),{\rm pr}^{(1)}\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,u,u_{1})=(\tilde{x},\tilde{u},\tilde{u}_{1}),\quad\tilde{u}_{1}=u_{1}+\varepsilon(u-xu_{1}),

and

pr(2)​Φε​(x,u,u1,u2)=(x~,u~,u1+ε⁡(u−x​u1),(1−ε​x)3​u2).{\rm pr}^{(2)}\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,u,u_{1},u_{2})=\left(\tilde{x},\tilde{u},u_{1}+\varepsilon(u-xu_{1}),(1-\varepsilon x)^{3}u_{2}\right).

Applying definition 2.2 we find the prolonged vector fields

pr(1)𝐯=𝐯+(u−xu1)∂u1,pr(2)𝐯=𝐯+(u−xu1)∂u1−3xu2∂u2.{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+(u-xu_{1})\partial_{u_{1}},\quad{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+(u-xu_{1})\partial_{u_{1}}-3xu_{2}\partial_{u_{2}}. (23)

The following theorem determines the Lie algebra of the symmetry group GG and known as the infinitesimal criterion of invariance of (11).

Theorem 2.4.

A connected local group of transformations GG is a symmetry group of the system ℰ\mathcal{E} of (11) if and only if the nn-th prolongation pr(n)​𝐯{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v} annihilates the system on solutions, namely

pr(n)𝐯(𝖤ν)=0,ν=1,2,…,N,{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{E}_{\nu})=0,\quad\nu=1,2,\ldots,N, (24)

whenever u=f⁡(x)u=f(x) is a solution to the system (11) for every infinitesimal generator 𝐯\mathbf{v} of GG.

Eqs. (24) are known as the determining equations of the symmetry group for the system. They form a large over-determining linear system of partial differential equations for the coefficients ξi\xi_{i} and φα\varphi_{\alpha} of 𝐯\mathbf{v}. This criterion has been applied to many differential equations arising in different branches of mathematics, physics and engineering to compute symmetry groups. The computation of symmetry group using the infinitesimal approach (Theorem (2.4)) have been implemented in several computer algebra systems, such as MATHEMATICA, MAPLE, REDUCE, MACSYMA (or freely available MAXIMA) [6, 16]. There are packages dedicated to the symmetry group calculations which make considerably easy the routine steps of finding the determining system and partial integration of them. Some packages are capable of triangularize the overdetermined system using differential Gröbner basis method. Packages equipped with automatic integrators can usually fail to provide the general solution of the determining system depending on the complexity of the system. We refer to [50] for the symbolic calculation of symmetries of differential equations.

There is an alternative formulation of the prolongation formula, which is useful in prolongation computations. This requires the formalism of the evolutionary vector fields. Given the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} as in (1), we define the qq-tuple Q⁡(x,u(1))=(Q1,…,Qq)Q(x,u^{(1)})=(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{q}) defined by

Qα​(x,u(1))=φα​(x,u)−∑i=1pξi​(x,u)​uα,iα=1,2,…,q.Q_{\alpha}(x,u^{(1)})=\varphi_{\alpha}(x,u)-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}(x,u)u_{\alpha,i}\quad\alpha=1,2,\ldots,q.

The functions QαQ_{\alpha} are called the characteristics of the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v}. Then, we have

φαJ=DJ​Qα+∑i=1pξi​uα,J,i,DJ=Dj1​…​Djk,1≤jν≤p\varphi_{\alpha}^{J}=D_{J}Q_{\alpha}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}u_{\alpha,J,i},\quad D_{J}=D_{j_{1}}\ldots D_{j_{k}},\quad 1\leq j_{\nu}\leq p (25)

and the nn-th prolongation of 𝐯\mathbf{v} can be expressed as

pr(n)​𝐯=pr(n)​𝐯Q+∑i=1pξi​Di,{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}={\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}_{Q}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i}D_{i},

where

𝐯Q=∑α=1qQα(x,u(1))∂uα,pr(n)𝐯Q=∑α=1q∑JDJQα∂uα,J.\mathbf{v}_{Q}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}Q_{\alpha}(x,u^{(1)})\partial_{u_{\alpha}},\quad{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}_{Q}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}\sum_{J}D_{J}Q_{\alpha}\partial_{u_{\alpha,J}}.

Obviously, 𝐯Q\mathbf{v}_{Q} and their prolongations do not act on the independent variables xix_{i}. In terms of characteristics QαQ_{\alpha}, the infinitesimal transformations can be written as

x~i=xi,u~α=uα+ε​Qα+𝒪⁡(ε2).\tilde{x}_{i}=x_{i},\quad\tilde{u}_{\alpha}=u_{\alpha}+\varepsilon Q_{\alpha}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2}).

Since Di​𝖤ν=0D_{i}\mathsf{E}_{\nu}=0 on solutions, we can replace the infinitesimal symmetry condition (24) by the simpler formula

pr(n)​𝐯Q|𝖤ν=0=0.{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}_{Q}\Big|_{\mathsf{E}_{\nu}=0}=0. (26)
Example 2.5.

We show that the Laplace equation Δ​u​(x,y)=ux​x+uy​y=0\Delta u(x,y)=u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0 in the plane is invariant under the symmetry group generated by the vector field

𝐯=ξ(x,y)∂x+η(x,y)∂y,\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,y)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,y)\partial_{y}, (27)

where ξ\xi and η\eta satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations ξx=ηy\xi_{x}=\eta_{y} , ξy=−ηx\xi_{y}=-\eta_{x}, in other words ξ\xi, η\eta are harmonic functions and therefore 𝐯\mathbf{v} generates an infinite-dimensional symmetry group of the two-dimensional Laplace equation. We recall that the general solution can be expressed in terms of two arbitrary analytic functions.

The second prolongation of 𝐯\mathbf{v} is

pr(2)𝐯=𝐯+φx∂ux+φy∂uy+φx​x∂ux​x+φx​y∂ux​y+φy​y∂uy​y.{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\varphi^{x}\partial_{u_{x}}+\varphi^{y}\partial_{u_{y}}+\varphi^{xx}\partial_{u_{xx}}+\varphi^{xy}\partial_{u_{xy}}+\varphi^{yy}\partial_{u_{yy}}.

The coefficients φx​x\varphi^{xx}, φy​y\varphi^{yy} are calculated from the general prolongation formulas (14)-(15)

φx​x=−(2​ηx​ux​y+2​ξx​ux​x+ηx​x​uy+ξx​x​ux),\varphi^{xx}=-(2\eta_{x}u_{xy}+2\xi_{x}u_{xx}+\eta_{xx}u_{y}+\xi_{xx}u_{x}),
φy​y=−(2​ξy​ux​y+2​ηy​uy​y+ηy​y​uy+ξy​y​ux).\varphi^{yy}=-(2\xi_{y}u_{xy}+2\eta_{y}u_{yy}+\eta_{yy}u_{y}+\xi_{yy}u_{x}).

So from the Cauchy–Riemann equations we find that the infinitesimal criterion of invariance (24) is satisfied

pr(2)​𝐯​(Δ​u)=φx​x+φy​y=−2​ξx​Δ​u=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}(\Delta u)=\varphi^{xx}+\varphi^{yy}=-2\xi_{x}\Delta u=0

on the solution surface. The linearity of the equation implies that it also admits the additional trivial symmetries u∂uu\partial_{u} and ρ(x,y)∂u\rho(x,y)\partial_{u} with Δ​ρ=0\Delta\rho=0 (one can multiply solutions by constants and add them). The symmetry condition then becomes pr(2)(u∂u)(Δu)=Δu=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}(u\partial_{u})(\Delta u)=\Delta u=0 and pr(2)(ρ∂u)(Δu)=Δρ=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}(\rho\partial_{u})(\Delta u)=\Delta\rho=0 on solutions. Obviously, the second one is satisfied if ρ\rho is an arbitrary harmonic function.

The special choice (ξ,η)=(x2−y2,2​x​y)(\xi,\eta)=(x^{2}-y^{2},2xy) leads to the conformal invariance of the Laplace equation. The one-parameter conformal symmetry group corresponding to the vector field 𝐜x=(x2−y2)∂x+2xy∂y\mathbf{c}_{x}=(x^{2}-y^{2})\partial_{x}+2xy\partial_{y} is easily obtained solving the following complex initial value problem for z~​(x,y,ε)\tilde{z}(x,y;\varepsilon) (more precisely, integrating the analytic vector field z2∂zz^{2}\partial_{z})

with the condition z~​(x,y,0)=z⁡(x,y)=x+i​y\tilde{z}(x,y;0)=z(x,y)=x+iy. The flow is given by

z~=z1−ε​z=z−ε​|z|2(1−ε​z)​(1−ε​z¯).\tilde{z}=\frac{z}{1-\varepsilon z}=\frac{z-\varepsilon|z|^{2}}{(1-\varepsilon z)(1-\varepsilon\bar{z})}.

x~=x−ε⁡(x2+y2)1−2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2),y~=y1−2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2),\tilde{x}=\frac{x-\varepsilon(x^{2}+y^{2})}{1-2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})},\quad\tilde{y}=\frac{y}{1-2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})}, (28)

possessing the invariant function ζ⁡(x,y)=y​(x2+y2)−1\zeta(x,y)=y(x^{2}+y^{2})^{-1}, satisfying the relation ζ⁡(x~,y~)=ζ⁡(x,y)\zeta(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})=\zeta(x,y) on ℝ2∖(0,0)\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus(0,0). ζ⁡(x,y)\zeta(x,y) is readily obtained by eliminating the group parameter ε\varepsilon in (28) (see the next Section for a more precise definition and infinitesimal derivation of invariant function of a symmetry group).

It is a well-know fact that the inversion map I⁡(x,y)=(x2+y2)−2​(x,y)I(x,y)=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{-2}(x,y), (x,y)≠0(x,y)\neq 0 (an involution: I−1=II^{-1}=I) is a discrete (not connected) symmetry, i.e. if f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) satisfies the Laplace equation, so does f⁡((x2+y2)−2​x,(x2+y2)−2​y)f((x^{2}+y^{2})^{-2}x,(x^{2}+y^{2})^{-2}y). Conjugating any symmetry of the equation by II will produce a new symmetry (a conformal mapping here). Indeed, the pushforward I∗I_{*} of the vector field −∂x-\partial_{x} through II is I∗(−∂x)=𝐜~x~I_{*}(-\partial_{x})=\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{\tilde{x}}, where tilde means that the vector field is written in the new coordinates. So exp⁡(ε​𝐜x)​(x,y)\exp(\varepsilon\mathbf{c}_{x})(x,y) can be recovered by conjugating the translational group along the xx-axis: x→x−εx\to x-\varepsilon by II

exp{ε𝐜x}(x,y)=I(x,y)∘exp{−ε∂x}∘I(x,y).\exp\left\{\varepsilon\mathbf{c}_{x}\right\}(x,y)=I(x,y)\circ\exp\left\{-\varepsilon\partial_{x}\right\}\circ I(x,y).

exp{ε𝐜y}(x,y)=I(x,y)∘exp{−ε∂y}∘I(x,y).\exp\left\{\varepsilon\mathbf{c}_{y}\right\}(x,y)=I(x,y)\circ\exp\left\{-\varepsilon\partial_{y}\right\}\circ I(x,y).

generates another conformal transformation

x~=x1−2​ε​y+ε2​(x2+y2),y~=y−ε⁡(x2+y2)1−2​ε​y+ε2​(x2+y2).\tilde{x}=\frac{x}{1-2\varepsilon y+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})},\quad\tilde{y}=\frac{y-\varepsilon(x^{2}+y^{2})}{1-2\varepsilon y+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})}. (29)

The one-parameter group transformations generated by the elements of the abelian subalgebra {𝐜x,𝐜y}\left\{\mathbf{c}_{x},\mathbf{c}_{y}\right\} are conformal because they leave form invariant the planar metric:

d​x~2+d​y~2=λ⁡(x,y,ε)​(d​x2+d​y2),d\tilde{x}^{2}+d\tilde{y}^{2}=\lambda(x,y;\varepsilon)(dx^{2}+dy^{2}),

Note that the inversion itself is also a conformal mapping with λ=(x2+y2)−2\lambda=(x^{2}+y^{2})^{-2}. The full (special) conformal transformations are given by the translation group conjugation I∘exp{ε1∂x+ε2∂y}∘I(x,y)I\circ\exp\{\varepsilon_{1}\partial_{x}+\varepsilon_{2}\partial_{y}\}\circ I(x,y) in the form

𝐱~=(x~,y~)=𝐱−𝜺⁡(x2+y2)1−2​𝜺⋅𝐱+ε2​(x2+y2),𝜺=(ε1,ε2),𝐱=(x,y).\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=(\tilde{x},\tilde{y})=\frac{\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}(x^{2}+y^{2})}{1-2\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})},\quad\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}=(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}),\quad\mathbf{x}=(x,y). (30)

Note that this transformation is not globally defined because the conformal factor λ⁡(x,y,ε1,ε2)=1−2​𝜺⋅𝐱+ε2​(x2+y2)=0\lambda(x,y;\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2})=1-2\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})=0 at the point 𝐱=𝜺/ε2\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon^{2}.

We conclude that action of this group on solutions states that u=f⁡(x~,y~)u=f(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) is also a solution, whenever f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) is solution to the Laplace equation. For example, with the help of the invariant ζ\zeta, the radial solution f⁡(x,y)=log⁡(x2+y2)f(x,y)=\log(x^{2}+y^{2}) or the angular solution f⁡(x,y)=arctan⁡(y/x)f(x,y)=\arctan(y/x), among many others (homogeneous harmonics) can be mapped to produce the new solutions

u=log⁡x2+y21−2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2),u=arctan⁡yx−ε⁡(x2+y2).u=\log\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{1-2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})},\quad u=\arctan\frac{y}{x-\varepsilon(x^{2}+y^{2})}.

Adding to 𝐜x\mathbf{c}_{x} and 𝐜y\mathbf{c}_{y} the subalgebras obtained by other choices (ξ,η)=(1,0),(0,1)(\xi,\eta)=(1,0),(0,1), (ξ,η)=(−y,x)(\xi,\eta)=(-y,x) and, (ξ,η)=(x,y)(\xi,\eta)=(x,y) leading to the translational, rotational and dilatational invariance, in terms of vector fields, 𝐩x=∂x\mathbf{p}_{x}=\partial_{x}, 𝐩y=∂y\mathbf{p}_{y}=\partial_{y}, 𝐣=−y∂x+x∂y\mathbf{j}=-y\partial_{x}+x\partial_{y}, 𝐝=x∂x+y∂y\mathbf{d}=x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y}, respectively, we obtain the 6-dimensional Lie algebra of the conformal group Conf⁡(ℝ2)\conf(\mathbb{R}^{2}) of the Euclidean plane ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, isomorphic to SO⁡(3,1)\Ort(3,1), the Lorentz group of four-dimensional Minkowski space [11]. Obviously, the subalgebra spanned by {𝐩x,𝐝,𝐜x}\left\{\mathbf{p}_{x},\mathbf{d},\mathbf{c}_{x}\right\} is sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}). This symmetry group is the two-dimensional analogue of the full conformal group in dimensions n≥3n\geq 3. Note that the full conformal group in the plane ℝ2≅ℂ\mathbb{R}^{2}\cong\mathbb{C} is infinite-dimensional, with the Lie group SO⁡(3,1)\Ort(3,1) as its maximal finite-dimensional subgroup, because any analytic function f:ℂ→ℂf:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} leads to a conformal transformation (In our case f⁡(z)=z,i​z,z2f(z)=z,iz,z^{2}). We have excluded the trivial symmetry algebra stemming from the linearity of the PDE. Their non-zero commutators satisfy

[𝐩x,y,𝐝]=𝐩x,y,[𝐣,𝐩x]=−𝐩y,[𝐣,𝐩y]=𝐩x,[𝐩1,𝐜x]=[𝐩2,𝐜y]=2​𝐝,[\mathbf{p}_{x,y},\mathbf{d}]=\mathbf{p}_{x,y},\quad[\mathbf{j},\mathbf{p}_{x}]=-\mathbf{p}_{y},\quad[\mathbf{j},\mathbf{p}_{y}]=\mathbf{p}_{x},\quad[\mathbf{p}_{1},\mathbf{c}_{x}]=[\mathbf{p}_{2},\mathbf{c}_{y}]=2\mathbf{d},
[𝐩x,𝐜y]=−[𝐩y,𝐜x]=−2​𝐣,[𝐝,𝐜x,y]=𝐜x,y,[𝐣,𝐜x]=−𝐜y,[𝐣,𝐜y]=𝐜x.[\mathbf{p}_{x},\mathbf{c}_{y}]=-[\mathbf{p}_{y},\mathbf{c}_{x}]=-2\mathbf{j},\quad[\mathbf{d},\mathbf{c}_{x,y}]=\mathbf{c}_{x,y},\quad[\mathbf{j},\mathbf{c}_{x}]=-\mathbf{c}_{y},\quad[\mathbf{j},\mathbf{c}_{y}]=\mathbf{c}_{x}.

A nonlinear variant of the Laplace equation, known as the conformal scalar curvature equation, or the elliptic Liouville’s equation, occurs in the study of isothermal coordinates in differential geometry and has the form

ux​x+uy​y=K​eu,u_{xx}+u_{yy}=Ke^{u}, (31)

where KK is constant (Gaussian curvature).

The conformal symmetry structure of this equation on the (x,y)(x,y)-plane is preserved. The vector field generating the symmetry group GG of the equation is given by

𝐯=ξ∂x+η∂y−2ξx∂u,\mathbf{v}=\xi\partial_{x}+\eta\partial_{y}-2\xi_{x}\partial_{u},

where ξ⁡(x,y)\xi(x,y), η⁡(x,y)\eta(x,y) satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations. For (ξ,η)=(x2−y2,2​x​y)(\xi,\eta)=(x^{2}-y^{2},2xy), 𝐯=(x2−y2)∂x+2xy∂y−4x∂u\mathbf{v}=(x^{2}-y^{2})\partial_{x}+2xy\partial_{y}-4x\partial_{u}. We solve the initial value problem d​u~/d​ε=−4​x~d\tilde{u}/d\varepsilon=-4\tilde{x}, u~​(x,y,0)=u​(x,y)\tilde{u}(x,y;0)=u(x,y) using (28) and find the transformation of uu under the group action:

u~​(x,y,ε)=2​ln⁡σ⁡(x,y,ε)+u⁡(x,y),σ⁡(x,y,ε)=1−2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2).\tilde{u}(x,y;\varepsilon)=2\ln\sigma(x,y;\varepsilon)+u(x,y),\quad\sigma(x,y;\varepsilon)=1-2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2}). (32)

We note that

σ⁡(x,y,ε)=σ​(x~,y~,−ε)−1=1+2​ε​x~+ε2​(x~2+y~2).\sigma(x,y;\varepsilon)=\sigma(\tilde{x},\tilde{y};-\varepsilon)^{-1}=1+2\varepsilon\tilde{x}+\varepsilon^{2}(\tilde{x}^{2}+\tilde{y}^{2}).

Application of the one-parameter transformation group defined by (28) and (32) to a solution f⁡(x,y)f(x,y), where the coordinates (x,y)(x,y) are written in terms of (x~,y~)(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) leads to the transformed new solution uε​(x,y)u_{\varepsilon}(x,y) (after the tildes are removed)

uε​(x,y)=−2​ln⁡σ⁡(x,y,−ε)+f⁡(x~,y~),u_{\varepsilon}(x,y)=-2\ln\sigma(x,y;-\varepsilon)+f(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}),

where

x~=x+ε⁡(x2+y2)1+2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2),y~=y1+2​ε​x+ε2​(x2+y2).\tilde{x}=\frac{x+\varepsilon(x^{2}+y^{2})}{1+2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})},\quad\tilde{y}=\frac{y}{1+2\varepsilon x+\varepsilon^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})}.
Remark 2.6.

The Laplace equation in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with n≥3n\geq 3 is invariant only under a finite dimensional conformal Lie symmetry group of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimension (n+22)=(n+1)​(n+2)/2\binom{n+2}{2}=(n+1)(n+2)/2, consisting of the groups of translations, rotations, dilation and conformal transformations (obtained by conjugating the nn-components of the translational group via inversion I⁡(𝐱)=|𝐱|−2​𝐱I(\mathbf{x})=|\mathbf{x}|^{-2}\mathbf{x}) on ℝn∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\left\{0\right\}.

The symmetry algebra of the Laplace equation (see [46] for its derivation)

Δn​u​(x)=0,x=(x1,x2,…,xn)∈ℝn\Delta_{n}u(x)=0,\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

is spanned by

𝐩i=∂xi,𝐝=∑j=1nxj∂xj,𝐣i​j=xi∂xj−xj∂xi,i≠j,𝐜i=2xi𝐝−r2∂xi+(2−n)xiu∂u,r2=∑j=1nxj2,𝐦=u∂u,𝐯(ρ)=ρ(x)∂u,Δnρ=0,\begin{split}&\mathbf{p}_{i}=\partial_{x_{i}},\quad\mathbf{d}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}\partial_{x_{j}},\quad\mathbf{j}_{ij}=x_{i}\partial_{x_{j}}-x_{j}\partial_{x_{i}},\quad i\neq j,\\ &\mathbf{c}_{i}=2x_{i}\mathbf{d}-r^{2}\partial_{x_{i}}+(2-n)x_{i}u\partial_{u},\quad r^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}^{2},\\ &\mathbf{m}=u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}(\rho)=\rho(x)\partial_{u},\quad\Delta_{n}\rho=0,\end{split} (33)

where i,j=1,2,…,ni,j=1,2,\ldots,n. The (n+1)​(n+2)/2(n+1)(n+2)/2-dimensional Lie algebra {𝐩i,𝐝,𝐣i​j,𝐜i}\{\mathbf{p}_{i},\mathbf{d},\mathbf{j}_{ij},\mathbf{c}_{i}\} generates the conformal group Conf⁡(ℝn)\conf(\mathbb{R}^{n}) of the Euclidean plane ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

We note that the conformal transformations of 𝐑n\mathbf{R}^{n} are generated by the conformal vector fields 𝐯=∑i=1nξi(x)∂xi\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}}, where the coefficients ξi\xi_{i} satisfy the conformal Killing equations

∂ξi∂xj+∂ξj∂xi=λ⁡(x)​δi​j,i,j=1,2,…,n\frac{\partial\xi_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}+\frac{\partial\xi_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}=\lambda(x)\delta_{ij},\quad i,j=1,2,\ldots,n

for some undetermined function λ\lambda (the conformal factor).

The linear wave equation ut​t=Δ​uu_{tt}=\Delta u, u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x), (t,x)∈ℝn+1(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} is invariant under a Lie point symmetry algebra isomorphic to the Lorentz group SO⁡(n+1,2)\Ort(n+1,2), of dimension (n+32)=(n+2)​(n+3)/2\binom{n+3}{2}=(n+2)(n+3)/2, n≥2n\geq 2 in a Minkowski space with an indefinite underlying metric d​s2=d​t2−d​x12−⋯−d​xn2ds^{2}=dt^{2}-dx_{1}^{2}-\cdots-dx_{n}^{2}.

The nonlinear wave (or Klein–Gordon) equation ut​t−ux​x=F⁡(u)u_{tt}-u_{xx}=F(u) is invariant under the Poincaré group P⁡(1,1)\PP(1,1) of 1+11+1-dimensional Minkowski plane for any F⁡(u)F(u) with F′′≠0F^{\prime\prime}\neq 0. Its Lie symmetry algebra is generated by the translational vector fields and Lorenz boost

𝐯1=∂t,𝐯2=∂x,𝐯3=t∂x+x∂t.\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=t\partial_{x}+x\partial_{t}.

For two specific forms of F⁡(u)F(u), the symmetry algebra is larger (see Section 4.1 for the group classification problem). The additional vector field for F⁡(u)=F0​ukF(u)=F_{0}u^{k} is 𝐯4=t∂t+x∂x+21−ku∂u\mathbf{v}_{4}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+\frac{2}{1-k}u\partial_{u}, and 𝐯4=t∂t+x∂x−2λ∂u\mathbf{v}_{4}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}-\frac{2}{\lambda}\partial_{u} for F⁡(u)=F0​eλ​uF(u)=F_{0}e^{\lambda u}.

The second special case is known as the hyperbolic Liouville equation, which in the light-cone (characteristic) coordinates r=t+xr=t+x, s=t−xs=t-x has the form

ur​s=a​eu.u_{rs}=ae^{u}. (34)

This equation is invariant under the infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra generated by the vector field

𝐯=ξ(r)∂r+η(s)∂s−(ξ′(r)+η′(s))∂u,\mathbf{v}=\xi(r)\partial_{r}+\eta(s)\partial_{s}-(\xi^{\prime}(r)+\eta^{\prime}(s))\partial_{u}, (35)

where ξ⁡(r)\xi(r) and η⁡(s)\eta(s) are arbitrary functions. This is true for any aa because

pr(2)​𝐯​(ur​s−a​eu)=−(ur​s−a​eu)​(ξ′​(r)+η′​(s)).{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}(u_{rs}-ae^{u})=-(u_{rs}-ae^{u})(\xi^{\prime}(r)+\eta^{\prime}(s)).

𝐯\mathbf{v} generates the infinite dimensional symmetry group depending on two arbitrary functions

r~=f⁡(r),s~=g⁡(s),u~=u−ln⁡(f′​(r)​g′​(s)),f′​g′≠0.\tilde{r}=f(r),\quad\tilde{s}=g(s),\quad\tilde{u}=u-\ln(f^{\prime}(r)g^{\prime}(s)),\quad f^{\prime}g^{\prime}\neq 0. (36)

The group action implies that if F⁡(r,s)F(r,s) is a solution, so is the function u=F⁡(r~,s~)+ln⁡(f′​g′)u=F(\tilde{r},\tilde{s})+\ln(f^{\prime}g^{\prime}). The general solution of (34) for a≠0a\neq 0 can be found by acting on a particular solution of the form

u=F⁡(r+s)=ln⁡2a​(r+s)2u=F(r+s)=\ln\frac{2}{a(r+s)^{2}}

as

u=F⁡(r~+s~)+ln⁡(f′​g′)=ln⁡(2a​f′​(r)​g′​(s)(f⁡(r)+g⁡(s))2).u=F(\tilde{r}+\tilde{s})+\ln(f^{\prime}g^{\prime})=\ln\left(\frac{2}{a}\frac{f^{\prime}(r)g^{\prime}(s)}{(f(r)+g(s))^{2}}\right). (37)

So the general solution of

ut​t−ux​x=a​euu_{tt}-u_{xx}=ae^{u}

can be expressed in terms of two arbitrary functions as

u=ln⁡(8a​f′​(t+x)​g′​(t−x)(f⁡(t+x)+g⁡(t−x))2).u=\ln\left(\frac{8}{a}\frac{f^{\prime}(t+x)g^{\prime}(t-x)}{(f(t+x)+g(t-x))^{2}}\right).

This solution was obtained by Liouville as early as 1853.

The linear case F′′=0F^{\prime\prime}=0 is quite different, the symmetry group is the infinite-dimensional conformal group.

3 Differential invariants

Given a Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, characterization of all invariant equations, equations that remain invariant under the symmetry group GG of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} requires the notion of differential invariants, which are functions unaffected by the action of GG on some manifold MM. An ordinary invariant is a C∞​(J​(x,u))C^{\infty}(J(x,u)) function I⁡(x,u)I(x,u) on J⁡(x,u)⊂MJ(x,u)\subset M, which satisfies I(g.(x,u))=I(x,u)I(g.(x,u))=I(x,u) for all group elements g∈Gg\in G and coordinates (x,u)(x,u).

Definition 3.1.

A differential invariant of order nn of a connected transformation group GG is a differential function I⁡(x,u(n))I(x,u^{(n)}) on the jet space JnJ^{n} if I(g(n).(x,u(n)))=I(x,u(n))I(g^{(n)}.(x,u^{(n)}))=I(x,u^{(n)}) for all g∈Gg\in G and (x,u(n))∈Jn(x,u^{(n)})\in J^{n}.

An ordinary invariant is a differential invariant of order 0. The following infinitesimal invariance criterion for differential invariants serves to determine differential invariants of a given connected group of transformations in a simple manner by just solving a system of linear first order PDEs.

Proposition 3.2.

A function II is a differential function for a connected group GG if and only if it is annihilated by all the prolonged vector fields (infinitesimal generators)

𝐯(n)​(I)≡pr(n)​𝐯​(I)=0\mathbf{v}^{(n)}(I)\equiv{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}(I)=0 (38)

for all 𝐯∈𝔤\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g}.

An function II is an ordinary invariant if and only if 𝐯⁡(I)=0\mathbf{v}(I)=0. For a general vector field

𝐯=∑i=1nξi(x)∂xi,\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}(x)\partial_{x_{i}},

the coordinates y=η⁡(x)y=\eta(x) rectifying 𝐯=∂y1\mathbf{v}=\partial_{y_{1}} are found by solving the first order partial differential equations 𝐯⁡(η1)=1\mathbf{v}(\eta_{1})=1, 𝐯⁡(ηi)=0\mathbf{v}(\eta_{i})=0, i>1i>1. So the new coordinates yi​(x)y_{i}(x) are the functionally independent invariants of the one-parameter group generated by 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Remark 3.3.

The dimension of the space JnJ^{n} is dimJn=p+q​(p+nn)\dim J^{n}=p+q\binom{p+n}{n}. The number of derivative coordinates of order exactly nn is given by qn=dimJn−dimJn−1=q​(p+n−1n)q_{n}=\dim J^{n}-\dim J^{n-1}=q\binom{p+n-1}{n}.

The number of functionally independent differential invariants of order nn is equal to

k=dimJn−(dimG−dimG0),k=\dim J^{n}-(\dim G-\dim G_{0}), (39)

where G0G_{0} is the stabilizer subgroup (also called the isotropy group) of a generic point on JnJ^{n}. d=dimG−dimG0d=\dim G-\dim G_{0} is the dimension of the orbit of GG at a generic point. An equivalent formula for knk_{n} is

kn=dimJn−rank⁡Z≥0,k_{n}=\dim J^{n}-\rank Z\geq 0,

where ZZ is the matrix of size r×dimJnr\times\dim J^{n} formed by the coefficients of the nn-th prolongations pr(n)​(𝐯ν){\rm pr}^{(n)}(\mathbf{v}_{\nu}), ν=1,2,…,r\nu=1,2,\ldots,r of the basis vector fields 𝐯1,…,𝐯r\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r} of the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of the group GG as rows

𝐯ν=∑i=1pξi,ν(x,u)∂xi+∑α=1qφα,ν(x,u)∂uα,ν=1,2,…,r.\mathbf{v}_{\nu}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi_{i,\nu}(x,u)\partial_{x_{i}}+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{q}\varphi_{\alpha,\nu}(x,u)\partial_{u_{\alpha}},\quad\nu=1,2,\ldots,r.

The rank mm of ZZ is calculated at a generic point of JnJ^{n}. For the special case of one independent and one dependent variable p=q=1p=q=1 we have dimJn=n+2\dim J^{n}=n+2 and the number of functionally independent invariants is kn=n+2−mk_{n}=n+2-m.

The set of nn-th order differential invariants I1,I2,…,IkI_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k} of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} will be denoted by ℐn​(𝔤)\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g}). This set is an ℝ\mathbb{R}-algebra. This means that ℐn​(𝔤)\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g}) is a vector space over the field ℝ\mathbb{R} and satisfies the property that any arbitrary smooth function H⁡(I1,…,Ik)H(I_{1},\ldots,I_{k}) of the set of differential invariants I1,I2,…,IkI_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k} is also a differential invariant, i.e. if I1,I2,…,Ik∈ℐn​(𝔤)I_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k}\in\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g}), then H⁡(I1,…,Ik)∈ℐn​(𝔤)H(I_{1},\ldots,I_{k})\in\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g}). They also satisfy the inclusions

ℐ0​(𝔤)⊂ℐ1​(𝔤)⊂…​ℐn​(𝔤)⊂…\mathcal{I}_{0}(\mathfrak{g})\subset\mathcal{I}_{1}(\mathfrak{g})\subset\ldots\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g})\subset\ldots

The algebra ⋃n=0∞ℐn​(𝔤)\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g}) is called the algebra of differential invariants.

3.1 Invariant differentiation

Lie [28, 27, 29] and Tresse [52] introduced the notion of ”invariant” differential operators to obtain (n+1)(n+1)-st order differential invariants from nn-th order ones. This enables one to produce all the higher order functionally independent differential invariants by successive application of the invariant operators to lower order invariants. The situation is easier when there is only one dependent variable. Let the group GG with Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} act on the basic space E=J0​(ℝ,ℝn)≃X×UE=J^{0}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^{n})\simeq X\times U.

Proposition 3.4.

Suppose that I⁡(x,u(n))I(x,u^{(n)}) and J⁡(x,u(n))J(x,u^{(n)}) are functionally independent invariants, at least one of which has order exactly nn. Then the ratio Dx​J/Dx​ID_{x}J/D_{x}I (the Tresse derivative) is an (n+1)(n+1)-st order differential invariant.

If I⁡(x,u(n))I(x,u^{(n)}) is any given differential invariant, then 𝒟=(Dx​I)−1​Dx\mathcal{D}=(D_{x}I)^{-1}D_{x} is an invariant differential operator so that iterating on 𝒟\mathcal{D} one can generate an hierarchy 𝒟k​J\mathcal{D}^{k}J, k=0,1,2,…,k=0,1,2,\ldots, of higher order differential invariants.

If z=I⁡(x,u)z=I(x,u) and w=J⁡(x,u,u1)w=J(x,u,u_{1}) are a complete set of functionally independent invariants of the first prolongation pr(1)​𝔤{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathfrak{g}, i.e. they form the basis of ℐ1​(𝔤)\mathcal{I}_{1}(\mathfrak{g}), then I,JI,J together with the derivatives 𝒟k​J=dk​w/d​zk\mathcal{D}^{k}J=d^{k}w/dz^{k}, k=1,2,…,n−1k=1,2,\ldots,n-1 generate a complete set of functionally independent invariants for the prolonged algebra pr(n)​𝔤{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathfrak{g} for n≥1n\geq 1. They all satisfy the infinitesimal invariant condition pr(n)​𝐯​(𝒟k​J)=0{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}(\mathcal{D}^{k}J)=0 for a vector field 𝐯∈𝔤\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g}.

Example 3.5.

We know from Example 2.3 that the algebra of vector fields 𝐯=x2∂x+xu∂u\mathbf{v}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xu\partial_{u} on J0​(ℝ,ℝ)J^{0}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) has the first order differential invariants I=u/xI=u/x, J=x​u1−uJ=xu_{1}-u, which satisfy 𝐯⁡(I)=0\mathbf{v}(I)=0, pr(1)​𝐯​(J)=0{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathbf{v}(J)=0. The Tresse derivative D​J/D​I=J−1​(x3​u2)DJ/DI=J^{-1}(x^{3}u_{2}) gives the second order differential invariant. We can take it as J2=J​D​J/D​I=x3​u2J_{2}=JDJ/DI=x^{3}u_{2} as it is needed only up to functional independence. Iterating the Tresse derivatives and multiplying by JJ we obtain the sequence of all other differential invariants as Jk=x2​Dx​Jk−1J_{k}=x^{2}D_{x}J_{k-1}, k=3,4,…k=3,4,\ldots.

Determination of a complete set of functionally independent differential invariants (the basis ℐn​(𝔤)\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g})) allows us to construct classes of differential equations with a prescribed symmetry algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}.

Theorem 3.6.

If the differential functions

I1​(x,u(n)),I2​(x,u(n)),…,Ik​(x,u(n))∈ℐn​(𝔤)⊂JnI_{1}(x,u^{(n)}),I_{2}(x,u^{(n)}),\ldots,I_{k}(x,u^{(n)})\in\mathcal{I}_{n}(\mathfrak{g})\subset J^{n}

form a set of functionally independent nn-th order differential invariants of GG, then a system of nn-th order differential equations are invariant under GG if and only if it can be written in terms of the differential invariants:

𝖤ν(x,u(n))=Hν(I1,I2,…,Ik)=0,ν=1,2,…,N.\mathsf{E}_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)})=H_{\nu}(I_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k})=0,\quad\nu=1,2,\ldots,N. (40)

Invariant equations obtained in this way are called strongly invariant (pr(n)​Hν​(I1,…,Ik)=0{\rm pr}^{(n)}H_{\nu}(I_{1},\ldots,I_{k})=0 is satisfied everywhere).

d​y11+y12=d​y23​y1​y2=d​y34​y1​y3+3​y22.\frac{dy_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{2}}=\frac{dy_{2}}{3y_{1}y_{2}}=\frac{dy_{3}}{4y_{1}y_{3}+3y_{2}^{2}}. (43)

This equation and other third order invariant equations can be integrated using three consecutive quadratures (see Example 4.14 for the integration procedure).

4 Reduction of order for ordinary differential equations

Theorem 4.1.

Let the scalar ODE

𝖤⁡(x,y(n))=𝖤⁡(x,y,y1,…,yn)=0,∂𝖤∂yn≠0\mathsf{E}(x,y^{(n)})=\mathsf{E}(x,y,y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})=0,\quad\frac{\partial\mathsf{E}}{\partial y_{n}}\neq 0

admit a one-parameter symmetry group GG generated by 𝐯∈𝔤\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g}. All nontangential solutions (𝐯∈𝔤\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g} is nowhere tangent to the graph of the solution) can be found by quadrature from the solutions to a reduced ODE (𝖤/G)​(x,y(n−1))(\mathsf{E}/G)(x,y^{(n-1)}).

Proof.

If we introduce rectifying (canonical or normal) coordinates r=r⁡(x,y)r=r(x,y) and s=s⁡(x,y)s=s(x,y) in which 𝐯\mathbf{v} generates a group of translation r→rr\to r, s→s+εs\to s+\varepsilon with the corresponding normal form 𝐯^=∂s\widehat{\mathbf{v}}=\partial_{s}. Its prolongation pr(n)𝐯^=∂s{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{\widehat{v}}=\partial_{s} and therefore the derivatives in the new coordinates remain unchanged so that from the invariance condition (24) it follows that the equation in normal form should be independent of the variable ss, but can depend on the derivatives. Therefore we have reduced our equation to one of order n−1n-1, (𝖤/G)​(r,s′,…,s(n−1))(\mathsf{E}/G)(r,s^{\prime},\ldots,s^{(n-1)}) for the derivative z=ϑ⁡(r)=d​s/d​r=s′​(r)z=\vartheta(r)=ds/dr=s^{\prime}(r). Once we know the solution of the reduced equation, the solution to the original one is obtained by a quadrature s=∫ϑ⁡(r)​𝑑rs=\int\vartheta(r)dr. ∎

The rectifying coordinates r,sr,s are constructed as solutions of the partial differential equations 𝐯⁡(r)=0\mathbf{v}(r)=0, 𝐯⁡(s)=1\mathbf{v}(s)=1. Note that the coordinate rr is an invariant of 𝐯⁡(r)\mathbf{v}(r) and r,sr,s can be replaced by any arbitrary functions of rr and ss. For a first order equation y′=F⁡(x,y)y^{\prime}=F(x,y) admitting the symmetry generated by 𝐯=ξ(x,y)∂x+η(x,y)∂y\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,y)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,y)\partial_{y}, the determining equation is

ξ​Fx+η​Fy=(ηy−ξx)​F−ξy​F2+ηx.\xi F_{x}+\eta F_{y}=(\eta_{y}-\xi_{x})F-\xi_{y}F^{2}+\eta_{x}. (48)

This equation admits the solution η=F​ξ\eta=F\xi. But the corresponding vector fields 𝐯=ξ(x,y)(∂x+F(x,y)∂y)\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,y)(\partial_{x}+F(x,y)\partial_{y}) are everywhere tangential to solutions and do not serve our purpose for reduction because finding canonical coordinates equally require integrating the equation itself. Other than these trivial symmetries, the above determining equation can allow particular solutions for given FF leading to one-parameter symmetry groups. Transforming to canonical coordinates reduces the equation to quadrature. It is quite straightforward to see that, if η−F​ξ≠0\eta-F\xi\neq 0, the infinitesimal symmetry condition (48) can be re-expressed as

μx+(μ​F)y=0,μ⁡(x,y)=(η−F​ξ)−1,\mu_{x}+(\mu F)_{y}=0,\quad\mu(x,y)=(\eta-F\xi)^{-1},

which implies the existence of an integrating factor μ⁡(x,y)\mu(x,y) of the equation.

In practise it is more feasible to solve the inverse problem of constructing the most general first order ODEs admitting a given group as a symmetry group. The same problem for higher order equations are equally useful.

Example 4.2.

We consider the following one-parameter local group of transformation (a special form of the so-called fiber-preserving transformation in which the changes in xx are not affected by the dependent variable yy)

Φε​(x,y):x~=X⁡(x,ε),y~=Y⁡(x,ε)​y\Phi_{\varepsilon}(x,y):\quad\tilde{x}=X(x;\varepsilon),\quad\tilde{y}=Y(x;\varepsilon)y (49)

with the infinitesimal generator

𝐯=ξ(x)∂x+η(x)y∂y,\mathbf{v}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\eta(x)y\partial_{y}, (50)

and its prolongation

pr(1)𝐯=𝐯+[η′y+(η−ξ′)y′]∂y′.{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+[\eta^{\prime}y+(\eta-\xi^{\prime})y^{\prime}]\partial_{y^{\prime}}.

Solving the characteristic equations of the first order PDE pr(1)​𝐯​(I)=0{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathbf{v}(I)=0

d​xξ⁡(x)=d​yη⁡(x)​y=d​y′η′​y+(η−ξ′)​y′\frac{dx}{\xi(x)}=\frac{dy}{\eta(x)y}=\frac{dy^{\prime}}{\eta^{\prime}y+(\eta-\xi^{\prime})y^{\prime}}

we find the first order fundamental invariants

r(x,y)=ν(x)y,w(x,y,y′)=ν(x)(ξy′−ηy),ν(x)=exp{−∫xη⁡(t)ξ⁡(t)dt}.r(x,y)=\nu(x)y,\quad w(x,y,y^{\prime})=\nu(x)(\xi y^{\prime}-\eta y),\quad\nu(x)=\exp\left\{-\int^{x}\frac{\eta(t)}{\xi(t)}dt\right\}. (51)

From Theorem 3.6, the corresponding ODE can be expressed in terms of invariants in the form F⁡(r,w)=0F(r,w)=0 or w=H⁡(r)w=H(r), more precisely

y′−η⁡(x)ξ⁡(x)​y=H⁡(ν⁡(x)​y)ν⁡(x)​ξ​(x),y^{\prime}-\frac{\eta(x)}{\xi(x)}y=\frac{H(\nu(x)y)}{\nu(x)\xi(x)}, (52)

where FF and HH are arbitrary functions of their arguments. In terms of canonical coordinates it has the form, which is independent of ss (invariant under the translations s→s+εs\to s+\varepsilon),

d​rd​s=H⁡(r),w=d​rd​s,s=∫xd​tξ⁡(t).\frac{dr}{ds}=H(r),\quad w=\frac{dr}{ds},\quad s=\int^{x}\frac{dt}{\xi(t)}. (53)

This means that Eq. (53) can be integrated by quadrature (separation of variables). This equation involves interesting types of ODEs like Abel equation of the second type or Riccati equation.

For example, if we choose ξ\xi arbitrary, η=−1\eta=-1 and H⁡(τ)=A+B​τ−1+τH(\tau)=A+B\tau^{-1}+\tau, A,B≠0A,B\neq 0 we have the Abel equation

y​y′=Aξ​ν​y+Bξ​ν2yy^{\prime}=\frac{A}{\xi\nu}y+\frac{B}{\xi\nu^{2}} (54)

with the one-parameter symmetry group generated by 𝐯=ξ(x)∂x−y∂y\mathbf{v}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}-y\partial_{y}. In terms of r,sr,s, its general solution in implicit form is given by the quadrature

∫r​d​rr2+A​r+B=s+c,\int\frac{rdr}{r^{2}+Ar+B}=s+c, (55)

where cc is an integration constant. If Δ=A2−4​B<0\Delta=A^{2}-4B<0, it is useful to use

∫r​d​rr2+A​r+B=12​ln⁡(r2+A​r+B)−A2​∫d​rr2+A​r+B\int\frac{rdr}{r^{2}+Ar+B}=\frac{1}{2}\ln(r^{2}+Ar+B)-\frac{A}{2}\int\frac{dr}{r^{2}+Ar+B}

together with the formula (60) for the integral on the right side.

For the choice ξ⁡(x)=x\xi(x)=x, A=1A=1, B=−2B=-2 (Δ=9>0\Delta=9>0), Eq. (54) specializes to

y​y′=1x2​y−2x3yy^{\prime}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}y-\frac{2}{x^{3}}

(x​y+2)2​(x​y−1)=k​x3.(xy+2)^{2}(xy-1)=kx^{3}.

The choice H⁡(τ)=A​τ2+B​τ+CH(\tau)=A\tau^{2}+B\tau+C leads to a Riccati equation depending on two arbitrary functions and three parameters

y′=a⁡(x)​y2+b⁡(x)​y+c⁡(x),y^{\prime}=a(x)y^{2}+b(x)y+c(x), (56)

where

a⁡(x)=A​νξ,b⁡(x)=η+Bξ,c⁡(x)=Cν​ξ,ξ≠0.a(x)=\frac{A\nu}{\xi},\quad b(x)=\frac{\eta+B}{\xi},\quad c(x)=\frac{C}{\nu\xi},\quad\xi\neq 0. (57)

Conversely, one can show that the most general Riccati equation of the form (56) invariant under the group (49) should have the coefficients given by (57). In (57), choosing, in particular, a⁡(x)=1,b⁡(x)=0a(x)=1,b(x)=0, ξ=A+B​x\xi=A+Bx, the following normal form of (57) is obtained

y′=y2+c⁡(x),c⁡(x)=CA​ν−2=CA​(A+B​x)−2y^{\prime}=y^{2}+c(x),\quad c(x)=\frac{C}{A}\nu^{-2}=\frac{C}{A}(A+Bx)^{-2} (58)

The integral on the left side depends on the discriminant Δ=B2−4​A​C\Delta=B^{2}-4AC

{−2Δ​arctanh⁡2​A​r+BΔ,Δ>0,−22​A​r+B,Δ=0,2−Δ​arctan⁡2​A​r+B−Δ,Δ<0.\begin{cases}\frac{-2}{\sqrt{\Delta}}\arctanh\frac{2Ar+B}{\sqrt{\Delta}},&\Delta>0,\\ \frac{-2}{2Ar+B},&\Delta=0,\\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{-\Delta}}\arctan\frac{2Ar+B}{\sqrt{-\Delta}},&\Delta<0.\end{cases} (60)

The particular choice ξ=1\xi=1, η=α=const.\eta=\alpha=\text{const.} (ν=e−α​x\nu=e^{-\alpha x}) leads to the Riccati equation

by redefining the parameter BB as B−αB-\alpha.

The other choice ξ=x2\xi=x^{2}, η=x\eta=x (ν=1/x\nu=1/x) gives the Riccati equation

y′=Ax3​y2+B+xx2​y+Cxy^{\prime}=\frac{A}{x^{3}}y^{2}+\frac{B+x}{x^{2}}y+\frac{C}{x} (63)

In the case Δ<0\Delta<0, the general solution of (56) from (59) has the explicit form

y=12​A​ν​{−Δ​tan⁡[−Δ2​(s+c)]−B},y=\frac{1}{2A\nu}\left\{\sqrt{-\Delta}\tan\left[\frac{\sqrt{-\Delta}}{2}(s+c)\right]-B\right\},

in the case Δ=0\Delta=0

y=−B⁡(s+c)+22​A​ν​(s+c),s=−1x.y=-\frac{B(s+c)+2}{2A\nu(s+c)},\quad s=-\frac{1}{x}.
Remark 4.3.

Lie showed that the Lie symmetry algebra of a second order ODE can be of dimension dim𝔤=0,1,2,3,8\dim\mathfrak{g}=0,1,2,3,8. The maximum dimension is attained if and only if and only if it can be mapped by a point transformation to the canonical linear equation y′′=0y^{\prime\prime}=0, which admits a symmetry group isomorphic to the SL⁡(3,ℝ)\SL(3,\mathbb{R}) group, acting as the group of projective transformations of the Euclidean plane with coordinates (x,y)(x,y). Moreover, he classified equations with point symmetries into equivalence classes under the action of the infinite dimensional group Diff⁡(2,ℂ)\Diff(2,\mathbb{C}) of all local diffeomorphisms of a complex plane ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Remark 4.4.

There are two isomorphism classes of two-dimensional Lie algebras exist (over ℝ\mathbb{R} and over ℂ\mathbb{C}): abelian and nonabelian

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=0,[𝐯1,𝐯2]=𝐯1.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=0,\qquad[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=\mathbf{v}_{1}. (64)

Their realizations in the plane are summarized as

A2,1:𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=∂y,A2,2:𝐯1=∂y,𝐯2=x∂y,A_{2,1}:\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{y},\quad A_{2,2}:\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{y}, (65)
A2,3:𝐯1=∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+y∂y,A2,4:𝐯1=∂y,𝐯2=y∂y.A_{2,3}:\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y},\quad A_{2,4}:\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=y\partial_{y}. (66)

They can be obtained by the following argument.

Abelian case: We first assume the algebra 𝔤={𝐯1,𝐯2}\mathfrak{g}=\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\} has rank 1. We start by assuming that 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} is in some canonical form, say 𝐯1=∂y\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{y} and 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} in its generic form

𝐯2=ξ(x,y)∂x+η(x,y)∂y.\mathbf{v}_{2}=\xi(x,y)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,y)\partial_{y}.

Then from the first commutation relation of (64) we have 𝐯2=η(x)∂y.\mathbf{v}_{2}=\eta(x)\partial_{y}. The transformation preserving 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}, but changing 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} (equivalence group) is given by

x~=f⁡(x),y~=y+g⁡(x),f′≠0.\tilde{x}=f(x),\quad\tilde{y}=y+g(x),\quad f^{\prime}\neq 0. (67)

Under such a transformation, we find 𝐯~2=η(x)∂y~\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\eta(x)\partial_{\tilde{y}}. We simply choose f⁡(x)=η⁡(x)f(x)=\eta(x) and obtain the A2,2A_{2,2} algebra.

Now assume that the rank of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is 2. Then we must have

𝐯2=ξ(x)∂x+η(x)∂y,ξ(x)≠0.\mathbf{v}_{2}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\eta(x)\partial_{y},\quad\xi(x)\neq 0.

Then 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} is transformed to

𝐯~2=ξf′∂x~+(ξg′+η)∂y~.\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\xi f^{\prime}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+(\xi g^{\prime}+\eta)\partial_{\tilde{y}}.

We choose ξ​f′=1\xi f^{\prime}=1 and ξ​g′+η=0\xi g^{\prime}+\eta=0 so that we have 𝐯~2=∂x~\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\partial_{\tilde{x}}, which gives A2,1A_{2,1} (in the reverse order).

Non-abelian case: First, rank⁡𝔤=1\rank\mathfrak{g}=1 realization. In this case, from the second commutation relation we find 𝐯2=(y+η(x))∂y\mathbf{v}_{2}=(y+\eta(x))\partial_{y}. The transformation (67) takes 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} to 𝐯~2=(y~+η−g)∂y~\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=(\tilde{y}+\eta-g)\partial_{\tilde{y}}. The choice g=η⁡(x)g=\eta(x) leads to the A2,4A_{2,4} realization of the algebra.

Finally, we consider the rank⁡𝔤=2\rank\mathfrak{g}=2 realization. In this case, we find

𝐯2=ξ(x)∂x+(y+η(x))∂y,ξ(x)≠0.\mathbf{v}_{2}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}+(y+\eta(x))\partial_{y},\quad\xi(x)\neq 0.

Again, using (67) with ff and gg satisfying

ξ​f′=f,ξ​g′−g+η=0\xi f^{\prime}=f,\quad\xi g^{\prime}-g+\eta=0

we arrive at A2,3A_{2,3}.

In the terminology of Lie, for the realizations A2,2A_{2,2}, A2,4A_{2,4}, the vector fields 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} and 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} are called linearly connected, for A2,1A_{2,1}, A2,3A_{2,3}, linearly unconnected.

The corresponding canonical invariant equations are

y′′=F⁡(y′),y′′=F⁡(x)y^{\prime\prime}=F(y^{\prime}),\qquad y^{\prime\prime}=F(x) (68)

for A2,1A_{2,1}, and A2,2A_{2,2}, and

x​y′′=F⁡(y′),y′′=F⁡(x)​y′xy^{\prime\prime}=F(y^{\prime}),\qquad y^{\prime\prime}=F(x)y^{\prime} (69)

for A2,3A_{2,3}, and A2,4A_{2,4}, respectively.

Any second order ODE with a symmetry group GG of dimension ≥2\geq 2 (a nonlinear second order ODE can be invariant at most under a three-dimensional Lie group) can be integrated by two quadratures except for the rotation group SO⁡(3,ℝ)\Ort(3,\mathbb{R}) when dimG=3\dim G=3, which has no two-dimensional subgroup. In the latter case, there is a method based on first integrals to find the general solution without integration, namely by purely algebraic manipulations (see [18, 51]).

Example 4.5.

We construct the most general second order ODE invariant under the rotation group SO⁡(3,ℝ)\Ort(3,\mathbb{R}). The Lie algebra so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) acting on the surface of the unit sphere 𝕊2={(x,y):x∈[0,2π),y∈(0,π)}⊂ℝ3\mathbb{S}^{2}=\left\{(x,y):x\in[0,2\pi),y\in(0,\pi)\right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} (See Remark 4.6) is realized by the vector fields

𝐯1=∂x,\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x}, (70)
𝐯2=cosxcoty∂x+sinx∂y,\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{2}=\cos x\cot y\partial_{x}+\sin x\partial_{y},
𝐯3=−sinxcoty∂x+cosx∂y\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{3}=-\sin x\cot y\partial_{x}+\cos x\partial_{y}

with the commutation relations

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=𝐯3,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=𝐯1,[𝐯3,𝐯1]=𝐯2.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=\mathbf{v}_{3},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{3},\mathbf{v}_{1}]=\mathbf{v}_{2}. (71)

Obviously, invariant function will be of the form I⁡(y,y1,y2)I(y,y_{1},y_{2}) because of

pr(2)​𝐯1​(I)=𝐯1​(I)=0.{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{1}(I)=\mathbf{v}_{1}(I)=0.

We solve the PDE pr(2)​𝐯2​(I)=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{2}(I)=0. Splitting it with respect to the set {cos⁡x,sin⁡x}\left\{\cos x,\sin x\right\} we find

tan⁡y​Iy+y1​Iy1−(tan⁡y+2​sec⁡y​csc⁡y​y12−y2)​Iy2=0,(1+csc2⁡y)​Iy1+y1​(cot⁡y−2​cot⁡y​csc2⁡y​y12+3​csc2⁡y2)​Iy2=0.\begin{split}&\tan yI_{y}+y_{1}I_{y_{1}}-(\tan y+2\sec y\csc yy_{1}^{2}-y_{2})I_{y_{2}}=0,\;\;\\ &(1+\csc^{2}y)I_{y_{1}}+y_{1}(\cot y-2\cot y\csc^{2}yy_{1}^{2}+3\csc^{2}y_{2})I_{y_{2}}=0.\end{split} (72)

A first integral is immediately obtained as τ=(csc⁡y)​y1\tau=(\csc y)y_{1}. The second independent integral is found by integrating the linear ODE

d​y2d​y−2​(cot⁡y)​y2=−(1+2​τ2)\frac{dy_{2}}{dy}-2(\cot y)y_{2}=-(1+2\tau^{2})

as

ω=(csc2⁡y)​y2−(1+2​τ2)​cot⁡y.\omega=(\csc^{2}y)y_{2}-(1+2\tau^{2})\cot y.

Expressing the second PDE of (72) in terms of τ,ω\tau,\omega gives

(1+τ2)​Iτ+3​τ​ω​Iω=0(1+\tau^{2})I_{\tau}+3\tau\omega I_{\omega}=0

possessing the single first integral ζ=ω(1+τ2)−3/2\zeta=\omega(1+\tau^{2})^{-3/2}. The condition pr(2)​𝐯3​(ζ)=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{3}(\zeta)=0 is automatically satisfied because

pr(2)​𝐯3=pr(2)​[𝐯1,𝐯2]=[pr(2)​𝐯1,pr(2)​𝐯2].{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{3}={\rm pr}^{(2)}[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=[{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{1},{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{2}].

Finally, a single invariant equation depending on an arbitrary parameter ν\nu is found from the relation ζ⁡(y,y1,y2)=ν=constant\zeta(y,y_{1},y_{2})=\nu=\text{constant}. In terms of the spherical angle variables (azimuth and polar angles) (x,y)(x,y) it can be written in the form

y2−2​(cot⁡y)​y12−sin⁡y​cos⁡y=ν​sin2⁡y​(1+(csc2⁡y)​y12)3/2.y_{2}-2(\cot y)y_{1}^{2}-\sin y\cos y=\nu\sin^{2}y\left(1+(\csc^{2}y)y_{1}^{2}\right)^{3/2}. (73)

The special case ν=0\nu=0 is the equation of the geodesics on the unit sphere

y2−2​(cot⁡y)​y12−sin⁡y​cos⁡y=0.y_{2}-2(\cot y)y_{1}^{2}-\sin y\cos y=0. (74)

In order to solve this equation, we can use the algorithmic method of first integrals based on symmetries suggested in [18] (see [51] for an alternative integration strategy). We first need the characteristic functions of the vector fields 𝐯1,𝐯2,𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}

Q1=−y1,Q2=sinx−cosx(coty)y1,Q3=cos⁡x+sin⁡x⁡(cot⁡y)​y1.\begin{split}&Q_{1}=-y_{1},\quad Q_{2}=\sin x-\cos x(\cot y)y_{1},\ \\ &Q_{3}=\cos x+\sin x(\cot y)y_{1}.\end{split} (75)

We next compute the quantities

W12=Q1​D^x​Q2−Q2​D^x​Q1,W13=Q1​D^x​Q3−Q3​D^x​Q1,W23=Q2​D^x​Q3−Q3​D^x​Q2,\begin{split}&W_{12}=Q_{1}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{2}-Q_{2}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{1},\\ &W_{13}=Q_{1}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{3}-Q_{3}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{1},\\ &W_{23}=Q_{2}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{3}-Q_{3}\widehat{D}_{x}Q_{2},\end{split} (76)

where D^x\widehat{D}_{x} is the total derivative operator restricted to the geodesic equation y2=F⁡(y,y1)=2​(cot⁡y)​y12+sin⁡y​cos⁡yy_{2}=F(y,y_{1})=2(\cot y)y_{1}^{2}+\sin y\cos y

D^x=∂x+y1∂y+F∂y2.\widehat{D}_{x}=\partial_{x}+y_{1}\partial_{y}+F\partial_{y_{2}}.

They are explicitly given by

W12=−(cos⁡x​csc2⁡y)​y13+(sin⁡x​cot⁡y)​y12−cos⁡x​y1+sin⁡x​sin⁡y​cos⁡y,W13=(sin⁡x​csc2⁡y)​y13+(cos⁡x​cot⁡y)​y12+sin⁡x​y1+cos⁡x​sin⁡y​cos⁡y,W23=12​(1−cos⁡2​y+2​y12).\begin{split}&W_{12}=-(\cos x\csc^{2}y)y_{1}^{3}+(\sin x\cot y)y_{1}^{2}-\cos xy_{1}+\sin x\sin y\cos y,\\ &W_{13}=(\sin x\csc^{2}y)y_{1}^{3}+(\cos x\cot y)y_{1}^{2}+\sin xy_{1}+\cos x\sin y\cos y,\\ &W_{23}=\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos 2y+2y_{1}^{2}).\end{split} (77)

The two nonconstant functionally independent first integrals then arise as the ratios

W12W23=c1,W13W23=c1\frac{W_{12}}{W_{23}}=c_{1},\qquad\frac{W_{13}}{W_{23}}=c_{1} (78)

because by construction

D^x​(W12W23)=0,D^x​(W13W23)=0.\widehat{D}_{x}\left(\frac{W_{12}}{W_{23}}\right)=0,\quad\widehat{D}_{x}\left(\frac{W_{13}}{W_{23}}\right)=0.

Eqs. (78) define the solution parametrically. It is possible to eliminate the parameter y1y_{1} between them as

c1​sin⁡x+c2​cos⁡x+cot⁡y=0c_{1}\sin x+c_{2}\cos x+\cot y=0 (79)

or in terms of new parameters α,β\alpha,\beta as

cot⁡y=α​cos⁡(x+β).\cot y=\alpha\cos(x+\beta). (80)

This is the equation of great circle (intersection of the plane passing through the origin with the unit sphere).

On the other hand, if ν≠0\nu\neq 0, then the solution can only be obtained in parametric form.

We note that the geodesic equation (74) is the Euler-Lagrange equation of the (first-order) arc-length functional on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}

J⁡[y]=∫x1x2L⁡(y,y1)​𝑑xJ[y]=\int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}L(y,y_{1})dx (81)

with Lagrangian

L⁡(y,y1)=y12+sin2⁡y.L(y,y_{1})=\sqrt{y_{1}^{2}+\sin^{2}y}.

It is easy to verify that the vector fields defined by (70) are also variational symmetries of the functional (81). This is indeed the case because infinitesimal invariance condition

pr(1)𝐯i(L)+Dx(ξi)L=0,i=1,2,3{\rm pr}^{(1)}\mathbf{v}_{i}(L)+{D}_{x}(\xi_{i})L=0,\quad i=1,2,3 (82)

is satisfied for each vector field 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} with ξi\xi_{i} being the xx-coefficients of the vector fields. The Noether theorem then can be used to find three first integrals ℐ1,ℐ2,ℐ3\mathscr{I}_{1},\mathscr{I}_{2},\mathscr{I}_{3} as

ℐi=ξi​L+Qi​∂L∂y1=ci.\mathscr{I}_{i}=\xi_{i}L+Q_{i}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_{1}}=c_{i}.

For an excellent discussion of this theorem with interesting applications the reader can consult the book [35]. A simple computation gives the first integrals

Remark 4.6.

The algebra spanned by (70) is the two dimensional rank-two realization of so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) that can be obtained by the following procedure. We may start with the locally smooth canonical form 𝐯1=∂x\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x}. Then with 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2}, 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} in the generic form

the commutation relations (71) give

ax=A,bx=B,a=−Ax,b=−Bxa_{x}=A,\quad b_{x}=B,\quad a=-A_{x},\quad b=-B_{x}

with solutions

A=−α⁡(y)​sin⁡(x+δ⁡(y)),B=β⁡(y)​cos⁡(x+λ⁡(y)).A=-\alpha(y)\sin(x+\delta(y)),\quad B=\beta(y)\cos(x+\lambda(y)).

We must have a,b,A,B≠0a,b,A,B\neq 0 for a rank-two realization because all wedge products (bivectors) 𝐯1∧𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{1}\wedge\mathbf{v}_{2}, 𝐯1∧𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{1}\wedge\mathbf{v}_{3}, 𝐯2∧𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{2}\wedge\mathbf{v}_{3} must be nonzero. Now the invertible transformation preserving the canonical form 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} is x~=x+X⁡(y)\tilde{x}=x+X(y), y~=Y⁡(y)\tilde{y}=Y(y), Y′≠0Y^{\prime}\neq 0 and maps 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} to

𝐯~2=[αcos(x~−X+δ)+βX′sin(x~−X+λ)]∂x~+βY′sin(x~−X+λ)∂y~.\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=[\alpha\cos(\tilde{x}-X+\delta)+\beta X^{\prime}\sin(\tilde{x}-X+\lambda)]\partial_{\tilde{x}}+\beta Y^{\prime}\sin(\tilde{x}-X+\lambda)\partial_{\tilde{y}}.

γ⁡(sin⁡σ)=0,−(1+γ2)−γ′​(cos⁡σ)+γ′​σ′​(sin⁡σ)=0.\gamma(\sin\sigma)=0,\quad-(1+\gamma^{2})-\gamma^{\prime}(\cos\sigma)+\gamma^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}(\sin\sigma)=0.

For cos⁡σ=1\cos\sigma=1, γ′=−(1+γ2)\gamma^{\prime}=-(1+\gamma^{2}) with solution γ=cot⁡(y+χ)\gamma=\cot(y+\chi) and cos⁡(x+σ⁡(y))=cos⁡x\cos(x+\sigma(y))=\cos x. The translation y~=y+χ\tilde{y}=y+\chi removes χ\chi in γ\gamma and consequently we find

We observe that the vector fields 𝐯1,𝐯2,𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3} are invariant under the transformation x~=x+2​n​π\tilde{x}=x+2n\pi, y~=y+n​π\tilde{y}=y+n\pi, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z} so we can restrict the coordinates (x,y)(x,y) onto the unit sphere.

As a result, we can state that any second order ordinary differential equation admitting a rank-two realization of so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) algebra is equivalent to (73) by point transformations.

We comment that there is no rank-one realization of so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) on the (x,y)(x,y)-space. If it were true, then there would exist real smooth functions f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) and g⁡(x,y)g(x,y) such that 𝐯1=𝐰\mathbf{v}_{1}=\mathbf{w}, 𝐯2=f​𝐰\mathbf{v}_{2}=f\mathbf{w}, 𝐯3=g​𝐰\mathbf{v}_{3}=g\mathbf{w}, where 𝐰\mathbf{w} is a smooth vector field. From the commutation relations we find that ff and gg must satisfy

f=−𝐰⁡(g),g=𝐰⁡(f),f​𝐰​(g)−g​𝐰​(f)=1.f=-\mathbf{w}(g),\quad g=\mathbf{w}(f),\quad f\mathbf{w}(g)-g\mathbf{w}(f)=1.

They imply the relation f2+g2+1=0f^{2}+g^{2}+1=0, which has no solution for real functions f,gf,g.

The following Theorem will be useful when performing reductions.

Theorem 4.8 ([36]).

Suppose 𝖤⁡(x,y(n))=0\mathsf{E}(x,y^{(n)})=0 is an nn-th order ODE with a symmetry group GG. Let HH be a one-parameter subgroup of GG. Then the ODE reduced by HH, 𝖤/H\mathsf{E}/H, admits the quotient group NorG⁡(H)/H\Nor_{G}(H)/H, where NorG(H)={g∈G:g.H.g−1⊂H}\Nor_{G}(H)=\left\{g\in G:g.H.g^{-1}\subset H\right\} is the normalizer subgroup of HH in GG, as a symmetry group (often called inherited symmetry group of 𝖤/H\mathsf{E}/H).

The normalizer algebra in 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of the subalgebra 𝔥⊂𝔤\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathfrak{g} is the maximal subalgebra satisfying

nor𝔤⁡𝔥={𝐯∈𝔤:[𝐯,𝔥]⊂𝔥}.\nor_{\mathfrak{g}}\mathfrak{h}=\left\{\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g}:[\mathbf{v},\mathfrak{h}]\subset\mathfrak{h}\right\}. (90)
Remark 4.9.

The normalizer of a subalgebra 𝔥⊂𝔤\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathfrak{g} in the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of dim𝔤=r\dim\mathfrak{g}=r with a basis {𝐯1,…,𝐯r}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r}\right\} is easily obtained by solving a linear algebra problem. Let the subalgebra 𝔥\mathfrak{h} of dim𝔥=k\dim\mathfrak{h}=k be spanned by {𝐯1,…​𝐯k}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots\mathbf{v}_{k}\right\}. Now for 𝐯=∑j=1raj​𝐯j\mathbf{v}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}, aj∈ℝa_{j}\in\mathbb{R} and 𝐯α∈𝔥\mathbf{v}_{\alpha}\in\mathfrak{h}, 1≤α≤k1\leq\alpha\leq k, we impose the requirement (90)

[𝐯,𝐯α]=[∑j=1raj​𝐯j,𝐯α]=∑j=1r[𝐯j,𝐯α]​aj[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}_{\alpha}]=[\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j},\mathbf{v}_{\alpha}]=\sum_{j=1}^{r}[\mathbf{v}_{j},\mathbf{v}_{\alpha}]a_{j}
=∑i=1r∑j=1rCj​αi​aj​𝐯i=∑i=1kλα,i​𝐯i=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sum_{j=1}^{r}C_{j\alpha}^{i}a_{j}\mathbf{v}_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{\alpha,i}\mathbf{v}_{i}

for some constants λα,i\lambda_{\alpha,i}. Here Cj​αiC_{j\alpha}^{i} are the structure constants of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. This implies that the following set of linear algebraic equations need to be solved for the coefficients aja_{j}, 1≤j≤r1\leq j\leq r

∑j=1rCj​αiaj=λα,i,i=1,…,k,α=1,…,k,\sum_{j=1}^{r}C_{j\alpha}^{i}a_{j}=\lambda_{\alpha,i},\quad i=1,\ldots,k,\quad\alpha=1,\ldots,k,
∑j=1rCj​αiaj=0,i=k+1,…,r.\sum_{j=1}^{r}C_{j\alpha}^{i}a_{j}=0,\quad i=k+1,\ldots,r.
Remark 4.10.

If 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is already an ideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, then nor𝔤⁡𝔥=𝔤\nor_{\mathfrak{g}}\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{g}. If nor𝔤⁡𝔥=𝔥\nor_{\mathfrak{g}}\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{h}, then 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is called self-normalizing.

Theorem 4.8 infinitesimally states that if the Lie symmetry algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of G has a basis 𝐯1,…,𝐯r\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r}. Then the ODE reduced by 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} can be reduced one more if 𝐯^2=span⁡{𝐯2,…,𝐯r}\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{2}=\Span\left\{\mathbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r}\right\} is chosen to satisfy [𝐯^2,𝐯1]=k​𝐯1[\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{1}]=k\mathbf{v}_{1} for some real constant kk, meaning that 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} is an ideal (normal subalgebra) of 𝐯^2\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{2}. One can reiterate this process to achieve a full reduction.

Theorem 4.8 applied to a two-parameter symmetry group with the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} being one of the isomorphy classes of Remark 4.3 and satisfying the commutation relation [𝐯1,𝐯2]=k​𝐯1[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=k\mathbf{v}_{1} ensures that given a second order ODE invariant under 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, reducing its order by one by the ideal (normal subalgebra) 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} in 𝔤\mathfrak{g} will lead to a first order ODE inheriting the one-parameter subgroup generated by 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} as a symmetry group. Note that the normalizer of {𝐯1}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\right\} is {𝐯1,𝐯2}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\} and 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} belongs to nor𝔤⁡𝔥/𝔥\nor_{\mathfrak{g}}\mathfrak{h}/\mathfrak{h}. This reduction procedure makes possible the integration of the ODE by two successive quadratures.

If the reduction is performed in the reverse order, the reduced ODE will in general not inherit the symmetry of the original equation, so we may not be able to complete the full integration.
