Eq. (97) is invariant under the two-dimensional symmetry algebra

𝐯1=x2∂x+xy∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+3y∂y.\mathbf{v}_{1}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xy\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+3y\partial_{y}. (98)

We can integrate (97) using differential invariants I=y/xI=y/x and J=x​y′−yJ=xy^{\prime}-y of 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}. The reduced first order equation is obtained by invariant differentiation

d​Jd​I=x3​y′′x​y′−y=K​x−2​y2x​y′−y=K​I2J,\frac{dJ}{dI}=\frac{x^{3}y^{\prime\prime}}{xy^{\prime}-y}=K\frac{x^{-2}y^{2}}{xy^{\prime}-y}=K\frac{I^{2}}{J}, (99)

whose integration gives

J2−2​K3​I3=c1J^{2}-\frac{2K}{3}I^{3}=c_{1}

or

(x​y′−y)2−2​K3​x−3​y3=c1.(xy^{\prime}-y)^{2}-\frac{2K}{3}x^{-3}y^{3}=c_{1}. (100)

Note that this equation is invariant under the scaling group (x,y)→(λ​x,λ3​y)(x,y)\to(\lambda x,\lambda^{3}y), λ>0\lambda>0 corresponding to 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2}. In terms of the normal coordinates r=y/xr=y/x, s=−1/xs=-1/x of 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} it has the form

r′​(s)2=2​K3​r3+c1.r^{\prime}(s)^{2}=\frac{2K}{3}r^{3}+c_{1}.

For c1≠0c_{1}\neq 0, the general solution can be expressed in terms of elliptic functions. It is elementary, when c1=0c_{1}=0, which is given by r=(1/(6)​s+c2)−2r=(1/(\sqrt{6})s+c_{2})^{-2} and in terms of (x,y)(x,y) variables

y⁡(x)=6​x3(K+6​c2​x)2.y(x)=\frac{6x^{3}}{(\sqrt{K}+\sqrt{6}c_{2}x)^{2}}. (101)

Moreover, the particular case n=−3n=-3 of (96) gives the celebrated Ermakov–Pinney equation

y′′=K​y−3y^{\prime\prime}=Ky^{-3} (102)

with solution

y=±A+2​B​x+C​x2,A​C−B2=K.y=\pm\sqrt{A+2Bx+Cx^{2}},\quad AC-B^{2}=K.

This equation admits the sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) algebra as the symmetry algebra with the basis

𝐰1=∂x,𝐰2=x∂x+12y∂y,𝐰3=x2∂x+xy∂y\mathbf{w}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{w}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{2}y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{w}_{3}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xy\partial_{y} (103)

satisfying the commutation relations

[𝐰1,𝐰2]=𝐰1,[𝐰1,𝐰3]=2​𝐰2,[𝐰2,𝐰3]=𝐰3.[\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{2}]=\mathbf{w}_{1},\quad[\mathbf{w}_{1},\mathbf{w}_{3}]=2\mathbf{w}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{w}_{2},\mathbf{w}_{3}]=\mathbf{w}_{3}. (104)

Just as in the previous case, the choice ξ=x2−k\xi=x^{2-k}, η=(1−k)​x1−k\eta=(1-k)x^{1-k} in 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} of (92), combined with the scaling group generated by

𝐯2=x∂x+δ+21−my∂y,m≠1\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+\frac{\delta+2}{1-m}y\partial_{y},\quad m\neq 1

can be shown to produce the following integrable variant of the generalized Lane–Emden–Fowler equation

y′′+kxy′=Kxδym,m≠0,1,K≠0,y^{\prime\prime}+\frac{k}{x}y^{\prime}=Kx^{\delta}y^{m},\quad m\neq 0,1,\quad K\neq 0, (105)

if the condition 3+δ+m−k⁡(m+1)=03+\delta+m-k(m+1)=0 is satisfied.

The case when δ=0\delta=0 (m=(k−3)/(1−k)m=(k-3)/(1-k)) appeared in [12] as one of the reductions of a radially symmetric nonlinear porous-medium equation. A suitable basis of the algebra in the case k≠1,2k\neq 1,2 is

𝐯~1=(1−k)𝐯1,𝐯~2=(1−k)−2𝐯2=1k−1x∂x+1k−2y∂y,\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=(1-k)\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=(1-k)^{-2}\mathbf{v}_{2}=\frac{1}{k-1}x\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{k-2}y\partial_{y},

with the commutation relation [𝐯~1,𝐯~2]=𝐯~1[\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}]=\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1} (type A2,3A_{2,3}). In terms of the canonical (or normal) coordinates

r=xk−2​y(k−2)/(k−1)k−1,s=xk−1k−1,r=\frac{x^{k-2}y^{(k-2)/(k-1)}}{k-1},\quad s=\frac{x^{k-1}}{k-1},

we find the standard form of the corresponding equation

r​s′′​(r)=−K⁡(k−2)​s′​(r)3+(k−1)3​s′​(r),rs^{\prime\prime}(r)=-K(k-2)s^{\prime}(r)^{3}+(k-1)^{3}s^{\prime}(r),

being invariant under the algebra {∂s,r∂r+s∂s}\left\{\partial_{s},r\partial_{r}+s\partial_{s}\right\}. On solving by two quadratures, implicit solution of the original equation is obtained.

Another particular case where m=−3m=-3 and δ=−2​k\delta=-2k leads to an sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant equation. Symmetry vector fields for k≠1k\neq 1 are

𝐯1=x2−k∂x+(1−k)x1−ky∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+1−k2y∂y,𝐯3=xk∂x,\mathbf{v}_{1}=x^{2-k}\partial_{x}+(1-k)x^{1-k}y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+\frac{1-k}{2}y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=x^{k}\partial_{x},

with the commutation relations

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=(k−1)​𝐯2,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=(k−1)​𝐯3,[𝐯1,𝐯3]=2​(k−1)​𝐯2.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=(k-1)\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=(k-1)\mathbf{v}_{3},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=2(k-1)\mathbf{v}_{2}.

If k=1k=1, they are given by

𝐯1=2xlnx∂x+y∂y,𝐯2=x(lnx)2∂x+ylnx∂y,𝐯3=x∂x\mathbf{v}_{1}=2x\ln x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x(\ln x)^{2}\partial_{x}+y\ln x\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=x\partial_{x}

and satisfy the commutation relations

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=2​𝐯2,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=−𝐯1,[𝐯1,𝐯3]=−2​𝐯3.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=2\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=-\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=-2\mathbf{v}_{3}.

This particular equation reduces to the standard Ermakov–Pinney equation y′′​(t)=K​y−3​(t)y^{\prime\prime}(t)=Ky^{-3}(t) by change of the independent variable, t=x1−k/(1−k)t=x^{1-k}/(1-k), k≠1k\neq 1, and t=ln⁡xt=\ln x for k=1k=1.

We can extract a similar integrable class from (92) by imposing invariance under a two-parameter symmetry group extended by 𝐯2=∂x\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x}. To do this we require that the commutation relation [𝐯2,𝐯1]=μ​𝐯1[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{1}]=\mu\mathbf{v}_{1}, μ≠0\mu\neq 0 be satisfied, which implies that ξ=eμ​x\xi=e^{\mu x}, η=α​eμ​x\eta=\alpha e^{\mu x} for some constant α\alpha and that Eq. (92) is autonomous. For this choice of ξ\xi, η\eta the left hand side of (92) is already independent of xx. We also require the right hand side to have the same property. This produces the PDE

y′′+py′+qy=ymG(ω),ω=y−(m+1)/2(y′−αy),μ=α⁡(1−m)2.y^{\prime\prime}+py^{\prime}+qy=y^{m}G(\omega),\quad\omega=y^{-(m+1)/2}(y^{\prime}-\alpha y),\quad\mu=\frac{\alpha(1-m)}{2}. (106)

The condition (93) is identically satisfied. The special choice G=K=constantG=K=\mbox{constant} and m≠1m\neq 1 (μ≠0\mu\neq 0) gives us the integrable equation (a type of Emden–Fowler equation known as force-free generalized Duffing oscillator)

y′′+p​y′+q​y=K​ym,p=−α⁡(m+3)2,q=α2​(m+1)2y^{\prime\prime}+py^{\prime}+qy=Ky^{m},\quad p=-\frac{\alpha(m+3)}{2},\quad q=\frac{\alpha^{2}(m+1)}{2} (107)

with symmetry algebra generated by

𝐯1=eμ​x(∂x+αy∂y),𝐯2=∂x,α=2​μ1−m.\mathbf{v}_{1}=e^{\mu x}(\partial_{x}+\alpha y\partial_{y}),\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\alpha=\frac{2\mu}{1-m}. (108)

If α\alpha is eliminated between the coefficients pp and qq we find the integrability condition

q=2​(m+1)(m+3)2​p2,m≠−3.q=\frac{2(m+1)}{(m+3)^{2}}p^{2},\quad m\neq-3. (109)

Under this condition, (107) passes the Painlevé test.

In terms of the canonical coordinates of 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}

x~=μ−1​e−μ​x,y~=y​e−α​x,μ=m−1m+3​p,α=−2​pm+3,\tilde{x}=\mu^{-1}e^{-\mu x},\qquad\tilde{y}=ye^{-\alpha x},\quad\mu=\frac{m-1}{m+3}p,\quad\alpha=-\frac{2p}{m+3},

Eq. (107) is reduced to d2​y~/d​x~2=K​y~md^{2}\tilde{y}/d\tilde{x}^{2}=K\tilde{y}^{m}, which is invariant under the symmetry group generated by

𝐯~1=∂x~,𝐯~2=x~∂x~+21−my~∂y~,\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=\partial_{\tilde{x}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=\tilde{x}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+\frac{2}{1-m}\tilde{y}\partial_{\tilde{y}},

and can be integrated by two quadratures.

The travelling wave solutions of Fisher’s (also called Kolmogorov– Petrovsky–Piscunov) equation satisfy the ODE [1]

y′′+c​y′+y⁡(1−y)=0.y^{\prime\prime}+cy^{\prime}+y(1-y)=0. (110)

If we identify (110) with (107) we find p=cp=c, q=1q=1 and m=2m=2, K=1K=1 and the integrability condition imposes a constraint c=±5/6c=\pm 5/\sqrt{6} on the wave speed. The corresponding solution is given in terms of Weierstrass function by y~=℘⁡(1/6​(x~+a),0,g3)\tilde{y}=\wp(1/\sqrt{6}(\tilde{x}+a);0,g_{3}) (see page 199).

The same type of solutions for the Newell–Whitehead–Segel equation satisfy

y′′+c​y′+y⁡(1−y2)=0.y^{\prime\prime}+cy^{\prime}+y(1-y^{2})=0. (111)

The integrability condition (109) for p=cp=c, q=1q=1 and m=3m=3 then requires c=±3/2c=\pm 3/\sqrt{2}. Solutions are found in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions.

Surprisingly, the special case m=3m=3 of (107) turns up in seeking localized stationary solutions of the form u⁡(x,t)=e−i​λ​t​u​(x)u(x,t)=e^{-i\lambda t}u(x) of the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation with inhomogeneous nonlinearity

i​ut+ux​x=V⁡(x)​u+g⁡(x)​|u|2​u,x∈ℝ,iu_{t}+u_{xx}=V(x)u+g(x)|u|^{2}u,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},

where V⁡(x)V(x) is an external potential and g⁡(x)g(x) describes the spatial modulation of the nonlinearity (see for example [3]). For some special choice of pairs (V,g)(V,g), dictated by the presence of a Lie point symmetry, u⁡(x)u(x) satisfies

u′′+2​C​u′+E​u=g0​u3.u^{\prime\prime}+2Cu^{\prime}+Eu=g_{0}u^{3}.

This equation is integrable if E=(8/9)​C2E=(8/9)C^{2}.

In Eqs. (110) and (111), there is no loss of generality in assuming c>0c>0, because using discrete transformation x→−xx\to-x, we can put c→−cc\to-c.

The case m=3m=3 (μ=−α≠0\mu=-\alpha\neq 0 arbitrary) of (107) is also known as the usual Duffing oscillator and under the condition q=(2/9)​p2q=(2/9)p^{2} its exact solutions can be found in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions from integrating the first integral (energy)

I=12​y~′2−K4​y~4=14​e−4​α​x​[2​y′2−4​α​y​y′+2​α2​y2−K​y4].I=\frac{1}{2}\tilde{y}^{\prime 2}-\frac{K}{4}\tilde{y}^{4}=\frac{1}{4}e^{-4\alpha x}\left[2y^{\prime 2}-4\alpha yy^{\prime}+2\alpha^{2}y^{2}-Ky^{4}\right].

On the other hand, the case m=−3m=-3 (p=0p=0, q=−α2q=-\alpha^{2}, μ=2​α\mu=2\alpha) is recognized to be the celebrated Ermakov–Pinney equation

y′′−α2​y=K​y−3,α≠0.y^{\prime\prime}-\alpha^{2}y=Ky^{-3},\quad\alpha\neq 0. (112)

Its symmetry algebra (108) is extended by one additional element

𝐯3=e−2​α​x(∂x−αy∂y),\mathbf{v}_{3}=e^{-2\alpha x}(\partial_{x}-\alpha y\partial_{y}),

or in coordinates (x~,y~)(\tilde{x},\tilde{y}) (up to multiple of −4​α2-4\alpha^{2}) by the projective element

𝐯~3=x~2∂x~+x~y~∂y~.\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\tilde{x}^{2}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+\tilde{x}\tilde{y}\partial_{\tilde{y}}.

It is isomorphic to the sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) algebra. The general solution depending on two independent arbitrary constants is given by

y2=A​e2​α​x+2​B+C​e−2​α​x,(A​C−B2)​α2=K.y^{2}=Ae^{2\alpha x}+2B+Ce^{-2\alpha x},\quad(AC-B^{2})\alpha^{2}=K. (113)
Remark 4.12.

We comment that as we mentioned above, differential equations may remain invariant under discrete symmetry groups. For example, the special Ermakov equation y2=K​y−3y_{2}=Ky^{-3} is invariant under the discrete transformation

x~=1x,y~=yx\tilde{x}=\frac{1}{x},\quad\tilde{y}=\frac{y}{x}

since

y~2=d2​y~d​x~2=x3​y2=K​x3​y−3=K​y~−3.\tilde{y}_{2}=\frac{d^{2}\tilde{y}}{d\tilde{x}^{2}}=x^{3}y_{2}=Kx^{3}y^{-3}=K\tilde{y}^{-3}.

More trivial ones are

(x,y)↦(−x,y),(x,y)↦(x,−y),(x,y)↦(−x,−y).(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y).

This type of symmetries can’t be obtained from the local Lie symmetry algebra so they can’t be characterized as a one-parameter group transformation.

In order to obtain another interesting subclass integrable by quadratures, we now let Eq. (92) be invariant under the scaling transformation generated by 𝐯2=y∂y\mathbf{v}_{2}=y\partial_{y}, or equivalently choosing H⁡(r,w)=r​G​(w/r)H(r,w)=rG(w/r). With further specialization G⁡(z)=A​z+BG(z)=Az+B, where A,BA,B are arbitrary constants, we obtain the variable coefficient linear invariant equation

y′′+p^​(x)​y′+q^​(x)​y=0,y^{\prime\prime}+\hat{p}(x)y^{\prime}+\hat{q}(x)y=0, (114)
p^​(x)=ξ−1​(ξ′−2​η−A),q^​(x)=ξ−2​(η2−ξ​η′+A​η−B).\hat{p}(x)=\xi^{-1}(\xi^{\prime}-2\eta-A),\quad\hat{q}(x)=\xi^{-2}(\eta^{2}-\xi\eta^{\prime}+A\eta-B). (115)

Eliminating η\eta results in the relation

(2​ξ​ξ′′−ξ′2)+4​ξ2​I​(x)=−(A2+4​B)≡−D2,(2\xi\xi^{\prime\prime}-\xi^{\prime 2})+4\xi^{2}I(x)=-(A^{2}+4B)\equiv-D^{2}, (116)

where I⁡(x)I(x) is the (semi)-invariant of (114), namely

I⁡(x)=q^​(x)−12​p^′​(x)−14​p^​(x)2.I(x)=\hat{q}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\hat{p}^{\prime}(x)-\frac{1}{4}\hat{p}(x)^{2}. (117)

Eq. (116) is related to the Ermakov–Pinney equation

χ′′+I⁡(x)​χ=−D24​χ−3\chi^{\prime\prime}+I(x)\chi=-\frac{D^{2}}{4}\chi^{-3} (118)

by the transformation ξ=χ2\xi=\chi^{2} and to the linear equation

ξ′′′+4​I​ξ′+2​I′​ξ=0\xi^{\prime\prime\prime}+4I\xi^{\prime}+2I^{\prime}\xi=0 (119)

by differentiation. The remarkable properties of (119) can be found in [5].

Eq. (114) admits a symmetry group isomorphic to the SL⁡(3,ℝ)\SL(3,\mathbb{R}) group (the projective group of the plane (x,y)(x,y), preserving straight lines in the (x,y)(x,y)-plane) as the symmetry group and can be integrated by quadratures using the two-parameter abelian subgroup generated by {𝐯1,𝐯2}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\}. Passing to the canonical coordinates rr and ss (as defined in Example 4.2) reduces (114) to the constant coefficient linear equation

r′′​(s)−A​r′​(s)−B​r​(s)=0,r^{\prime\prime}(s)-Ar^{\prime}(s)-Br(s)=0, (120)

preserving the homogeneity property in rr (invariance under the scaling r∂rr\partial_{r}).

In the special case of the inversional group (ξ=x2\xi=x^{2}, η=x\eta=x), the corresponding invariant ODE becomes

y′′−Ax2​y′+A​x−Bx4​y=0.y^{\prime\prime}-\frac{A}{x^{2}}y^{\prime}+\frac{Ax-B}{x^{4}}y=0. (121)

Its normal form is easy to obtain from the relation (116) as

v′′+I⁡(x)​v=0,I⁡(x)=−D24​x4,y=exp⁡{−A2​x}​v.v^{\prime\prime}+I(x)v=0,\quad I(x)=-\frac{D^{2}}{4x^{4}},\quad y=\exp\left\{-\frac{A}{2x}\right\}v. (122)

Then, we have r=y/xr=y/x, s=−1/xs=-1/x, and we can easily solve (120) to find the general solution of (121)

y⁡(x)=x⁡[c1​exp⁡(−λ+x)+c2​exp⁡(−λ−x)],y(x)=x\left[c_{1}\exp\left(-\frac{\lambda_{+}}{x}\right)+c_{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\lambda_{-}}{x}\right)\right], (123)

where λ±=(A±D)/2\lambda_{\pm}=(A\pm D)/2, D2=A2+4​B>0D^{2}=A^{2}+4B>0 are the real roots of the characteristic equation P⁡(λ)=λ2−A​λ−B=0P(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-A\lambda-B=0. If the discriminant D2D^{2} is zero or negative, the solution should be modified appropriately.

Alternatively, we can use the differential invariant approach. By means of the differential invariant z=y′/y=v′/vz=y^{\prime}/y=v^{\prime}/v of 𝐯2(1)=y∂y+y′∂y′\mathbf{v}_{2}^{(1)}=y\partial_{y}+y^{\prime}\partial_{y^{\prime}} we can express (122) as a Riccati equation

d​zd​x+z2=D24​x4,\frac{dz}{dx}+z^{2}=\frac{D^{2}}{4x^{4}}, (124)

which inherits the symmetry 𝐯~1=x2∂x+(1−2xz)∂z\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+(1-2xz)\partial_{z}. Using the canonical coordinates ρ=x⁡(x​z−1)\rho=x(xz-1), s=−1/xs=-1/x satisfying 𝐯~1​(ρ)=0\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}(\rho)=0, 𝐯~1​(s)=1\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}(s)=1, it can be written as a separable equation, invariant under the group of translations (ρ,s)→(ρ,s+ε)(\rho,s)\to(\rho,s+\varepsilon),

d​ρd​s=D24−ρ2\frac{d\rho}{ds}=\frac{D^{2}}{4}-\rho^{2}

with solution

ρ⁡(s)={D2​tanh⁡[D2​(s+c0)],D2>0,D2​cot⁡[D2​(s+c0)],D2<0,(s+c0)−1,D2=0.\rho(s)=\begin{cases}\frac{D}{2}\tanh[\frac{D}{2}(s+c_{0})],&D^{2}>0,\\ \frac{D}{2}\cot[\frac{D}{2}(s+c_{0})],&D^{2}<0,\\ (s+c_{0})^{-1},&D^{2}=0.\end{cases} (125)

Finally, from the relation

z=y′y=1x+ρx2z=\frac{y^{\prime}}{y}=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{\rho}{x^{2}}

by another integration we recover the general solution of (121), and in particular solution (123) after some manipulation with the arbitrary constants. For the special case A=0A=0, B=−1B=-1 and D2=−4D^{2}=-4, the solution of (124) is given by

z=x−2​[x−cot⁡(1x+c0)].z=x^{-2}\left[x-\cot\left(\frac{1}{x}+c_{0}\right)\right].

Consequently, we obtain the solution of

y′′+x−4​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+x^{-4}y=0

as

y=c1​x​sin⁡(1x+c0).y=c_{1}x\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}+c_{0}\right).

The following equation arises in the integrability analysis of the variable coefficient Basener–Ross model [13]

y′′​(x)+I⁡(x)​y=0,I⁡(x)=−e2​x+4​τ​ex+τ24​(τ+2​ex)2,y^{\prime\prime}(x)+I(x)y=0,\quad I(x)=-\frac{e^{2x}+4\tau e^{x}+\tau^{2}}{4(\tau+2e^{x})^{2}}, (126)

where τ\tau is a constant. The relation (116) for the choice A=1A=1, B=−3/16B=-3/16 (D2=A2+4​B=1/4D^{2}=A^{2}+4B=1/4) and

ξ=12​(2+τ​e−x)\xi=\frac{1}{2}(2+\tau e^{-x})

gives precisely I⁡(x)I(x) as above. One can check that

𝐯1=ξ(x)(∂x−12y∂y)\mathbf{v}_{1}=\xi(x)\left(\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{2}y\partial_{y}\right)

generates one-parameter symmetry group of (126). So we have η(x)=−ξ(x)/2\eta(x)=-\xi(x)/2, ν⁡(x)=ex/2\nu(x)=e^{x/2}, s⁡(x)=ln⁡(τ+2​ex)s(x)=\ln(\tau+2e^{x}), and r⁡(x)=ν⁡(x)​yr(x)=\nu(x)y. In canonical coordinates (s,r)(s,r), rr satisfies the constant coefficient equation (ODE (120))

r′′​(s)−r′​(s)+316​r​(s)=0.r^{\prime\prime}(s)-r^{\prime}(s)+\frac{3}{16}r(s)=0.

Solving this equation and changing to (x,y)(x,y) coordinates we obtain the general solution

y(x)=e−x/2[c1(τ+2ex)1/4+c2(τ+2ex)3/4].y(x)=e^{-x/2}\left[c_{1}(\tau+2e^{x})^{1/4}+c_{2}(\tau+2e^{x})^{3/4}\right].

In general, given ξ⁡(x)\xi(x), A,BA,B, one can solve (116) for I⁡(x)I(x) and thus construct an invariant equation of the form (114) with symmetry 𝐯=ξ∂x+ηy∂y\mathbf{v}=\xi\partial_{x}+\eta y\partial_{y}. The coefficient η⁡(x)\eta(x) is found from solving p^​(x)=0\hat{p}(x)=0 as η⁡(x)=(ξ′−A)/2\eta(x)=(\xi^{\prime}-A)/2. If η⁡(x)\eta(x) is substituted into q^​(x)\hat{q}(x) of (115) it follows that q^=I⁡(x)\hat{q}=I(x) as expected. We conclude that

y′′+I⁡(x)​y=0,I⁡(x)=−14​ξ2​(2​ξ​ξ′′−ξ′2+A2+4​B)y^{\prime\prime}+I(x)y=0,\quad I(x)=-\frac{1}{4\xi^{2}}(2\xi\xi^{\prime\prime}-\xi^{\prime 2}+A^{2}+4B) (127)

is invariant under

𝐯=ξ(x)∂x+12(ξ′(x)−A)y∂y.\mathbf{v}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(\xi^{\prime}(x)-A)y\partial_{y}.

Solution is readily obtained by transforming this equation into the constant coefficient equation (120) by the linear transformation

y⁡(x)=ξ​exp⁡[−(A/2)​s]​r​(s),s=∫d​xξ⁡(x).y(x)=\sqrt{\xi}\exp[-(A/2)s]r(s),\quad s=\int\frac{dx}{\xi(x)}.

For an equation of the form (114) with p^≠0\hat{p}\neq 0, ξ,A,B\xi,A,B given we take η=(ξ′−p^​ξ−A)/2\eta=(\xi^{\prime}-\hat{p}\xi-A)/2 and y(x)=ξexp[−(∫p^dx+As)/2)]r(s)y(x)=\sqrt{\xi}\exp[-(\int\hat{p}dx+As)/2)]r(s).

The knowledge of invariance of an nn-th order ODE under an rr-parameter symmetry group can be useful in reducing in order more than once. But the full reduction to an equation of order n−rn-r can only be guaranteed if the symmetry group is solvable.

A Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is solvable if the derived series defined recursively by the chain of subalgebras

𝔤=𝔤(0)⊇𝔤(1)​…⊇𝔤(k)⊇…,𝔤(k)=[𝔤(k−1),𝔤(k−1)]\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}^{(0)}\supseteq\mathfrak{g}^{(1)}\ldots\supseteq\mathfrak{g}^{(k)}\supseteq\ldots,\quad\mathfrak{g}^{(k)}=[\mathfrak{g}^{(k-1)},\mathfrak{g}^{(k-1)}] (128)

terminates, namely there exists k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that 𝔤(k)=0\mathfrak{g}^{(k)}=0. The algebra of commutators D​𝔤=𝔤(1)=[𝔤,𝔤]D\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}^{(1)}=[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}] is called the derived algebra. For the solvable algebra Dk​𝔤={0}D^{k}\mathfrak{g}=\left\{0\right\} holds.

Theorem 4.13 ([35]).

Let 𝖤⁡(x,y(n))=0\mathsf{E}(x,y^{(n)})=0 be an nn-th order ODE. If 𝖤⁡(x,y(n))=0\mathsf{E}(x,y^{(n)})=0 admits a solvable rr-parameter group of symmetries GG such that , then the general solution of the equation can be found by quadratures from the general solution of an (n−r)(n-r)-th order reduced ODE 𝖤/G\mathsf{E}/G. In particular, if the ODE admits a solvable nn-parameter group of symmetries, then the general solutions can be found by quadratures alone.

A solvable three-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} always contains a two-dimensional abelian ideal, which is unique up to conjugacy under inner automorphisms unless 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is abelian or nilpotent. An integration strategy for an ODE with a three-parameter solvable symmetry group is to first reduce the equation by this two-dimensional ideal and then to use the remaining symmetry to complete the integration by quadratures.

Example 4.14.

We turn to Eq. (44). As this equation admits a three-dimensional solvable algebra 𝔤=e⁡(2)\mathfrak{g}=\e(2) as the symmetry algebra we can integrate it by three consecutive quadratures. The derived series of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is

𝔤⊃D​𝔤={𝐯1,𝐯2},D2​𝔤=𝔤(2)={0}.\mathfrak{g}\supset D\mathfrak{g}=\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\},\quad D^{2}\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}^{(2)}=\left\{0\right\}.

The third order differential invariants of the ideal {𝐯1,𝐯2}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\} are z=y1z=y_{1}, ρ=y2\rho=y_{2}, ρ′​(z)=d​ρ/d​z=z2/z1\rho^{\prime}(z)=d\rho/dz=z_{2}/z_{1}, in terms of which Eq. (44) reduces to the first order ODE

(1+z2)ρ′(z)−3zρ=ρH(κ),κ=(1+z2)−3/2ρ.(1+z^{2})\rho^{\prime}(z)-3z\rho=\rho H(\kappa),\quad\kappa=(1+z^{2})^{-3/2}\rho. (129)

This equation should retain the final (inherited) symmetry 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3}, which, in terms of z,ρz,\rho, has the reduced form (from restriction of pr(2)​𝐯3{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{3} to z,ρz,\rho coordinates)

𝐯~3=(1+z2)∂z+3zρ∂ρ.\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=(1+z^{2})\partial_{z}+3z\rho\partial_{\rho}.

The coordinates κ=(1+z2)−3/2ρ\kappa=(1+z^{2})^{-3/2}\rho, χ=arctan⁡z\chi=\arctan z rectifies the vector field 𝐯~3=∂z\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\partial_{z}. In terms of κ\kappa, χ\chi, (129) becomes a separable equation

d​κd​χ=κ​H​(κ)\frac{d\kappa}{d\chi}=\kappa H(\kappa) (130)

with implicit solution H^​(κ)=χ+c1\hat{H}(\kappa)=\chi+c_{1} or solving for ρ=y2=G⁡(y1,c1)\rho=y_{2}=G(y_{1},c_{1}), which is invariant under the translational algebra {𝐯1,𝐯2}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\} and can be integrated by two further quadratures.

The special case H=λ=const.H=\lambda=\mbox{const.} leads to the similitude invariant equation

(1+y12)​y3=(3​y1+λ)​y22(1+y_{1}^{2})y_{3}=(3y_{1}+\lambda)y_{2}^{2}

with the additional symmetry 𝐯4=x∂x+y∂y\mathbf{v}_{4}=x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y}. From (130), the solution of the reduced equation is κ=c1​eλ​χ\kappa=c_{1}e^{\lambda\chi}, and with the original variables, it is the second order ODE

y2=c1​(1+y12)3/2​exp⁡{λ​arctan⁡y1}.y_{2}=c_{1}(1+y_{1}^{2})^{3/2}\exp\left\{\lambda\arctan y_{1}\right\}.

For λ=0\lambda=0, the solutions are curves with the constant curvature κ=c1\kappa=c_{1}, i.e. the family of circles with radius c1−1c_{1}^{-1}

(x−c2)2+(y−c3)2=c1−2.(x-c_{2})^{2}+(y-c_{3})^{2}=c_{1}^{-2}.

In this case the equation admits two further additional symmetries

𝐯5=(x2−y2)∂x+2xy∂y,𝐯6=2xy∂x+(y2−x2)∂y.\mathbf{v}_{5}=(x^{2}-y^{2})\partial_{x}+2xy\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{6}=2xy\partial_{x}+(y^{2}-x^{2})\partial_{y}.

The maximal symmetry algebra of the equation is the six-dimensional Lorentz algebra so⁡(3,1)\ort(3,1) (see also Example 2.5).

When λ≠0\lambda\neq 0, the corresponding second order ODE can be integrated using two-parameter translational group. More conveniently, a parametric solution can be produced by the introduction of the parametrization τ=arctan⁡y1\tau=\arctan y_{1} in the form

x⁡(τ)=c1​e−λ​τ​(λ​cos⁡τ−sin⁡τ)+c2,y⁡(τ)=c1​e−λ​τ​(λ​sin⁡τ+cos⁡τ)+c3.x(\tau)=c_{1}e^{-\lambda\tau}(\lambda\cos\tau-\sin\tau)+c_{2},\quad y(\tau)=c_{1}e^{-\lambda\tau}(\lambda\sin\tau+\cos\tau)+c_{3}.

To see what happens when the symmetry group is not solvable we consider the following example of a third-order ODE, known as the Schwarzian equation,

y3y1−32​(y2y1)2=F⁡(x),\frac{y_{3}}{y_{1}}-\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{y_{2}}{y_{1}}\right)^{2}=F(x), (131)

where FF is any function of its argument, admitting the nonsolvable symmetry group SL⁡(2,ℝ)\SL(2,\mathbb{R}), with Lie algebra having the basis

𝐯1=∂y,𝐯2=y∂y,𝐯3=y2∂y.\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=y^{2}\partial_{y}. (132)

The corresponding Lie group SL⁡(2,ℝ)\SL(2,\mathbb{R}) is the group of linear fractional transformations

(x,y)→(x,a​y+bc​y+d),(abcd)∈SL⁡(2,ℝ).(x,y)\to\left(x,\frac{ay+b}{cy+d}\right),\qquad\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{R}).

The expression on the left-hand side of (131) is called the Schwarzian derivative of yy with respect to xx and is denoted by the symbol {y,x}\left\{y,x\right\}. It is invariant under the Möbius transformation in yy:

{a​y+bc​y+d;x}={y,x},a​d−b​c=1\left\{\frac{ay+b}{cy+d};x\right\}=\left\{y,x\right\},\quad ad-bc=1

(a unique differential invariant of order ≤3\leq 3 of the algebra (132)). A two-dimensional solvable subalgebra 𝔤0\mathfrak{g}_{0} generated by {𝐯1,𝐯2}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}\right\} can be used to reduce the equation to one of first order. The second-order differential invariants of 𝔤0\mathfrak{g}_{0} are xx and w=y2/y1w=y_{2}/y_{1}, in terms of which the reduced equation becomes

d​wd​x=12​w2+F⁡(x),\frac{dw}{dx}=\frac{1}{2}w^{2}+F(x),

which is recognized as a Riccati equation. This equation does not inherit the symmetry 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} of the original equation. Indeed, the reduced vector field 𝐯~3\mathbf{\tilde{v}}_{3} in terms of the invariants xx and ww is nonlocal (the so-called exponential vector field)

𝐯~3=2e∫w​𝑑x∂w.\mathbf{\tilde{v}}_{3}=2e^{\int wdx}\partial_{w}.

On the other hand, the well-known Hopf–Cole transformation w=−2​θ′​(x)θ⁡(x)w=-2\frac{\theta^{\prime}(x)}{\theta(x)} (y1=y′=θ−2y_{1}=y^{\prime}=\theta^{-2}) linearizes to

θ′′+F⁡(x)2​θ=0.\theta^{\prime\prime}+\frac{F(x)}{2}\theta=0. (133)

Let θ\theta and ψ\psi be two independent solutions of (133). Then, we have ψ/θ=W​∫θ−2​𝑑x+c\psi/\theta=W\int\theta^{-2}dx+c, where WW is the (constant) Wronskian of θ\theta and ψ\psi, (we can put W=1W=1 by scaling ψ\psi) and cc is an arbitrary constant, that can be absorbed to ψ\psi so that we can put c=0c=0 without loss of generality. The solution yy can now be expressed as a ratio y=ψ/θy=\psi/\theta of two linearly independent solutions to (133).

When F⁡(x)=0F(x)=0 (known as the Kummer–Schwarz equation; this equation is also encountered in the study of geodesic curves in spaces of constant curvature), the symmetry algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} becomes six-dimensional and has a direct-sum structure 𝔤=sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊕sl⁡(2,ℝ)\mathfrak{g}=\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) spanned by the vector fields (132) and

𝐯4=∂x,𝐯5=x∂x,𝐯6=x2∂x.\mathbf{v}_{4}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=x\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{6}=x^{2}\partial_{x}. (134)

The symmetry group is then a linear fractional group of both xx and yy coordinates. The corresponding solution is the linear fractional (or Möbius) transformation in xx: y=(a​x+b)/(c​x+d)y=(ax+b)/(cx+d), a​d−b​c≠0ad-bc\neq 0.

Remark 4.15.

There are only two types of third order ODE admitting 6-dimensional symmetry groups:

(1+y12)​y3=3​y1​y22and{y,x}=0.(1+y_{1}^{2})y_{3}=3y_{1}y_{2}^{2}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\left\{y,x\right\}=0.

The maximal symmetry algebra for a third order ODE is seven-dimensional and is attained if and only if it is equivalent to the linear equation y3=0y_{3}=0 up to a linear point (equivalence) transformation.

In general, for any ODE of order n≥3n\geq 3, the symmetry group has dimension ≤n+4\leq n+4. The maximal dimension n+4n+4 is attained if and only if the equation is linear or linearizable by a point transformation.

4.1 Group classification problem

When a system involves an arbitrary parameter or arbitrary function, the symmetry group can have a richer symmetry for certain specific forms of these arbitrary terms. The problem of identifying such arbitrary parameters or functions is known as the group classification problem. When there are only parameters or arbitrary functions of a single argument of independent or dependent variable then the problem is easily tackled solving the determining system where splitting is almost always possible. The arbitrary functions are found by solving an ODE (the so-called classifying ODE). The situation becomes rather complicated when the system depends on arbitrary functions of more than one argument. In this case, the group classification problem is often solved by reducing it to the classification of realizations of low-dimensional abstract Lie algebras combined with the notion of equivalence group and the knowledge of abstract Lie theory.

Example 4.16.

A classification problem: We wish to determine all possible forms of F⁡(y)F(y) for which the following ODE allows a two-dimensional symmetry algebra:

y′′=μ​y′+F⁡(y),μ≠0,F′′≠0.y^{\prime\prime}=\mu y^{\prime}+F(y),\quad\mu\not=0,\quad F^{\prime\prime}\neq 0. (135)

Under the reflection x→−xx\to-x, we have μ→−μ\mu\to-\mu so we can assume μ>0\mu>0 without loss of generality. The special nonlinearity F⁡(y)=a​y3+b​yF(y)=ay^{3}+by is recognized as Duffing’s equation (see page 4.11). The trivial case μ=0\mu=0 is clearly integrable. It has the energy first integral (Hamiltonian)

H=12​y′2+V⁡(y)=constant,F⁡(y)=−V′​(y).H=\frac{1}{2}y^{\prime 2}+V(y)=\text{constant},\quad F(y)=-V^{\prime}(y).

The symmetry classification for μ≠0\mu\neq 0 naturally characterizes all possible integrable cases. Eq. (135) arises in obtaining travelling-wave solutions of the nonlinear heat (diffusion) equation

ut=ux​x+F⁡(u),F′′≠0.u_{t}=u_{xx}+F(u),\quad F^{\prime\prime}\neq 0. (136)

These are solutions of the form u⁡(x,t)=y⁡(z)=y⁡(x−c​t)u(x,t)=y(z)=y(x-ct), being invariant under a combination of time and space translational symmetries. In what follows we take z≡xz\equiv x.

We can put μ=1\mu=1 in (135) by scaling the independent variable x→μ−1​xx\to\mu^{-1}x and redefining μ−2​F\mu^{-2}F as FF. The equation is invariant under translation of xx so that 𝐯1=∂x\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x} generates a symmetry. For certain functions FF, the symmetry group will be two-dimensional. The general symmetry algebra is generated by vector fields of the form

𝐯=ξ(x,y)∂x+η(x,y)∂y.\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,y)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,y)\partial_{y}. (137)

The second prolongation formula for vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} is

pr(2)𝐯=ξ(x,y)∂x+η(x,y)∂y+η(1)(x,y,y′)∂y′+η(2)(x,y,y′,y′′)∂y′′,{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}=\xi(x,y)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,y)\partial_{y}+\eta^{(1)}(x,y,y^{\prime})\partial_{y^{\prime}}+\eta^{(2)}(x,y,y^{\prime},y^{\prime\prime})\partial_{y^{\prime\prime}},

where

η(1)=Dx​η−y′​Dx​ξ,η(2)=Dx​η(1)−y′′​Dx​ξ.\eta^{(1)}=D_{x}\eta-y^{\prime}D_{x}\xi,\quad\eta^{(2)}=D_{x}\eta^{(1)}-y^{\prime\prime}D_{x}\xi.

Higher order prolongation coefficients can be calculated from the recursion formula (18)

η(k)=Dx​η(k−1)−yk​Dx​ξ,yk=y(k),\eta^{(k)}=D_{x}\eta^{(k-1)}-y_{k}D_{x}\xi,\quad y_{k}=y^{(k)},

or in terms of the characteristic Q⁡(x,y,y′)=η−y′​ξQ(x,y,y^{\prime})=\eta-y^{\prime}\xi as

η(k)=Dxk​Q+ξ​yk+1.\eta^{(k)}=D^{k}_{x}Q+\xi y_{k+1}.

From the infinitesimal symmetry requirement (24) we find η(2)−η(1)−η​F′=0\eta^{(2)}-\eta^{(1)}-\eta F^{\prime}=0 on solutions. This condition, replacing y′′y^{\prime\prime} by y′+F⁡(y)y^{\prime}+F(y), is a cubic polynomial in the first derivative y′y^{\prime} with coefficients depending on xx and yy. Setting these coefficients equal to zero we obtain the determining system for the coefficients ξ\xi, η\eta

3​F​ξy+ξx−2​ηx​y+ξx​x\displaystyle 3F\xi_{y}+\xi_{x}-2\eta_{xy}+\xi_{xx} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (138)
2​ξy−ηy​y+2​ξx​y\displaystyle 2\xi_{y}-\eta_{yy}+2\xi_{xy} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (139)
ξy​y\displaystyle\xi_{yy} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (140)
F′​η−(ηy−2​ξx)​F−ηx​x+ηx\displaystyle F^{\prime}\eta-(\eta_{y}-2\xi_{x})F-\eta_{xx}+\eta_{x} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (141)

Differentiating twice the first two equations with respect to yy and using the third one and the condition F′′≠0F^{\prime\prime}\neq 0 (FF is not linear) we find

ξy=0,ηy​y=0.\xi_{y}=0,\quad\eta_{yy}=0.

So this gives ξ=b⁡(x)\xi=b(x) and η=c⁡(x)​y+d⁡(x)\eta=c(x)y+d(x), and then (137) takes the form

𝐯=b(x)∂x+[c(x)y+d(x)]∂y,b≠0.\mathbf{v}=b(x)\partial_{x}+[c(x)y+d(x)]\partial_{y},\quad b\neq 0. (142)

(c​y+d)​F′−(c−2​b′)​F=(c′′−c′)​y+d′′−d′(cy+d)F^{\prime}-(c-2b^{\prime})F=(c^{\prime\prime}-c^{\prime})y+d^{\prime\prime}-d^{\prime} (143)

with the relation

2​c′−(b′+b′′)=02c^{\prime}-(b^{\prime}+b^{\prime\prime})=0 (144)

from which we have

c=12​(L+b′+b),c=\frac{1}{2}(L+b^{\prime}+b), (145)

where LL is a constant.

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=k𝐯2,𝐯1=∂x.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=k\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x}. (146)

b=b0​ek​x,c=c0​ek​x,d=d0​ek​x,b=b_{0}e^{kx},\quad c=c_{0}e^{kx},\quad d=d_{0}e^{kx},

(c0​y+d0)​F′−(c0−2​k​b0)​F=k⁡(k−1)​(c0​y+d0),(c_{0}y+d_{0})F^{\prime}-(c_{0}-2kb_{0})F=k(k-1)(c_{0}y+d_{0}), (148)

y′′=y′+e2​y−1.y^{\prime\prime}=y^{\prime}+e^{2y}-1. (152)

F=α(y+δ)−1,𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=ex[∂x+(y+δ)∂y].F=\alpha(y+\delta)^{-1},\quad\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=e^{x}[\partial_{x}+(y+\delta)\partial_{y}].

(y+δ)​F′−γ​F=2​(γ2−1)(γ+3)2​(y+δ),γ=1−3​kk+1.(y+\delta)F^{\prime}-\gamma F=\frac{2(\gamma^{2}-1)}{(\gamma+3)^{2}}(y+\delta),\quad\gamma=\frac{1-3k}{k+1}. (153)

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=ek​x[∂x+k+12(y+δ)∂y],k=1−γγ+3.\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=e^{kx}\left[\partial_{x}+\frac{k+1}{2}(y+\delta)\partial_{y}\right],\quad k=\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma+3}. (155)

The form of (154) is not changed by the linear transformation y~=p​y+q\tilde{y}=py+q. The arbitrary coefficient F⁡(y)F(y) gets changed into F~​(y~)=p​F​(y~−qp)\tilde{F}(\tilde{y})=pF(\frac{\tilde{y}-q}{p}). By a suitable choice of pp and qq we can set M=1M=1 and δ=0\delta=0.

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=ek​x[∂x+k+12y∂y].\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=e^{kx}\left[\partial_{x}+\frac{k+1}{2}y\partial_{y}\right]. (156)

According to Theorem 4.8, we start to reduce by the normal subalgebra 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2}, which, in terms of the coordinates

s=k−1e−k​x,r=ye−(k+1)x/2,s=k^{-1}e^{-kx},\quad r=ye^{-(k+1)x/2}, (158)

d2​rd​s2=e(3​k−1)2​x​[−k2−14​y+F⁡(y)]=rγ,\frac{d^{2}r}{ds^{2}}=e^{\frac{(3k-1)}{2}x}\left[-\frac{k^{2}-1}{4}y+F(y)\right]=r^{\gamma}, (159)

which retains the symmetry 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}. In terms of the invariants rr and ρ=d​r/d​s\rho=dr/ds of 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}, it reduces to the first order ODE ρ​d​ρ/d​r=rγ\rho d\rho/dr=r^{\gamma} with solution ρ2=2​ln⁡r+c1\rho^{2}=2\ln r+c_{1} if γ=−1\gamma=-1; ρ2=2​(γ+1)−1​rγ+1+c1\rho^{2}=2(\gamma+1)^{-1}r^{\gamma+1}+c_{1}, otherwise. The general solution is obtained implicitly after a second quadrature from (d​r/d​s)2=ρ2​(r)(dr/ds)^{2}=\rho^{2}(r). The alterative way is to integrate directly using the integrating factor I=r′​(s)I=r^{\prime}(s). When γ=2,3\gamma=2,3, the solutions are obtained in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions or Weierstrass ℘\wp function, when γ>3\gamma>3 in terms of hyperelliptic integrals.

The case k=−1k=-1 is treated similarly. The canonical coordinates r=y−xr=y-x, s=exs=e^{x} maps Eq. (152) to r′′​(s)=e2​rr^{\prime\prime}(s)=e^{2r} with symmetry {∂s,s∂s−∂r}\left\{\partial_{s},s\partial_{s}-\partial_{r}\right\}. The corresponding solution is given by

y=x+ln⁡{2​c1​c2exp⁡{−c1​ex}−c22​exp⁡{c1​ex}},c1>0y=x+\ln\left\{\frac{2\sqrt{c_{1}}c_{2}}{\exp\left\{-\sqrt{c_{1}}e^{x}\right\}-c_{2}^{2}\exp\left\{\sqrt{c_{1}}e^{x}\right\}}\right\},\quad c_{1}>0

or

y=x+ln⁡{−c1​sec⁡[−c1​(ex+c2)]},c1<0.y=x+\ln\left\{\sqrt{-c_{1}}\sec[\sqrt{-c_{1}}(e^{x}+c_{2})]\right\},\quad c_{1}<0.
Remark 4.17.

We note that Example 4.16 does not provide a complete group (or symmetry) classification. Rather, it identifies classes of F⁡(y)F(y) for which the equation is invariant only under a two-dimensional symmetry group which is sufficient for reduction to quadratures.

For an equation depending on arbitrary functions of more than a single variable, to solve the problem of complete classification with respect to its Lie point symmetries it is imperative to use equivalence group of the equation. In this framework, let us consider the group classification of the more general equation

y′′=f⁡(x,y).y^{\prime\prime}=f(x,y). (160)

Due to the absence of the first derivative y′y^{\prime} in ff, invariance under the general symmetry group generated by (137) constrains considerably infinitesimal generators ξ,η\xi,\eta

ξ⁡(x,y)=α⁡(x)​y+ξ⁡(x),η⁡(x,y)=α′​(x)​y2+η⁡(x)​y+β⁡(x),\xi(x,y)=\alpha(x)y+\xi(x),\quad\eta(x,y)=\alpha^{\prime}(x)y^{2}+\eta(x)y+\beta(x), (161)

where the functions α⁡(x),β⁡(x),ξ⁡(x),η⁡(x)\alpha(x),\beta(x),\xi(x),\eta(x) are subject to the following equations

ξ′′−2​η′+3​(α​f−α′′​y)=0,ξ​fx+η​fy=(η−2​ξ′)​f+α′′′​y2+η′′​y+β′′.\begin{split}&\xi^{\prime\prime}-2\eta^{\prime}+3(\alpha f-\alpha^{\prime\prime}y)=0,\\ &\xi f_{x}+\eta f_{y}=(\eta-2\xi^{\prime})f+\alpha^{\prime\prime\prime}y^{2}+\eta^{\prime\prime}y+\beta^{\prime\prime}.\end{split} (162)

From the first equation by taking differentiation twice with respect to yy we find

α​fy​y=0.\alpha f_{yy}=0. (163)

Hence, if α=0\alpha=0, then ξ′′−2​η′=0\xi^{\prime\prime}-2\eta^{\prime}=0 and η=ξ′/2+c0\eta=\xi^{\prime}/2+c_{0}. We have a single classification relation between ff, ξ\xi and β\beta.

ξ⁡(x)​fx+(η⁡(x)​y+β⁡(x))​fy=(η−2​ξ′)​f+η′′​y+β′′.\xi(x)f_{x}+(\eta(x)y+\beta(x))f_{y}=(\eta-2\xi^{\prime})f+\eta^{\prime\prime}y+\beta^{\prime\prime}. (164)

For given ξ\xi, β\beta and c0c_{0}, the first order linear PDE (164) can be integrated using method of characteristics to find the most general form of ff. For c0=0c_{0}=0, f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) is given by

f(x,y)=(ξ)′′ξy+1ξ(βξ)′+ξ−3/2F(σ),σ=yξ−∫ξ−3/2β(x)dx,f(x,y)=\frac{(\sqrt{\xi})^{\prime\prime}}{\sqrt{\xi}}y+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\xi}}\left(\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{\xi}}\right)^{\prime}+\xi^{-3/2}F(\sigma),\quad\sigma=\frac{y}{\sqrt{\xi}}-\int\xi^{-3/2}\beta(x)dx, (165)

where FF (F′′≠0F^{\prime\prime}\neq 0) is an arbitrary function of its argument. We note that for ξ=x2\xi=x^{2}, β=0\beta=0 we recover (95) with the arbitrary function HH independent of the differential invariant ww.

Imposing a further symmetry on the equation (165) one can generate a second order differential equation invariant under a two-parameter group of symmetries with the arbitrary function FF restricted. As an example, we require invariance under the scaling group (x,y)→(λ​x,λk​y)(x,y)\to(\lambda x,\lambda^{k}y), λ>0\lambda>0 and pick ξ,β\xi,\beta for c0=0c_{0}=0 such that the generators

𝐯1=ξ∂x+(ξ′2y+β)∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+ky∂y\mathbf{v}_{1}=\xi\partial_{x}+(\frac{\xi^{\prime}}{2}y+\beta)\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+ky\partial_{y} (166)

form a two-dimensional Lie algebra with commutator

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=(ξ−xξ′)∂x+(kβ−xβ′−ξ′′2xy)∂y=−𝐯1,[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=(\xi-x\xi^{\prime})\partial_{x}+\left(k\beta-x\beta^{\prime}-\frac{\xi^{\prime\prime}}{2}xy\right)\partial_{y}=-\mathbf{v}_{1},

which implies

x​ξ′−2​ξ=0,(k+1)​β−x​β′+12​(ξ′−x​ξ′′)​y=0x\xi^{\prime}-2\xi=0,\quad(k+1)\beta-x\beta^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2}(\xi^{\prime}-x\xi^{\prime\prime})y=0

with solutions ξ=x2\xi=x^{2}, β=δ​xk+1\beta=\delta x^{k+1} so we find the generators

𝐯1=x2∂x+(xy+δxk+1)∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+ky∂y.\mathbf{v}_{1}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+(xy+\delta x^{k+1})\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+ky\partial_{y}.

With these choices of ξ,β\xi,\beta, invariance under 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} will restrict the arbitrary FF to

F⁡(σ)=F0​σ(k+1)/(k−1),σ=yx−δk−1​xk−1,k≠1.F(\sigma)=F_{0}\sigma^{(k+1)/(k-1)},\quad\sigma=\frac{y}{x}-\frac{\delta}{k-1}x^{k-1},\quad k\neq 1. (167)

In conclusion, the corresponding invariant differential equation becomes

y′′=δ​k​xk−2+F0​x−3​σ(k+1)/(k−1)y^{\prime\prime}=\delta kx^{k-2}+F_{0}x^{-3}\sigma^{(k+1)/(k-1)} (168)

and can be integrated by two quadratures in the order of 𝐯1,𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}. The special case δ=0\delta=0 of (168) agrees with the Emden–Fowler equation (96) for n=(k+1)/(k−1)n=(k+1)/(k-1) and in particular with (97) for k=2k=2.

When k=1k=1,

F⁡(σ)=F0​e−(2/δ)​σ,σ=yx−δ​log⁡x,δ≠0F(\sigma)=F_{0}e^{-(2/\delta)\sigma},\quad\sigma=\frac{y}{x}-\delta\log x,\quad\delta\neq 0 (169)

the equation assumes the form

y′′=x−1​[δ+F0​e−(2/δ)​(y/x)],y^{\prime\prime}=x^{-1}\left[\delta+F_{0}e^{-(2/\delta)(y/x)}\right], (170)

invariant under a rank-2 Lie algebra with generators

𝐯1=x2∂x+x(δx+y)∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+y∂y.\mathbf{v}_{1}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+x(\delta x+y)\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y}.

Using the normal coordinates r=σr=\sigma and s=−1/xs=-1/x of 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1} satisfying 𝐯1​(σ)=0\mathbf{v}_{1}(\sigma)=0, 𝐯1​(s)=1\mathbf{v}_{1}(s)=1 we can write (170) as

d2​σd​s2=F0​e−(2/δ)​σ,\frac{d^{2}\sigma}{ds^{2}}=F_{0}e^{-(2/\delta)\sigma},

which is certainly invariant under 𝐯~1=∂s\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=\partial_{s} and 𝐯~2=s∂s+δ∂σ\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=s\partial_{s}+\delta\partial_{\sigma}.

We can form an equivalent realization of the Lie algebra spanned by the elements (166) satisfying the commutation relation

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=(ξ−xξ′)∂x+(kβ−xβ′−ξ′′2xy)∂y=(1−m)𝐯1.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=(\xi-x\xi^{\prime})\partial_{x}+\left(k\beta-x\beta^{\prime}-\frac{\xi^{\prime\prime}}{2}xy\right)\partial_{y}=(1-m)\mathbf{v}_{1}. (171)

In this case, we have

ξ=xm,β=δ​xk+m−1\xi=x^{m},\quad\beta=\delta x^{k+m-1}

for which Eq. (165) remains remains invariant under 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} when FF is limited to a power function of σ\sigma

F=F0σν,σ=x−m/2(y+2​δ​xkm−2​k),ν=4−3​m−2​km−2​k,m≠2k.F=F_{0}\sigma^{\nu},\quad\sigma=x^{-m/2}\left(y+\frac{2\delta x^{k}}{m-2k}\right),\quad\nu=\frac{4-3m-2k}{m-2k},\quad m\neq 2k. (172)

The corresponding invariant equation is significantly simplified for ν=2\nu=2 or m=2/5​(k+2)m=2/5(k+2) (k≠1/2k\neq 1/2). In this case, there are two values of the pairs (m,k)(m,k), that are worth examining.

First we choose (m,k)=(6/7,1/7)(m,k)=(6/7,1/7) so that ν=2\nu=2, β=δ\beta=\delta (constant). After some calculation, we find the invariant equation as

y′′=F0x−15/7y2+(343​F0​δ−12)196​x2(7δx1/7+4y).y^{\prime\prime}=F_{0}x^{-15/7}y^{2}+\frac{(343F_{0}\delta-12)}{196x^{2}}(7\delta x^{1/7}+4y). (173)

admitting the symmetry algebra

𝐯1=x6/7∂x+(37x−1/7y+12343​F0)∂y,𝐯2=x∂x+17y∂y\mathbf{v}_{1}=x^{6/7}\partial_{x}+(\frac{3}{7}x^{-1/7}y+\frac{12}{343F_{0}})\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=x\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{7}y\partial_{y}

with commutation relation [𝐯1,𝐯2]=1/7​𝐯1[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=1/7\mathbf{v}_{1}.

y′′=F0x−20/7y2+(343​F0​δ+12)196​x2(7δx6/7−4y).y^{\prime\prime}=F_{0}x^{-20/7}y^{2}+\frac{(343F_{0}\delta+12)}{196x^{2}}(7\delta x^{6/7}-4y). (175)

admitting the symmetry algebra

with commutation relation [𝐯1,𝐯2]=−1/7𝐯1[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=-1/7\mathbf{v}_{1}. We recall that all possible forms of the equation y′′=F0​xn​y2y^{\prime\prime}=F_{0}x^{n}y^{2} invariant under a two-dimensional nonabelian symmetry algebra are attained only for three values of the exponents n∈{−5,−15/7,−20/7}n\in\left\{-5,-15/7,-20/7\right\} (see page 4.11).

In the Abelian case [𝐯1,𝐯2]=0[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=0 (ν=1\nu=1), we find ξ=x\xi=x, β=δ​xk\beta=\delta x^{k} and this leads to a linear equation.

On the other hand, if ff has some specific form, this linear PDE allows us to find all possible symmetries. For example, if f⁡(x,y)=q⁡(x)​y2f(x,y)=q(x)y^{2}, then we find that ξ\xi, β\beta should satisfy

ξ′′′=4​q​β,β′′=0,2​ξ​q′+(5​ξ′+2​c0)​q=0.\xi^{\prime\prime\prime}=4q\beta,\quad\beta^{\prime\prime}=0,\quad 2\xi q^{\prime}+(5\xi^{\prime}+2c_{0})q=0.

Once ξ\xi, β\beta are solved form the first two equations, the last one serves as a compatibility condition. For the choice q=exq=e^{x}, it can be shown that there is only one symmetry given by 𝐯=∂x−y∂y\mathbf{v}=\partial_{x}-y\partial_{y} which reduces the corresponding equation to an Abel equation of second type. For another special case q=K​xmq=Kx^{m} see the discussion on page 4.11.

In the nonlinear case fy​y≠0f_{yy}\neq 0, the complete group classification of (160) was carried out in [39]. The interested reader is referred to this paper for the details of the classification procedure. We here present the complete classification results in Table 1.

If α\alpha is not identically zero then fy​y=0f_{yy}=0 (linear ODE). The pair of equations (162) for f=−q⁡(x)​yf=-q(x)y by splitting with respect to powers of yy gives:

η⁡(x)=12​ξ′​(x)+c0,ξ′′′+4​q​ξ′+2​q′​ξ=0,\eta(x)=\frac{1}{2}\xi^{\prime}(x)+c_{0},\quad\xi^{\prime\prime\prime}+4q\xi^{\prime}+2q^{\prime}\xi=0,

and α,β\alpha,\beta are solutions to the original linear ODE y′′+q⁡(x)​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+q(x)y=0. Consequently, we find that infinitesimals depend on eight arbitrary constants. We recall that general solution of ξ\xi can be expressed in terms of two linearly independent solutions of the original ODE (see formula (288)). We list the eight vector fields found above as

𝐯1=yy1∂x+y1′y2∂y,𝐯2=yy2∂x+y2′y2∂y,𝐯3=y∂y,𝐯4=y12∂x+y1y1′y∂y,𝐯5=y1y2∂x+12(y1y2)′y∂y,𝐯6=y22∂x+y2y2′y∂y,𝐯7=y1∂y,𝐯8=y2∂y,\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=yy_{1}\partial_{x}+y_{1}^{\prime}y^{2}\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=yy_{2}\partial_{x}+y_{2}^{\prime}y^{2}\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=y\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{4}=y_{1}^{2}\partial_{x}+y_{1}y_{1}^{\prime}y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=y_{1}y_{2}\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(y_{1}y_{2})^{\prime}y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{6}=y_{2}^{2}\partial_{x}+y_{2}y_{2}^{\prime}y\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{7}=y_{1}\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{8}=y_{2}\partial_{y},\end{split} (177)

where y1,y2y_{1},y_{2} are solutions to the ODE y′′+q⁡(x)​y=0y^{\prime\prime}+q(x)y=0. They span a Lie algebra isomorphic to the sl⁡(3,ℝ)\Sl(3,\mathbb{R}) algebra.

For the special case q=0q=0 we have y1=1y_{1}=1, y2=xy_{2}=x and upon taking a suitable combination of 𝐯5\mathbf{v}_{5} with 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3}, the vector fields (177) turn to the standard basis of sl⁡(3,ℝ)\Sl(3,\mathbb{R}) in the form

𝐯1=y∂x,𝐯2=xy∂x+y2∂y,𝐯3=y∂y,𝐯4=∂x,𝐯5=x∂x,𝐯6=x2∂x+xy∂y,𝐯7=∂y,𝐯8=x∂y.\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=y\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=xy\partial_{x}+y^{2}\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=y\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{4}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=x\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{6}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xy\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{7}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{8}=x\partial_{y}.\end{split} (178)

This algebra is admitted if and only if a second order ODE is either linear or linearizable by a point transformation. See Example 5.11.

We comment that the nonhomogeneous linear ODE

y′′+q⁡(x)​y=r⁡(x)y^{\prime\prime}+q(x)y=r(x)

remains invariant under the sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) subalgebra generated by

𝐯=ξ(x)∂x+ξ′​(x)2y∂y\mathbf{v}=\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\frac{\xi^{\prime}(x)}{2}y\partial_{y}

if r(x)=r0ξ(x)−3/2r(x)=r_{0}\xi(x)^{-3/2}.

Moreover, the change of independent variable τ=eμ​x\tau=e^{\mu x} converts Eq. (135) to

yτ​τ=τ−2​f​(y),y_{\tau\tau}=\tau^{-2}f(y),

where f⁡(y⁡(τ))f(y(\tau)) should be obtained from F⁡(y⁡(x))F(y(x)) by the inverse transformation. This equivalent equation belongs to the class (160). For nonconstant μ=A⁡(x)\mu=A(x), the classification problem was solved in [32].

Finally, we comment that the quadratic Liénard equation

y′′+f⁡(y)​y′2+g⁡(y)=0,y^{\prime\prime}+f(y)y^{\prime 2}+g(y)=0, (179)

where f⁡(y)f(y) and g⁡(y)g(y) are arbitrary smooth functions of yy, can be transformed to a subclass of (160) of the form

Y′′​(x)+G⁡(Y)=0,G⁡(Y)=W′​(y)​g​(y)Y^{\prime\prime}(x)+G(Y)=0,\quad G(Y)=W^{\prime}(y)g(y) (180)

by the invertible change of dependent variable Y=W⁡(y)Y=W(y), W′​(y)≠0W^{\prime}(y)\neq 0 where W⁡(y)W(y) is chosen as a solution of W′′−f⁡(y)​W′=0W^{\prime\prime}-f(y)W^{\prime}=0. So complete group classification of (179) can be extracted from Table 1.

However, the classification problem for the standard Liénard equation, which is a possible extension of (135)

y′′+f⁡(y)​y′+g⁡(y)=0y^{\prime\prime}+f(y)y^{\prime}+g(y)=0 (181)

is more complicated. Such a classification, but without effective use of the equivalence group to obtain the simplest forms of ff and gg and the corresponding symmetry algebras, was treated in [41] excluding linearizable equations that occur when f′′=0f^{\prime\prime}=0 and 3​g′−f2=const.3g^{\prime}-f^{2}=\text{const.} (see Example (5.11) and Subsection 5.2). In the nonlinearizable case, when f≠0f\neq 0, the maximal symmetry algebra is two-dimensional (The trivial symmetry 𝐯1=∂x\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x} is extended by an additional symmetry 𝐯2\mathbf{v}_{2} of the form (142)). The algebra can not be abelian, otherwise the equation would have to be constant coefficient linear. A remarkable exception occurs when f=0f=0 (see Table 1 and formulae (185)-(186)).

An alternative classification of (181) can be done by solving the inverse problem: Require invariance under (147) and split the resulting condition with respect to y′y^{\prime}. We distinguish between two cases:

I. c0≠0c_{0}\neq 0, b0≠0b_{0}\neq 0: Without loss of generality we put b0=1b_{0}=1 and d0=0d_{0}=0. We find that f⁡(y)f(y) and g⁡(y)g(y) satisfy the first order linear ODEs

c0​y​f′+k​f+k⁡(2​c0−k)=0,c0​y​g′+(2​k−c0)​g=−c0​k​y​f−c0​k2​y.\begin{split}&c_{0}yf^{\prime}+kf+k(2c_{0}-k)=0,\\ &c_{0}yg^{\prime}+(2k-c_{0})g=-c_{0}kyf-c_{0}k^{2}y.\end{split} (182)

Solving this system, we obtain

f(y)=C1y−k/c0+k−2c0,g(y)=y[C2y−2k/c0−c0C1y−k/c0+c02−kc0],f(y)=C_{1}y^{-k/c_{0}}+k-2c_{0},\quad g(y)=y\left[C_{2}y^{-2k/c_{0}}-c_{0}C_{1}y^{-k/c_{0}}+c_{0}^{2}-kc_{0}\right], (183)

where C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} are integration constants. Letting 1−(2​k)/(c0)=γ≠11-(2k)/(c_{0})=\gamma\neq 1 we can re-express (183) in the form

f⁡(y)=C1​y(γ−1)/2+k⁡(γ+3)γ−1,g⁡(y)=C2​yγ+2​k​C1γ−1​y(γ+1)/2+2​k2​(γ+1)(1−γ)2​yf(y)=C_{1}y^{(\gamma-1)/2}+\frac{k(\gamma+3)}{\gamma-1},\quad g(y)=C_{2}y^{\gamma}+\frac{2kC_{1}}{\gamma-1}y^{(\gamma+1)/2}+\frac{2k^{2}(\gamma+1)}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}y (184)

allowing the two-dimensional nonabelian symmetry algebra spanned by the vector fields

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=ek​x[∂x+2​k1−γy∂y].\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=e^{kx}[\partial_{x}+\frac{2k}{1-\gamma}y\partial_{y}].

The case f=0f=0, namely C1=0C_{1}=0, γ=−3\gamma=-3, is in particular interesting. The nonlinearity g⁡(y)g(y) becomes

g⁡(y)=C2​y−3−k24​y,g(y)=C_{2}y^{-3}-\frac{k^{2}}{4}y, (185)

and c0=k/2c_{0}=k/2. The corresponding invariant equation is exactly (112) for α=k/2\alpha=k/2, namely, Ermakov–Pinney equation with symmetry algebra spanned by the vector fields

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=ek​x(∂x+k2y∂y),𝐯3=e−k​x(∂x−k2y∂y),k≠0.\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=e^{kx}(\partial_{x}+\frac{k}{2}y\partial_{y}),\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=e^{-kx}(\partial_{x}-\frac{k}{2}y\partial_{y}),\quad k\neq 0. (186)

This is the only case when the symmetry algebra of (181) is three-dimensional.

If f⁡(y)=−1f(y)=-1, g⁡(y)=−F⁡(y)g(y)=-F(y) we recover the group classification of (135). Then the first equation of (182) gives the condition k⁡(1+k−2​c0)=0k(1+k-2c_{0})=0. We discard the abelian case k=0k=0 to eliminate the linearity of g⁡(y)g(y). For the choice c0=(1+k)/2c_{0}=(1+k)/2 (k≠−1k\neq-1) we find

g⁡(y)=14​[C1​y(1−3​k)/(1+k)+(1−k2)​y].g(y)=\frac{1}{4}[C_{1}y^{(1-3k)/(1+k)}+(1-k^{2})y].

Compare this result with (157). When k=±i​κk=\pm i\kappa, we can replace g⁡(y)g(y) by g⁡(y)=C2​y−3+(κ2/4)​yg(y)=C_{2}y^{-3}+(\kappa^{2}/4)y and we then have

Remark 4.18.

The special case γ=2\gamma=2, k=−1/5k=-1/5 and F⁡(y)=y⁡(y−6/25)F(y)=y(y-6/25) of (157) deserves a special attention, because this relates, up to a scaling of yy, to the travelling-wave solutions of Fisher’s equation (or nonlinear reaction-diffusion equation)

ut=ux​x+a​u​(1−u).u_{t}=u_{xx}+au(1-u). (198)

This equation originated in 1936 to model the propagation of a gene in a population. Notice that under the change of variable u→1−uu\to 1-u, the parameter aa changes sign. The corresponding travelling-wave solutions are then reduced to integrating the second order ODE r′′​(s)=r2r^{\prime\prime}(s)=r^{2}. The general solution of this equation is r=℘⁡(s/6+a,0,g3)r=\wp(s/\sqrt{6}+a;0,g_{3}), where a,g3a,g_{3} are arbitrary constants. Here ℘⁡(s,g2,g3)\wp(s;g_{2},g_{3}) is the Weierstrass ℘\wp function with invariants g2g_{2} and g3g_{3}.

Changing to the original variables using s=−5​ex/5s=-5e^{x/5}, r=ye−2x/5r=ye^{-2x/5} from (158), for g3≠0g_{3}\neq 0, the solutions can be written as

y⁡(x)=e2​x/5​℘​(56​ex/5+a,0,g3).y(x)=e^{2x/5}\wp\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{6}}e^{x/5}+a;0,g_{3}\right). (199)

We note that ℘\wp is an even function since g2=0g_{2}=0 and g3g_{3} is arbitrary. They are doubly periodic with an infinite number of poles on the real axis. The solutions of biological interest are obtained for g3=0g_{3}=0. Using the fact that ℘⁡(s,0,0)=s−2\wp(s;0,0)=s^{-2} we find

y(x)=[56+ae−x/5]−2y(x)=\left[\frac{5}{\sqrt{6}}+ae^{-x/5}\right]^{-2}

satisfying the boundary conditions limx→∞y⁡(x)=6/25\lim_{x\to\infty}y(x)=6/25 and limx→−∞y⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to-\infty}y(x)=0. In [1], it was shown that for the special wave speed c=5/6c=5/\sqrt{6}, for which the Fisher’s equation passes the necessary condition to be of Painlevé type (we already discussed this constraint on page 4.11 as a condition of integrability by quadratures), can be reduced to the canonical form r′′=6​r2r^{\prime\prime}=6r^{2} by a transformation of the independent and dependent variables of the form y⁡(x)=f⁡(x)​r​(s)y(x)=f(x)r(s), s=h⁡(x)s=h(x) with ff and hh appropriately chosen.

Another context in which γ=2\gamma=2 appears is the study of travelling solutions of the two-dimensional Korteweg–de Vries–Burgers (μ≠0\mu\neq 0) and Kadomtsev–Petviashvili (μ=0\mu=0) equations for the special quadratic nonlinearity F⁡(u)F(u) [9]. In this paper, factorization technique was applied to obtain solution (199).

We recall that the case γ=3\gamma=3, k=−1/3k=-1/3 corresponds to the travelling wave solutions for the Newell–Whitehead–Segel equation. The rectifying transformation is r=−3​ex/3r=-3e^{x/3}, s=e−x/3ys=e^{-x/3}y.

5 Group-invariant solutions

One of the main applications of the notion of symmetry group to PDEs is to construct group-invariant solutions. Suppose that GG is a symmetry group of the system (11). A solution u=f⁡(x)u=f(x) is called group-invariant if g.f=fg.f=f for all g∈Gg\in G. This means that a group-invariant solution does not change under the symmetry group transformations. For example, if GG is the group of rotations in the space of independent variables xx, then a solution invariant under GG will be a function of the radius alone in the form u=F⁡(|x|)u=F(|x|). Travelling wave solutions are solutions invariant under the group of translations. Self-similar (or similarity) solutions that frequently arise in applications correspond to scaling symmetries.

Theorem 5.1.

Suppose that the symmetry group GG acts on the space of independent and dependent variables E=X×UE=X\times U and sweeps out generic orbits of dimension dd and of codimension p+q−dp+q-d (the number of functionally independent invariants of the group GG). Then all the group-invariant solutions to 𝖤=0\mathsf{E}=0 can be found by solving a reduced system of differential equations 𝖤/G=0\mathsf{E}/G=0 in dd fewer independent variables.

For example, if we have a system of partial differential equations in two independent variables, then the solutions invariant under a one-parameter symmetry group can all be found by integrating a system of ordinary differential equations.

Reduction in the number of independent variables will be possible if the orbit dimension dd satisfies the inequality p≤dp\leq d. When d=pd=p, the reduced system 𝖤/G=0\mathsf{E}/G=0 is a system of algebraic equations, while if d>pd>p there are no group-invariant solutions. In particular, if d=p−1d=p-1 we have a system of ODEs.

Let G be a local Lie group of transformations with infinitesimal generators 𝐯1,…,𝐯r\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r}, and the associated characteristics Q1,…,QrQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{r}. Then a function is invariant under GG if and only if it is a solution to the system of quasilinear first order partial differential equations characterizing the functions invariant under GG

Qα,l(x,u(1))=0,α=1,2,…,q,l=1,2,…,r.Q_{\alpha,l}(x,u^{(1)})=0,\quad\alpha=1,2,\ldots,q,\quad l=1,2,\ldots,r. (200)

The group-invariant solution thus will satisfy both the original system together with the invariance constraints (200), which form an overdetermined system of PDEs. The method of symmetry reduction consists of solving (200) in terms of invariant coordinates and substituting these into the original system. In the final step all non-invariant coordinates will drop out of the resulting reduced system. What remains to derive group-invariant solutions is to solve the reduced system depending on fewer independent variables.

Given a solution invariant under a subgroup HH of the full symmetry group GG of a system, it can be transformed to other group-invariant solutions by elements g∈Gg\in G not in the subgroup HH. Two group-invariant solutions are called inequivalent if one can not be transformed to the other by some group transformation g∈Gg\in G. The corresponding reduced systems also have to be inequivalent. Two subgroups which are conjugate under the symmetry group GG will produce equivalent reduced systems (systems connected with a transformation in the symmetry group).

Let H⊂GH\subset G be a ss-parameter subgroup. If u=f⁡(x)u=f(x) is a solution invariant under HH and g∈Gg\in G is any other group element, then the transformed function u=f~​(x)=g.f​(x)u=\tilde{f}(x)=g.f(x) is a solution invariant under the conjugate subgroup Kg​(H)=g.H.g−1K_{g}(H)=g.H.g^{-1}.

For example, the stationary solutions u=f⁡(x)u=f(x) of an evolution equation such as heat equation and KdV (Korteweg–de Vries) equation invariant under Galilean group 𝐯b\mathbf{v}_{b} can be conjugated by the Galilean boosts e−c​𝐯b​∂tec​𝐯be^{-c\mathbf{v}_{b}}\partial_{t}e^{c\mathbf{v}_{b}} to map to travelling wave solutions u=f⁡(x−c​t)u=f(x-ct) and vice versa.

So the collection of all group-invariant solutions are partitioned into equivalence classes. If 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is the Lie algebra of GG, we are interested in obtaining a representative list of subalgebras of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} (also called an optimal system of subalgebras) such that every subalgebra of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is conjugate to precisely one algebra in the list and no two subalgebras in the list are conjugate. Two algebras 𝔤\mathfrak{g} and 𝔤′\mathfrak{g}^{\prime} are conjugate under GG if 𝔤=G​𝔤′​G−1\mathfrak{g}=G\mathfrak{g}^{\prime}G^{-1}. Consequently, the problem of classifying group-invariant solutions is completely tantamount to finding the optimal system of subalgebras. When this task has been finished, it is sufficient to construct only group-invariant solutions corresponding to these representative subalgebras in the list. All other solutions can be obtained by applying the symmetry transformations to the representative classes of solutions.

For a finite dimensional Lie algebra of dimension ≥2\geq 2, this is in general a complicated problem. If 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is a direct sum of two or more algebras, there is an algorithmic classification method [55, 42, 45], which is an adaptation to Lie algebras of the Goursat’s method for direct products of discrete groups. When 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is semidirect sum of two algebras, for example when 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is a Levi decomposition of a semi-simple algebra and its radical (maximal solvable ideal) a method has been proposed in [44] (see also [54]). In physical applications, one usually encounters with low-dimensional algebras as symmetry algebras. In such cases, subalgebras of real three- and four-dimensional Lie algebras [43] can be of great use in the classification of group-invariant solutions.

In the one-dimensional case, subalgebra classification problem is solved by using the adjoint transformations using the Baker–Campbell–Housedorff formula (or the Lie series)

Ad⁡(exp⁡(ε​𝐯))​𝐰=exp⁡(ε​𝐯)​𝐰​exp⁡(−ε​𝐯)=𝐰+ε⁡[𝐯,𝐰]+ε22!​[𝐯,[𝐯,𝐰]]+…,\Ad(\exp(\varepsilon\mathbf{v}))\mathbf{w}=\exp{(\varepsilon\mathbf{v})}\mathbf{w}\exp{(-\varepsilon\mathbf{v})}=\mathbf{w}+\varepsilon[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}]+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2!}[\mathbf{v},[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}]]+\ldots, (201)

where 𝐯,𝐰∈𝔤\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{g} and ε\varepsilon is the group parameter. This series terminates or can be easily summed up when the vector field 𝐯\mathbf{v} is a nilpotent element or generates a translation, rotation or scaling group. The basic idea is to take a general vector field 𝐯=span⁡{𝐯1,…,𝐯r}\mathbf{v}=\Span\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{v}_{r}\right\} in 𝔤\mathfrak{g} and to simplify it as much as possible using adjoint transformations.

Example 5.2.

We give an example of one-dimensional subalgebras for the simple algebra so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) with commutation relations

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=𝐯3,[𝐯3,𝐯1]=𝐯2,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=𝐯1.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=\mathbf{v}_{3},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{3},\mathbf{v}_{1}]=\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=\mathbf{v}_{1}.

and from the linearity of the adjoint transformation

𝐯′=Ad⁡(exp⁡(ε​𝐯2))​𝐯=a1′​𝐯1+a2′​𝐯2+a3′​𝐯3,\mathbf{v}^{\prime}=\Ad(\exp(\varepsilon\mathbf{v}_{2}))\mathbf{v}=a_{1}^{\prime}\mathbf{v}_{1}+a_{2}^{\prime}\mathbf{v}_{2}+a_{3}^{\prime}\mathbf{v}_{3},

where

a1′=a1​cos⁡ε+a3​sin⁡ε,a2′=a2,a3′=−a1​sin⁡ε+a3​cos⁡ε.a_{1}^{\prime}=a_{1}\cos\varepsilon+a_{3}\sin\varepsilon,\quad a_{2}^{\prime}=a_{2},\quad a_{3}^{\prime}=-a_{1}\sin\varepsilon+a_{3}\cos\varepsilon.

Note that a1′2+a2′2+a3′2=a12+a22+a32a_{1}^{\prime 2}+a_{2}^{\prime 2}+a_{3}^{\prime 2}=a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+a_{3}^{2} for any ε∈ℝ\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}. This means that the positive-definite function I⁡(𝐯)=a12+a22+a32>0I(\mathbf{v})=a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+a_{3}^{2}>0 (unless a1=a2=a3=0a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=0) is an invariant of the corresponding adjoint transformation. It can be seen that II is an invariant of the full adjoint action: I⁡(Adg⁡(𝐯))=I⁡(𝐯)I(\Ad_{g}(\mathbf{v}))=I(\mathbf{v}), g∈SO⁡(3,ℝ)g\in\Ort(3,\mathbb{R}), the Lie group of so⁡(3,ℝ)\ort(3,\mathbb{R}). If a3≠0a_{3}\neq 0, we can choose ε\varepsilon such that the coefficient a3′a_{3}^{\prime} is zero. So we may assume that a3=0a_{3}=0 and 𝐯=a1​𝐯1+a2​𝐯2\mathbf{v}=a_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}+a_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}. If a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0, we further conjugate this form of 𝐯\mathbf{v} by 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} (or equivalently apply an inner automorphism of the algebra) and find

𝐯′=Ad⁡(exp⁡(α​𝐯3))​𝐯=(a1​cos⁡α−a2​sin⁡α)​𝐯1+(a1​sin⁡α+a2​cos⁡α)​𝐯2.\mathbf{v}^{\prime}=\Ad(\exp(\alpha\mathbf{v}_{3}))\mathbf{v}=(a_{1}\cos\alpha-a_{2}\sin\alpha)\mathbf{v}_{1}+(a_{1}\sin\alpha+a_{2}\cos\alpha)\mathbf{v}_{2}.

The optimal system contains only one vector field 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}. Any solution invariant under the one-parameter group generated by 𝐯∈so⁡(3,ℝ)\mathbf{v}\in\ort(3,\mathbb{R}) is equivalent to a solution invariant under the group generated by 𝐯1\mathbf{v}_{1}.

The example of one-dimensional subalgebras of the sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) algebra can be found in [35, 38, 18]. For the subalgebra classification of the symmetry algebra of the heat equation, which will be needed in the following example, see for example [53, 54, 35].

Example 5.3.

We consider the diffusion equation with constant drift bb

ut=x​ux​x+b​ux,b>0.u_{t}=xu_{xx}+bu_{x},\quad b>0. (202)

As this equation contains a parameter the structure of its symmetry group will crucially depend on the parameter. The problem of determination of all possible symmetries can be regarded as a group classification problem. Let the symmetry group of (202) be generated by the vector fields

φt=Dt​Q+ξ​ux​t+τ​ut​t,φx=Dx​Q+ξ​ux​x+τ​ux​t,\varphi^{t}=D_{t}Q+\xi u_{xt}+\tau u_{tt},\quad\varphi^{x}=D_{x}Q+\xi u_{xx}+\tau u_{xt},

and

φx​x=Dx2​Q+ξ​ux​x​x+τ​ux​x​t.\varphi^{xx}=D_{x}^{2}Q+\xi u_{xxx}+\tau u_{xxt}.

Eliminating ux​xu_{xx} using 𝖤=0\mathsf{E}=0 and splitting with respect to the derivatives utu_{t}, uxu_{x}, ux​tu_{xt} we find that τx=τu=0\tau_{x}=\tau_{u}=0, ξu=0\xi_{u}=0 and φu​u=0\varphi_{uu}=0, which mean τ=τ⁡(t)\tau=\tau(t), ξ=ξ⁡(t,x)\xi=\xi(t,x), φ=ϕ⁡(t,x)​u+ψ⁡(t,x)\varphi=\phi(t,x)u+\psi(t,x). Using this information and setting equal to zero the coefficients of uu, utu_{t}, uxu_{x}, the determining system is simplified to

2​x​ξx−τ˙​x−ξ=0,x2​(ξx​x−2​ϕx)−x​ξt−b​x​ξx+b​ξ=0,2x\xi_{x}-\dot{\tau}x-\xi=0,\quad x^{2}(\xi_{xx}-2\phi_{x})-x\xi_{t}-bx\xi_{x}+b\xi=0, (204a)
ϕt=x​ϕx​x+b​ϕx,ψt=x​ψx​x+b​ψx.\phi_{t}=x\phi_{xx}+b\phi_{x},\quad\psi_{t}=x\psi_{xx}+b\psi_{x}. (204b)

ξ⁡(t,x)=f⁡(t)​x+τ˙​x.\xi(t,x)=f(t)\sqrt{x}+\dot{\tau}x.

4​x3/2​(2​ϕx+τ¨)+4​f˙​x+(1−2​b)​f=0,4x^{3/2}(2\phi_{x}+\ddot{\tau})+4\dot{f}x+(1-2b)f=0,

from which on integrating we have

ϕ⁡(t,x)=−14​[2​τ¨​x+4​f˙​x+(2​b−1)​fx]+g⁡(t).\phi(t,x)=-\frac{1}{4}\left[2\ddot{\tau}x+4\dot{f}\sqrt{x}+\frac{(2b-1)f}{\sqrt{x}}\right]+g(t).
