(2​b−1)​(2​b−3)​f=0,f¨=0,τ˙˙˙=0,b​τ¨+2​g˙=0.(2b-1)(2b-3)f=0,\quad\ddot{f}=0,\quad\dddot{\tau}=0,\quad b\ddot{\tau}+2\dot{g}=0. (205)

The last two equations specify τ\tau and gg as

τ⁡(t)=τ2​t2+τ1​t+τ0,g⁡(t)=−b2​τ˙+g0,\tau(t)=\tau_{2}t^{2}+\tau_{1}t+\tau_{0},\quad g(t)=-\frac{b}{2}\dot{\tau}+g_{0},

where τ2,τ1,τ0,g0\tau_{2},\tau_{1},\tau_{0},g_{0} are the integration constants. Finally, the last equation in (204b) decouples from the others, therefore we find that for any solution ψ⁡(t,x)\psi(t,x) of (202), the vector field 𝐯ψ=ψ∂u\mathbf{v}_{\psi}=\psi\partial_{u} gives rise to a symmetry, which simply reflects the superposition rule of the linear equations. Hereafter, we shall factor out this infinite-dimensional algebra. The constant g0g_{0} corresponds to the scaling symmetry 𝐯0=u∂u\mathbf{v}_{0}=u\partial_{u}. This means we can multiply solutions by constants. There are two cases to consider:

b∉{1/2,3/2}b\not\in\left\{1/2,3/2\right\} (f=0f=0): 𝐯\mathbf{v} depends on four integration constants. The symmetry algebra 𝔤4\mathfrak{g}_{4} is four-dimensional. A suitable basis is given by

𝐯1=∂t,𝐯2=t∂t+x∂x,𝐯3=t2∂t+2tx∂x−(x+bt)u∂u,𝐯0=u∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{3}=t^{2}\partial_{t}+2tx\partial_{x}-(x+bt)u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{0}=u\partial_{u}.\end{split} (206)

b∈{1/2,3/2}b\in\left\{1/2,3/2\right\} (f≠0f\neq 0): We have f⁡(t)=f1​t+f0f(t)=f_{1}t+f_{0}. The symmetry algebra 𝔤6\mathfrak{g}_{6} is six-dimensional. In this case, the basis (206) for b=1/2b=1/2 is extended by two additional elements

𝐯4=x∂x,𝐯5=t𝐯4−xu∂u,\mathbf{v}_{4}=\sqrt{x}\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=t\mathbf{v}_{4}-\sqrt{x}u\partial_{u}, (207)

and for b=3/2b=3/2 by the following two

𝐯4=x∂x−12​xu∂u,𝐯5=t𝐯4−xu∂u.\mathbf{v}_{4}=\sqrt{x}\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=t\mathbf{v}_{4}-\sqrt{x}u\partial_{u}. (208)

𝐯0\mathbf{v}_{0} is the center element of the symmetry algebra.

From the commutator table (2) we see that the algebra 𝔤4\mathfrak{g}_{4} has the structure of a direct sum 𝔤4=sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊕{𝐯0}\mathfrak{g}_{4}=\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\left\{\mathbf{v}_{0}\right\}, where sl⁡(2,ℝ)≃{𝐯1,𝐯2,𝐯3}\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\simeq\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}\right\}, whereas the algebra 𝔤6\mathfrak{g}_{6} has the semidirect sum structure 𝔤6=sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊎h⁡(1)\mathfrak{g}_{6}=\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\uplus\Heis(1), where h⁡(1)≃{𝐯0,𝐯4,𝐯5}\Heis(1)\simeq\left\{\mathbf{v}_{0},\mathbf{v}_{4},\mathbf{v}_{5}\right\} is the three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra with center 𝐯0\mathbf{v}_{0}. The symmetry algebra 𝔤6\mathfrak{g}_{6} is isomorphic to the well-known symmetry algebra of the constant coefficient heat equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx}. The existence of such an isomorphism is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for a point transformation Φ:(t,x,u)→(t~,x~,u~)\Phi:(t,x,u)\to(\tilde{t},\tilde{x},\tilde{u}) to exist, mapping equations into each other. Indeed, in the case of b=1/2b=1/2, there is a point transformation (not necessarily unique)

Φ:t~=−1t,x~=2​xt,u~=t​exp⁡(xt)​u,\Phi:\quad\tilde{t}=-\frac{1}{t},\quad\tilde{x}=\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{t},\quad\tilde{u}=\sqrt{t}\exp\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)u, (209)

and

Φ:t~=−1t,x~=2​xt,u~=t​x​exp⁡(xt)​u,\Phi:\quad\tilde{t}=-\frac{1}{t},\quad\tilde{x}=\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{t},\quad\tilde{u}=\sqrt{tx}\exp\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)u, (210)

if b=3/2b=3/2, mapping (202) to the first canonical form u~t~=u~x~​x~\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}. If b=1/2b=1/2, a simple change of space variable x~=2​x\tilde{x}=2\sqrt{x} alone also does the job.

Let b=3/2b=3/2. The pushforwards 𝐯~i=Φ∗​(𝐯i)\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{i}=\Phi_{*}(\mathbf{v}_{i}) of the vector fields 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}, i=0,…,5i=0,\ldots,5 of the algebra 𝔤6\mathfrak{g}_{6} via the map Φ\Phi are easily calculated:

𝐯~1=t2∂t+tx∂x−14(x2+2t)u∂u,𝐯~2=−(t∂t+x2∂x)+12𝐯~0,𝐯~3=∂t,𝐯~4=−(t∂x−x2u∂u),𝐯~5=∂x,𝐯~0=𝐯0=u∂u,\begin{split}&\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=t^{2}\partial_{t}+tx\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{4}(x^{2}+2t)u\partial_{u},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=-\left(t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{2}\partial_{x}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\\ &\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=\partial_{t},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=-\left(t\partial_{x}-\frac{x}{2}u\partial_{u}\right),\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{5}=\partial_{x},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{0}=\mathbf{v}_{0}=u\partial_{u},\end{split} (211)

where all coordinates should be replaced by tildes (written in the new coordinates). The Lie algebra 𝔤~\tilde{\mathfrak{g}} spanned by {𝐯~i}\left\{\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{i}\right\} is recognized to be the symmetry algebra of ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx}, having the Levi decomposition 𝔤~={𝐯~3,𝐯~2,𝐯~1}⊎{𝐯~5,𝐯~4,𝐯~0}≃sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊎h⁡(1)\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}=\left\{\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}\right\}\uplus\left\{\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{5},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{4},\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{0}\right\}\simeq\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\uplus\Heis(1). This can be verified by using the same steps of symmetry calculation done for Eq. (202).

For b=1/2b=1/2, the pushforwards 𝐯~i=Φ∗​(𝐯i)\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{i}=\Phi_{*}(\mathbf{v}_{i}) of the vector fields 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i}, i=0,1,2,…,5i=0,1,2,\ldots,5 of the algebra 𝔤6\mathfrak{g}_{6} spanned by (206)-(207) via the map Φ:(t,x,u)→(t,2​x,u)\Phi:(t,x,u)\to(t,2\sqrt{x},u) are exactly the basis vectors of the heat equation algebra:

𝐯~1=∂t,𝐯~2=t∂t+x2∂x,𝐯~3=t2∂t+xt∂x−14(x2+2t)𝐯0,𝐯~4=∂x,𝐯~5=t∂x−x2𝐯0,𝐯0=u∂u.\begin{split}&\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{2}=t\partial_{t}+\frac{x}{2}\partial_{x},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{3}=t^{2}\partial_{t}+xt\partial_{x}-\frac{1}{4}(x^{2}+2t)\mathbf{v}_{0},\\ &\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=\partial_{x},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{5}=t\partial_{x}-\frac{x}{2}\mathbf{v}_{0},\quad\mathbf{v}_{0}=u\partial_{u}.\end{split} (212)

The corresponding one-parameter symmetry groups are time translations, scaling in t,xt,x, projective (or inversional) transformation, Galilei boosts, space translations and scaling in uu, respectively.

In the case b∉{1/2,3/2}b\notin\left\{1/2,3/2\right\}, the equation transforms to the second canonical form

u~t~=u~x~​x~+μx~2​u~,μ=(2​b−1)​(2​b−3)4\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}+\frac{\mu}{\tilde{x}^{2}}\tilde{u},\qquad\mu=\frac{(2b-1)(2b-3)}{4} (213)

via the transformation

t~=t,x~=2​x,u=x(1−2​b)/4​u~,\tilde{t}=t,\quad\tilde{x}=2\sqrt{x},\quad u=x^{(1-2b)/4}\tilde{u},

admitting the symmetry algebra spanned by

𝐯1=∂t~,𝐯2=t~∂t~+x~2∂x~,𝐯3=t~2∂t~+t~x~∂x~−14(x~2+2t~)u~∂u~,𝐯0=u~∂u~.\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{\tilde{t}},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\tilde{t}\partial_{\tilde{t}}+\frac{\tilde{x}}{2}\partial_{\tilde{x}},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{3}=\tilde{t}^{2}\partial_{\tilde{t}}+\tilde{t}\tilde{x}\partial_{\tilde{x}}-\frac{1}{4}(\tilde{x}^{2}+2\tilde{t})\tilde{u}\partial_{\tilde{u}},\quad\mathbf{v}_{0}=\tilde{u}\partial_{\tilde{u}}.\end{split} (214)

We thus have given the identification of the symmetry algebras of two locally equivalent differential equations, (202) and ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx}. In general, two equivalent differential equations have isomorphic symmetry groups. If a differential equation with a symmetry gg is mapped to another one by a point transformation Φ\Phi, then g~=Φ⋅g⋅Φ−1\tilde{g}=\Phi\cdot g\cdot\Phi^{-1} is a symmetry of the second equation.

The well-known solutions of ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx} can be mapped to solutions of (202) when b=1/2,3/2b=1/2,3/2. We note that the given equation is also invariant under the discrete group of simultaneous time and space reflections: (t,x,u)→(−t,−x,u)(t,x,u)\to(-t,-x,u).

Symmetry group of the equation will now be used to derive explicit group-invariant solutions. We illustrate how to construct group-invariant fundamental solution of (202) for any value of bb using the most general element 𝐯=a0​𝐯0+a1​𝐯1+a2​𝐯2+a3​𝐯3\mathbf{v}=a_{0}\mathbf{v}_{0}+a_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}+a_{2}\mathbf{v}_{2}+a_{3}\mathbf{v}_{3} of the Lie algebra 𝔤4\mathfrak{g}_{4}. A fundamental solution K⁡(t,x,y)K(t,x;y) as distributions satisfies (202) with the initial condition limt↘0K⁡(t,x,y)=δ⁡(x−y)\lim_{t\searrow 0}K(t,x;y)=\delta(x-y), where δ⁡(x−y)\delta(x-y) is the Dirac distribution with singularity at yy. The initial condition puts the following restrictions on the coefficients of (203) (see [7, 8, 14, 15] for details)

τ⁡(0)=0,ξ⁡(0,y)=0,ϕ⁡(0,y)+τ˙​(0)+ξx​(0,y)=0.\tau(0)=0,\quad\xi(0,y)=0,\quad\phi(0,y)+\dot{\tau}(0)+\xi_{x}(0,y)=0. (215)

These conditions are satisfied by the vector field (a projective type symmetry)

𝐯=t2∂t+2tx∂x−(x−y+bt)u∂u.\mathbf{v}=t^{2}\partial_{t}+2tx\partial_{x}-(x-y+bt)u\partial_{u}. (216)

The fundamental solution will be looked for as a solution invariant the symmetry group generated by (216). Its invariants are found by solving the invariance condition Q⁡(x,t,u,ut,ux)=φ−τ​ut−ξ​ux=0Q(x,t,u,u_{t},u_{x})=\varphi-\tau u_{t}-\xi u_{x}=0 as η=x/t2\eta=x/t^{2}, ζ=u​tb​exp⁡[(x+y)/t]\zeta=ut^{b}\exp[(x+y)/t]. The group-invariant solution has the form

u=t−b​exp⁡{−x+yt}​F​(η).u=t^{-b}\exp\left\{-\frac{x+y}{t}\right\}F(\eta).

Substituting the above solution uu into (202) we find that FF satisfies

η​F′′+b​F′−y​F=0.\eta F^{\prime\prime}+bF^{\prime}-yF=0.

We note that this ODE is free of the non-invariant coordinates. The solution FF, which is bounded near zero is given by

F=(ηy)(1−b)/2​Ib−1​(2​y​η),F=\left(\frac{\eta}{y}\right)^{(1-b)/2}I_{b-1}(2\sqrt{y\eta}),

where IνI_{\nu} denotes the usual modified Bessel function of the first kind and order ν\nu. We recall the following asymptotic relations for small values of xx

Iν∼12ν​ν!​xν,I−ν∼2ν(−ν)!​x−ν,ν∉ℤ.I_{\nu}\sim\frac{1}{2^{\nu}\nu!}x^{\nu},\quad I_{-\nu}\sim\frac{2^{\nu}}{(-\nu)!}x^{-\nu},\quad\nu\not\in\mathbb{Z}.

We thus have constructed the following fundamental solution, up to a nonzero multiplicative constant CC,

K⁡(t,x,y)=Ct​(xy)1−b2​exp⁡{−x+yt}​Ib−1​(2​x​yt).K(t,x;y)=\frac{C}{t}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{\frac{1-b}{2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{x+y}{t}\right\}I_{b-1}\left(\frac{2\sqrt{xy}}{t}\right).

The value of CC is determined from the normalization condition.

The special case b=1/2b=1/2 with C=π−1/2C=\pi^{-1/2} produces the elementary solution

K⁡(t,x,y)=1π​t​y​exp⁡{−x+yt}​cosh⁡(2​x​yt).K(t,x;y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi ty}}\exp\left\{-\frac{x+y}{t}\right\}\cosh\left(\frac{2\sqrt{xy}}{t}\right). (217)

Translation along tt gives the full heat kernel K⁡(t,x,t0,x0)=K⁡(t−t0,x,x0)K(t,x;t_{0},x_{0})=K(t-t_{0},x;x_{0}).

Similarly, in the case b=3/2b=3/2 with C=π−1/2C=\pi^{-1/2}, KK is again elementary

K⁡(t,x,y)=1π​t​x​exp⁡{−x+yt}​sinh⁡(2​x​yt).K(t,x;y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi tx}}\exp\left\{-\frac{x+y}{t}\right\}\sinh\left(\frac{2\sqrt{xy}}{t}\right). (218)

Both fundamental solutions satisfy the normalization condition

∫0∞K⁡(0,x,y)​𝑑x=1.\int_{0}^{\infty}K(0,x;y)dx=1.

We remark that solutions (217)-(218) can be recovered using the transformations (209)-(210) and the separable solutions (solutions invariant under 𝐯~3+y​𝐯0\mathbf{\tilde{v}}_{3}+y\mathbf{v}_{0}, y>0y>0 a parameter)

u~​(t~,x~)=C​ey​t~​{cosh⁡(y​x~),sinh⁡(y​x~),\tilde{u}(\tilde{t},\tilde{x})=Ce^{y\tilde{t}}\begin{cases}\cosh(\sqrt{y}\,\tilde{x}),&\\ \sinh(\sqrt{y}\,\tilde{x}),&\end{cases}

of the heat equation u~t~=u~x~​x~\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}.

In the case when b≠1/2,3/2b\neq 1/2,3/2, group-invariant solutions can be derived using the one dimensional subalgebras (an optimal system of subalgebras) of the algebra 𝔤4\mathfrak{g}_{4} (see (256)).

Now let us look at the action of a subgroup, say 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} of (206), on the solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x), exp⁡{ε​𝐯3}​u​(t,x)\exp\left\{\varepsilon\mathbf{v}_{3}\right\}u(t,x). We find by exponentiating 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} the group action generated by 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3}

u~ε​(t,x)=(1+ε​t)−b​exp⁡{−ε​x1+ε​t}​u​(x(1+ε​t)2,t1+ε​t).\tilde{u}_{\varepsilon}(t,x)=(1+\varepsilon t)^{-b}\exp\left\{\frac{-\varepsilon x}{1+\varepsilon t}\right\}u\left(\frac{x}{(1+\varepsilon t)^{2}},\frac{t}{1+\varepsilon t}\right). (219)

Formula (219) states that if u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is a solution of (202), then u~ε​(t,x)\tilde{u}_{\varepsilon}(t,x) is also a solution. Simple solutions like stationary (time-independent) solutions can be mapped to new solutions. A stationary solution u⁡(x)u(x) satisfies the linear ODE x​ux​x+b​ux=0xu_{xx}+bu_{x}=0 with two-parameter solution u⁡(x)=c0+c1​x1−bu(x)=c_{0}+c_{1}x^{1-b} if b≠1b\neq 1, and u⁡(x)=c0+c1​ln⁡xu(x)=c_{0}+c_{1}\ln x if b=1b=1. They get mapped to the following new solutions, respectively:

uε(t,x)=(1+εt)−bexp{−ε​x1+ε​t}[c0+c1(1+εt)2​(b−1)x1−b],b≠1,uε(t,x)=(1+εt)−1exp{−ε​x1+ε​t}[c0+c1logx1+ε​t],b=1.\begin{split}&u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)=(1+\varepsilon t)^{-b}\exp\left\{\frac{-\varepsilon x}{1+\varepsilon t}\right\}\left[c_{0}+c_{1}(1+\varepsilon t)^{2(b-1)}x^{1-b}\right],\quad b\neq 1,\\ &u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)=(1+\varepsilon t)^{-1}\exp\left\{\frac{-\varepsilon x}{1+\varepsilon t}\right\}\left[c_{0}+c_{1}\log\frac{\sqrt{x}}{1+\varepsilon t}\right],\quad b=1.\end{split} (220)

The remaining symmetry group of translation in tt and scaling in tt and xx: (t,x)→(λ⁡(t+t0),λ​x)(t,x)\to(\lambda(t+t_{0}),\lambda x) can be applied to these solutions to obtain new ones depending on two more group parameters t0,λt_{0},\lambda (solutions invariant under the group SL⁡(2,ℝ)\SL(2,\mathbb{R})).

Example 5.4.

([24]) A tricky classification problem for the generalized Fokker–Planck–Kolmogorov equation with a varying coefficient

ut−ux​x+p⁡(x)​uy=0.u_{t}-u_{xx}+p(x)u_{y}=0. (221)

We assume that pp is not constant, otherwise by a simple change of variable u=U⁡(t,x,z),z=t−p−1​yu=U(t,x,z),z=t-p^{-1}y, it would be equivalent to the heat equation Ut=Ux​xU_{t}=U_{xx}. The special case p⁡(x)=xp(x)=x is known as the celebrated Kolmogorov equation. In the sequel we shall show that in this case the Lie point symmetry group is maximal.

The general element of the symmetry algebra is written in the form

𝐯=τ(t,x,y,u)∂t+ξ(t,x,y,u)∂x+η(t,x,y,u)∂y+φ(t,x,y,u)∂u.\mathbf{v}=\tau(t,x,y,u)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u}. (222)

The linearized symmetry condition

φt−φx​x+p′​(x)​ξ​uy+p⁡(x)​φy=0\varphi^{t}-\varphi^{xx}+p^{\prime}(x)\xi u_{y}+p(x)\varphi^{y}=0

should be satisfied on solutions. Here φt,φx​x,φy\varphi^{t},\varphi^{xx},\varphi^{y} are the coefficients in the appropriate prolongation of 𝐯\mathbf{v}

φt=Dt​Q+τ​ut​t+ξ​ut​x+η​ut​y,φy=Dy​Q+τ​uy​t+ξ​uy​x+η​uy​y,\varphi^{t}=D_{t}Q+\tau u_{tt}+\xi u_{tx}+\eta u_{ty},\quad\varphi^{y}=D_{y}Q+\tau u_{yt}+\xi u_{yx}+\eta u_{yy},
φx​x=Dx2​Q+τ​ux​x​t+ξ​ux​x​x+η​ux​x​y,\varphi^{xx}=D^{2}_{x}Q+\tau u_{xxt}+\xi u_{xxx}+\eta u_{xxy},

where Q=φ−τ​ut−ξ​ux−η​uyQ=\varphi-\tau u_{t}-\xi u_{x}-\eta u_{y} is the characteristic function.

We find it more convenient to substitute utu_{t} from (221), rather than ux​xu_{xx} as was done in the previous example. The coefficients of the terms involving ux​x​xu_{xxx} imply that

τ=τ⁡(t,y),ξ=ξ⁡(t,x,y),η=η⁡(t,y),φ=f⁡(t,x,y)​u+g⁡(t,x,y).\tau=\tau(t,y),\quad\xi=\xi(t,x,y),\quad\eta=\eta(t,y),\quad\varphi=f(t,x,y)u+g(t,x,y).

From the linearity of the equation we a priori know that gg must solve the equation. Using this simplification and setting the coefficients of the terms ux​x,uy,uxu_{xx},u_{y},u_{x}, and uu equal to zero lead to the overdetermined system of homogeneous linear PDEs

2​ξx−τt−p​τy=0,ξ​p′+p2​τy−ηt+p⁡(τt−ηy)=0,ξt−ξx​x+p​ξy+2​fx=0,ft−fx​x+p​fy=0.\begin{split}&2\xi_{x}-\tau_{t}-p\tau_{y}=0,\\ &\xi p^{\prime}+p^{2}\tau_{y}-\eta_{t}+p(\tau_{t}-\eta_{y})=0,\\ &\xi_{t}-\xi_{xx}+p\xi_{y}+2f_{x}=0,\\ &f_{t}-f_{xx}+pf_{y}=0.\end{split} (223)

Inspection of the determining system (223) suggests that while the principal symmetry algebra 𝔤0\mathfrak{g}_{0} (valid for any pp) is obvious

𝔤0={𝐯1,𝐯2,𝐯3,𝐯4}={∂t,∂y,u∂u,g∂u},\mathfrak{g}_{0}=\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3},\mathbf{v}_{4}\right\}=\left\{\partial_{t},\partial_{y},u\partial_{u},g\partial_{u}\right\}, (224)

where gg is a solution of (221), it is not straightforward to obtain a classifying equation for pp. To remedy this situation we pass to use the equivalence group and algebra of the equation. It is quite simple to find the equivalence transformations (including the discrete ones) for a linear equation as such and is given by

t~=α2t+t0,x~=αx+x0,y~=βy+δt+y0,u~=γu+ρ(t,x),p~=α−2​(β​p+δ),\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=\alpha^{2}t+t_{0},\quad\tilde{x}=\alpha x+x_{0},\quad\tilde{y}=\beta y+\delta t+y_{0},\quad\tilde{u}=\gamma u+\rho(t,x),\\ &\tilde{p}=\alpha^{-2}(\beta p+\delta),\end{split} (225)

where α,β,γ,δ,t0,x0,y0\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,t_{0},x_{0},y_{0} are parameters and ρ⁡(t,x)\rho(t,x) solves ρt−ρx​x=0\rho_{t}-\rho_{xx}=0. The continuous part of this group is generated by the equivalence algebra 𝔤ℰ\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{E}} with basis

𝐞1=∂t,𝐞2=∂x,𝐞3=∂y,𝐞4=t∂y+∂p,𝐞5=y∂y+p∂p,𝐞6=t∂t+x∂x−2p∂p,𝐞7=u∂u,𝐞8=ρ(t,x)∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{e}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{e}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{e}_{3}=\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{e}_{4}=t\partial_{y}+\partial_{p},\quad\mathbf{e}_{5}=y\partial_{y}+p\partial_{p},\\ &\mathbf{e}_{6}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}-2p\partial_{p},\quad\mathbf{e}_{7}=u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{e}_{8}=\rho(t,x)\partial_{u}.\end{split} (226)

Now the idea is to project the algebra 𝔤ℰ\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{E}} to the space (x,p)(x,p) so that we have 𝔤~ℰ=proj(x,p)⁡𝔤ℰ\tilde{\mathfrak{g}}_{\mathcal{E}}=\proj_{(x,p)}\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{E}} with basis

𝐞~2=∂x,𝐞~4=∂p,𝐞~5=p∂p,𝐞~6=x∂x−2p∂p.\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{4}=\partial_{p},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{5}=p\partial_{p},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{6}=x\partial_{x}-2p\partial_{p}. (227)

for all possible choices of the parameters c2,c4,c5,c6c_{2},c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}. The possible invariants result from the following combinations

𝐞(1)=x∂x+∂p,𝐞(2)=∂x+p∂p,𝐞(3)=x∂x+kp∂p,\mathbf{e}^{(1)}=x\partial_{x}+\partial_{p},\quad\mathbf{e}^{(2)}=\partial_{x}+p\partial_{p},\quad\mathbf{e}^{(3)}=x\partial_{x}+kp\partial_{p},

Remark 5.5.

In general, the time independent solutions of (221) satisfy the heat equation with diffusivity a⁡(x)=1/p⁡(x)a(x)=1/p(x) (yy plays the role of time)

Uy=a⁡(x)​Ux​x.U_{y}=a(x)U_{xx}.

It can be shown that such an equation is equivalent to the standard one by a point transformation if and only if a⁡(x)=(a2​x2+a1​x+a0)2a(x)=(a_{2}x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0})^{2} [14], which of course includes the case p=x−2p=x^{-2} discussed above.

Uy=x4​Ux​xU_{y}=x^{4}U_{xx} (236)

to the heat equation (233) is given by

U⁡(x,y)=x​V​(y,z),z=−1x.U(x,y)=xV(y,z),\quad z=-\frac{1}{x}.

A particular extension of the equation under study allowing power diffusivity

One can transform time independent solutions u=U⁡(x,y)u=U(x,y) of (237)

to new time dependent solutions using some appropriate subalgebra of the symmetry algebra.

where H⁡(t)H(t) is the Heaviside function and CC is a constant. This solution is invariant under the 4-dimensional subalgebra

𝐰1=3x02ty∂t−x02x(3tx+y)∂x+x02y2∂y+[1−x02x2−3x02tx−3x02y]u∂u,𝐰2=[3t(x0+5x03y)−y]∂t+[5x03y−x0x−(15x03t−1)x2]∂x++x0y(5x02y+2)∂y+[x−5​x02x2−15x03tx−15x03y]u∂u,𝐰3=12(3x0t−y)y∂t−x2[3x0tx+(x0−2x)y]∂x+x02y2∂y++12​x2[x−x0−3x0x2y+(2y−3x0t)x3]u∂u,𝐰4=𝐯8,\begin{split}&\mathbf{w}_{1}=3x_{0}^{2}ty\partial_{t}-x_{0}^{2}x(3tx+y)\partial_{x}+x_{0}^{2}y^{2}\partial_{y}+\left[1-\frac{x_{0}^{2}}{x^{2}}-3x_{0}^{2}tx-3x_{0}^{2}y\right]u\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{w}_{2}=[3t(x_{0}+5x_{0}^{3}y)-y]\partial_{t}+[5x_{0}^{3}y-x_{0}x-(15x_{0}^{3}t-1)x^{2}]\partial_{x}+\\ &\qquad+x_{0}y(5x_{0}^{2}y+2)\partial_{y}+\left[x-\frac{5x_{0}^{2}}{x^{2}}-15x_{0}^{3}tx-15x_{0}^{3}y\right]u\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{w}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}(3x_{0}t-y)y\partial_{t}-\frac{x}{2}[3x_{0}tx+(x_{0}-2x)y]\partial_{x}+\frac{x_{0}}{2}y^{2}\partial_{y}+\\ &\qquad+\frac{1}{2x^{2}}[x-x_{0}-3x_{0}x^{2}y+(2y-3x_{0}t)x^{3}]u\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{w}_{4}=\mathbf{v}_{8},\end{split} (240)

leaving invariant the PDE

Example 5.6.

The nonlinear diffusion (porous medium) equation

ut=u4​ux​xu_{t}=u^{4}u_{xx} (243)

is invariant under a five dimensional symmetry group generated by

𝐯1=∂t,𝐯2=∂x,𝐯3=2t∂t+x∂x,𝐯4=x∂x+u2∂u,𝐯5=x2∂x+xu∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=2t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{4}=x\partial_{x}+\frac{u}{2}\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{5}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+xu\partial_{u}.\end{split} (244)

u=t−1/4F(x)=±t−1/4(A+2Bx+Cx2)1/2,4(B2−AC)=1.u=t^{-1/4}F(x)=\pm t^{-1/4}(A+2Bx+Cx^{2})^{1/2},\quad 4(B^{2}-AC)=1.

We now consider the (2+1)-dimensional nonlinear Darboux equation

□​u+bt​ut+a​uk=0,\square u+\frac{b}{t}u_{t}+au^{k}=0, (245)

where a,b,ka,b,k are arbitrary real parameters and □=∂t2−Δ2=∂t2−∂x2−∂y2\square=\partial_{t}^{2}-\Delta_{2}=\partial_{t}^{2}-\partial_{x}^{2}-\partial_{y}^{2} is the wave (also called d’Alembert) operator in the (2+1)-dimensional Minkowski space with metric d​t2−d​x2−d​y2dt^{2}-dx^{2}-dy^{2}.

The linear wave equation □​u=0\square u=0 obtained for a=0a=0, b=0b=0 (see Example 2.43 of [35]) is known to be invariant under the ten-dimensional conformal group Conf⁡(ℝ1,2)\conf(\mathbb{R}^{1,2}) of the pseudo-Euclidean space ℝ1,2\mathbb{R}^{1,2}. A suitable basis of the corresponding Lie algebra (conformal algebra) is given by the seven elements of the Poincaré-similitude subalgebra

𝐩t=∂t,𝐩x=∂x,𝐩y=∂y,𝐤x​t=t∂x+x∂t,𝐤y​t=t∂y+y∂t,𝐣x​y=y∂x−x∂y,𝐝=t∂t+x∂x+y∂y,\begin{split}&\mathbf{p}_{t}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{p}_{x}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{p}_{y}=\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{k}_{xt}=t\partial_{x}+x\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{k}_{yt}=t\partial_{y}+y\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{j}_{xy}=y\partial_{x}-x\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{d}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y},\end{split} (246)

plus the three conformal generators

𝐜t=(x2+y2+t2)∂t+2xt∂x+2yt∂y−tu∂u,𝐜x=2xt∂t+(t2+x2−y2)∂x+2xy∂y−xu∂u,𝐜y=2yt∂t+2xy∂x+(t2−x2+y2)∂y−yu∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{c}_{t}=(x^{2}+y^{2}+t^{2})\partial_{t}+2xt\partial_{x}+2yt\partial_{y}-tu\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{c}_{x}=2xt\partial_{t}+(t^{2}+x^{2}-y^{2})\partial_{x}+2xy\partial_{y}-xu\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{c}_{y}=2yt\partial_{t}+2xy\partial_{x}+(t^{2}-x^{2}+y^{2})\partial_{y}-yu\partial_{u}.\end{split} (247)

Eq. (245) can be viewed as a special case of the nonlinear perturbation of the singular operator □+(b/t)∂t=0\square+(b/t)\partial_{t}=0

□​u+bt​ut+f⁡(t,u)=0.\square u+\frac{b}{t}u_{t}+f(t,u)=0. (248)

In this case the symmetry gets considerably reduced:

𝐩x=∂x,𝐩y=∂y,𝐣x​y=y∂x−x∂y.\mathbf{p}_{x}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{p}_{y}=\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{j}_{xy}=y\partial_{x}-x\partial_{y}. (249)

In the special case f⁡(t,u)=f⁡(u)f(t,u)=f(u), invariance under the dilation

𝐝=t∂t+x∂x+y∂y+qu∂u,q=21−k,k≠1\mathbf{d}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+y\partial_{y}+qu\partial_{u},\quad q=\frac{2}{1-k},\quad k\neq 1 (250)

restricts ff to f⁡(u)=a​ukf(u)=au^{k} and the corresponding equation becomes (245). With the condition k=(b+5)/(b+1)k=(b+5)/(b+1), b≠−1b\neq-1 (q=−(b+1)/2q=-(b+1)/2), it admits further the following two conformal transformations

𝐜x=2xt∂t+(t2+x2−y2)∂x+2xy∂y−(b+1)xu∂u,𝐜y=2yt∂t+2xy∂x+(t2−x2+y2)∂y−(b+1)yu∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{c}_{x}=2xt\partial_{t}+(t^{2}+x^{2}-y^{2})\partial_{x}+2xy\partial_{y}-(b+1)xu\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{c}_{y}=2yt\partial_{t}+2xy\partial_{x}+(t^{2}-x^{2}+y^{2})\partial_{y}-(b+1)yu\partial_{u}.\end{split} (251)

We comment that the singularly perturbed linear version of (248) with f⁡(t,u)=a​t−2​uf(t,u)=at^{-2}u preserves the same symmetry without any restriction on qq which can be taken zero. If, in addition, 2​b−b2+4​a=02b-b^{2}+4a=0 then there is an additional generator

𝐩t=∂t−b2​tu∂u,\mathbf{p}_{t}=\partial_{t}-\frac{b}{2t}u\partial_{u},

which is mapped to the translational vector field ∂t\partial_{t} by the transformation u=t−b/2vu=t^{-b/2}v and the new equation becomes the usual wave equation □​v=0\square v=0.

On the other hand, the maximal symmetry algebra of (245) is achieved when b=0b=0 (k=5k=5), which reduces to the Klein–Gordon equation (also called classical ϕ6\phi^{6}-field equation)

□​u=a​u5.\square u=au^{5}. (252)

Its symmetry algebra is precisely the 10-dimensional conformal algebra with basis given by (246)-(247), excluding the linearity reflecting symmetry.

The 1+1-dimensional linear variant of (245) is known as the Euler–Poisson–Darboux (EPD) equation:

ut​t+bt​ut−ux​x=0.u_{tt}+\frac{b}{t}u_{t}-u_{xx}=0. (253)

The values b=0,2b=0,2 are exceptional (Eq. is equivalent to the wave equation as mentioned above. See (35) for its symmetry algebra). The EPD equation admits a four-dimensional symmetry algebra with basis ([30])

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=t∂t+x∂x,𝐯3=2tx∂t+(x2+t2)∂x−bxu∂u,𝐯4=u∂u.\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{3}=2tx\partial_{t}+(x^{2}+t^{2})\partial_{x}-bxu\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=u\partial_{u}.\end{split} (254)

The non-zero commutation relations are

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=𝐯1,[𝐯1,𝐯3]=2​𝐯2,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=𝐯3.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=2\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=\mathbf{v}_{3}. (255)

The symmetry algebra has the direct-sum structure 𝔤=sl⁡(2,ℝ)⊕{𝐯4}\mathfrak{g}=\Sl(2,\mathbb{R})\oplus\{\mathbf{v}_{4}\}.

The one-dimensional subalgebras of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} ([43]) are

{𝐯1},{𝐯4},{𝐯2+p​𝐯4},p≥0,{𝐯1+𝐯3+q​𝐯4},{𝐯1+ϵ​𝐯4},ϵ=±1,q∈ℝ.\begin{split}&\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\right\},\quad\left\{\mathbf{v}_{4}\right\},\quad\left\{\mathbf{v}_{2}+p\mathbf{v}_{4}\right\},\quad p\geq 0,\\ &\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1}+\mathbf{v}_{3}+q\mathbf{v}_{4}\right\},\quad\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1}+\epsilon\mathbf{v}_{4}\right\},\quad\epsilon=\pm 1,\quad q\in\mathbb{R}.\end{split} (256)

We can put ϵ=1\epsilon=1 by invariance under x→−xx\to-x. All solutions invariant under these subalgebras can be found by symmetry reduction technique [30]. For example, the solution corresponding to the subalgebra {𝐯𝟏+𝐯𝟒}\left\{\mathbf{v_{1}}+\mathbf{v_{4}}\right\} has the form u=ex​F​(t)u=e^{x}F(t), where F⁡(t)F(t) satisfies the ODE

t​F′′+b​F′−t​F=0tF^{\prime\prime}+bF^{\prime}-tF=0

with solution in terms of modified Bessel functions of the form

F(t)=t(1−b)/2I±(b−1)/2(t).F(t)=t^{(1-b)/2}I_{\pm(b-1)/2}(t).

For even integer bb, this solution is elementary.

Solution invariant under the third subalgebra admits the reduction formula u=(x−t)p​F​(τ)u=(x-t)^{p}F(\tau), τ=(x+t)/(x−t)\tau=(x+t)/(x-t). Substitution into the EPD equation gives the hypergeometric equation

τ⁡(1−τ)​F′′+[1−p−b2−(1−p+b2)​τ]​F′+b​p2​F=0.\tau(1-\tau)F^{\prime\prime}+\left[1-p-\frac{b}{2}-\left(1-p+\frac{b}{2}\right)\tau\right]F^{\prime}+\frac{bp}{2}F=0. (257)

So the solution can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric function as

u=(x−t)p​F12​(−p,b2,1−p−b2,τ),1−p−b2∉ℤ≤0.u=(x-t)^{p}{}_{2}F_{1}\left(-p,\frac{b}{2},1-p-\frac{b}{2};\tau\right),\quad 1-p-\frac{b}{2}\not\in\mathbb{Z}^{\leq 0}.

Solutions invariant under {𝐯1+𝐯3}\left\{\mathbf{v}_{1}+\mathbf{v}_{3}\right\} will have the form u=t−b/2F(τ)u=t^{-b/2}F(\tau), τ=(1+x2−t2)/t\tau=(1+x^{2}-t^{2})/t where F⁡(τ)F(\tau) satisfies

(τ2+4)​F′′+2​τ​F′−b⁡(b−2)4​F=0.(\tau^{2}+4)F^{\prime\prime}+2\tau F^{\prime}-\frac{b(b-2)}{4}F=0.

The special cases b=0,2b=0,2 are trivially integrated. Otherwise, the general solution of this equation can be expressed in terms of Legendre functions with imaginary argument i​τ/2i\tau/2 and order (b−2)/2(b-2)/2, known as oblate spheroidal harmonics for τ>0\tau>0 and b=2​(n+1)b=2(n+1), n∈ℤ0n\in\mathbb{Z}^{0}.

The sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) invariance can be used to derive identities for hypergeometric and Bessel functions, and transformation formulas for other solutions of the EPD equation.

The symmetry group corresponding to 𝐯3\mathbf{v}_{3} is found by integrating the following Cauchy problem

dd​ϵ​t~​(t,x,ϵ)=2​t~​x~,dd​ϵ​x~​(t,x,ϵ)=t~2+x~2,dd​ϵ​u~​(t,x,ϵ)=−b​x~​u~\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\tilde{t}(t,x;\epsilon)=2\tilde{t}\tilde{x},\quad\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\tilde{x}(t,x;\epsilon)=\tilde{t}^{2}+\tilde{x}^{2},\quad\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\tilde{u}(t,x;\epsilon)=-b\tilde{x}\tilde{u} (258)

subject to the initial conditions t~​(t,x,0)=t\tilde{t}(t,x;0)=t, x~​(t,x,0)=x\tilde{x}(t,x;0)=x, u~​(t,x,0)=u\tilde{u}(t,x;0)=u. The first two equations written in canonical coordinates gives the translational group r~=r\tilde{r}=r and s~=s+ϵ\tilde{s}=s+\epsilon, where

r=tt2−x2,s=xt2−x2r=\frac{t}{t^{2}-x^{2}},\quad s=\frac{x}{t^{2}-x^{2}}

satisfying 𝐯3​(r)=0\mathbf{v}_{3}(r)=0, 𝐯3​(s)=1\mathbf{v}_{3}(s)=1. Solving for t~\tilde{t} and x~\tilde{x} we find the transformation of (t,x)(t,x):

t~=t1−2​ϵ​x−ϵ2​(t2−x2),x~=x+ϵ⁡(t2−x2)1−2​ϵ​x−ϵ2​(t2−x2).\tilde{t}=\frac{t}{1-2\epsilon x-\epsilon^{2}(t^{2}-x^{2})},\quad\tilde{x}=\frac{x+\epsilon(t^{2}-x^{2})}{1-2\epsilon x-\epsilon^{2}(t^{2}-x^{2})}.

Finally integrating the last equation in (258) we find

u~=σ​(t,x,ϵ)b/2​u,σ⁡(t,x,ϵ)=1−2​ϵ​x−ϵ2​(t2−x2).\tilde{u}=\sigma(t,x;\epsilon)^{b/2}u,\quad\sigma(t,x;\epsilon)=1-2\epsilon x-\epsilon^{2}(t^{2}-x^{2}).

The factor σ\sigma has the property σ⁡(t,x,ϵ)=σ​(t~,x~,−ϵ)−1\sigma(t,x;\epsilon)=\sigma(\tilde{t},\tilde{x};-\epsilon)^{-1}. The symmetry group action on a solution U⁡(t,x)U(t,x) induces the transformation formula for solutions

u(t,x)=σ(t,x;−ϵ)−b/2U(tσ⁡(t,x,−ϵ),x−ϵ⁡(t2−x2)σ⁡(t,x,−ϵ)).u(t,x)=\sigma(t,x;-\epsilon)^{-b/2}U\left(\frac{t}{\sigma(t,x;-\epsilon)},\frac{x-\epsilon(t^{2}-x^{2})}{\sigma(t,x;-\epsilon)}\right).

In Ref. [30], transformations leaving EPD equation invariant but changing the parameter bb to derive a variety of generating functions for the standard hypergeometric functions F12{}_{2}F_{1} were also considered.

The Euler–Darboux (ED) equation

uξ​η+1ξ+η​(α​uξ+β​uη)=0u_{\xi\eta}+\frac{1}{\xi+\eta}(\alpha u_{\xi}+\beta u_{\eta})=0 (259)

includes the EPD equation (253) as a special case. This equation has important applications in aerodynamics. The change of coordinates ξ=t+x\xi=t+x, η=t−x\eta=t-x transforms (253) to (259) with α=β=b/2\alpha=\beta=b/2. Eq. (259) for α=β=N∈ℤ\alpha=\beta=N\in\mathbb{Z} admits a general solution

u⁡(ξ,η)=∂N−1∂ξN−1​f⁡(ξ)ξ+η+∂N−1∂ηN−1​g⁡(η)ξ+η,u(\xi,\eta)=\frac{\partial^{N-1}}{\partial\xi^{N-1}}\frac{f(\xi)}{\xi+\eta}+\frac{\partial^{N-1}}{\partial\eta^{N-1}}\frac{g(\eta)}{\xi+\eta}, (260)

where ff and gg are arbitrary functions. This implies that the general solution of (253) can be obtained for b=2​Nb=2N. For example, for N=1N=1 (b=2b=2), the d’Alembert solution of the radial wave equation is obtained

u=f⁡(ξ)+g⁡(η)ξ+η=12​t​(f⁡(t+x)+g⁡(t−x)).u=\frac{f(\xi)+g(\eta)}{\xi+\eta}=\frac{1}{2t}(f(t+x)+g(t-x)).

A basis for the symmetry algebra of (259) is

𝐯1=∂ξ−∂η,𝐯2=ξ∂ξ+η∂η−(α+β)2u∂u,𝐯3=ξ2∂ξ−η2∂η−(βξ−αη)u∂u,𝐯4=u∂u\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{\xi}-\partial_{\eta},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\xi\partial_{\xi}+\eta\partial_{\eta}-\frac{(\alpha+\beta)}{2}u\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{3}=\xi^{2}\partial_{\xi}-\eta^{2}\partial_{\eta}-(\beta\xi-\alpha\eta)u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=u\partial_{u}\end{split} (261)

with the same non-zero commutation relations (255). The EPD and ED equations have isomorphic symmetry algebras. For values α=β≠2​N\alpha=\beta\not=2N, we have symmetry methods at our disposal for producing exact solutions of the ED equation.

A complete classification of group invariant solutions of (252) would go far beyond the scope of these notes. Instead, we will focus on the solutions invariant under one-parameter subgroup generated by the conformal elements

𝐜=α0​𝐜t+α1​𝐜x+α2​𝐜y,\mathbf{c}=\alpha_{0}\mathbf{c}_{t}+\alpha_{1}\mathbf{c}_{x}+\alpha_{2}\mathbf{c}_{y},

where α0,α1,α2\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} are arbitrary parameters. Invariance under this subalgebra leads to the reduction formula

u=r−1​f​(ξ),ξ=r−2​(β0​t+β1​x+β2​y),r2=t2−x2−y2u=r^{-1}f(\xi),\quad\xi=r^{-2}(\beta_{0}t+\beta_{1}x+\beta_{2}y),\quad r^{2}=t^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2} (262)

with the constraint among the parameters

β0​α0−β1​α1−β2​α2=0.\beta_{0}\alpha_{0}-\beta_{1}\alpha_{1}-\beta_{2}\alpha_{2}=0.

Substitution of (262) into (252) gives the second order ODE

β2​f′′=a​f5,β2=β02−β12−β22≠0,\beta^{2}f^{\prime\prime}=af^{5},\qquad\beta^{2}=\beta_{0}^{2}-\beta_{1}^{2}-\beta_{2}^{2}\neq 0, (263)

which has the first integral

f′2=a3​β2​(f6+c).f^{\prime 2}=\frac{a}{3\beta^{2}}(f^{6}+c).

A further change of the dependent variable f=F−1/2f=F^{-1/2} simplifies it to

F′2=4​a3​β2​(c​F3+1),F^{\prime 2}=\frac{4a}{3\beta^{2}}(cF^{3}+1),

whose solution for c≠0c\neq 0 can be expressed in terms of Weierstrass ℘\wp function as

F=℘⁡(z,0,g3),z=a​c3​β2​(ξ+ξ0),g3=−4​c−1.F=\wp(z;0,g_{3}),\quad z=\sqrt{\frac{ac}{3\beta^{2}}}(\xi+\xi_{0}),\quad g_{3}=-4c^{-1}.

In addition to the invariant solutions, the subgroup action on solutions obtained through the exponentiation exp⁡{ε0​𝐜t+ε1​𝐜x+ε2​𝐜y}\exp\left\{\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{c}_{t}+\varepsilon_{1}\mathbf{c}_{x}+\varepsilon_{2}\mathbf{c}_{y}\right\} can be utilized to derive a formula for the transformation of solutions. More precisely, whenever U⁡(𝐫)=U⁡(t,x,y)U(\mathbf{r})=U(t,x,y) is a solution to (252), so is

u(𝐫)=σ−1/2U(𝐫~),σ(𝐫;𝜺)=1−2𝜺.𝐫+ε2r2,𝐫~=σ−1(𝐫−r2𝜺),𝐫=(t,x,y),u({\bf r})=\sigma^{-1/2}U({\bf\tilde{r}}),\quad\sigma(\mathbf{r};\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=1-2{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}.{\bf r}+\varepsilon^{2}r^{2},\quad\tilde{\bf r}=\sigma^{-1}({\bf r}-r^{2}{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}),\quad{\bf r}=(t,x,y),

where 𝜺=(ε0,ε1,ε2)\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}=(\varepsilon_{0},\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}) is the vector of group parameters, r2=t2−x2−y2r^{2}=t^{2}-x^{2}-y^{2} and ε2=|𝜺|2=ε02+ε12+ε22\varepsilon^{2}=|\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}|^{2}=\varepsilon_{0}^{2}+\varepsilon_{1}^{2}+\varepsilon_{2}^{2}. Note the relation σ⁡(𝐫,𝜺)=σ​(𝐫~,−𝜺)−1\sigma(\mathbf{r};\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})=\sigma(\mathbf{\tilde{r}};-\boldsymbol{\varepsilon})^{-1}. The reader can compare the conformal transformations 𝐫~=σ−1​(𝐫−r2​𝜺)\tilde{\bf r}=\sigma^{-1}({\bf r}-r^{2}{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}) of the ℝ1,2\mathbb{R}^{1,2} space leaving its metric form invariant, d​𝐫~2=σ−2​d​𝐫2d\tilde{\mathbf{r}}^{2}=\sigma^{-2}d\mathbf{r}^{2}, with those of the Euclidean plane ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} given by (28)-(29).

Remark 5.8.

The (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional conformally invariant extension of Eq. (252) [10] is

□​u​(x)=ux0​x0−Δn​u=a​u(n+3)/(n−1),n≥2,\square u(x)=u_{x_{0}x_{0}}-\Delta_{n}u=au^{(n+3)/(n-1)},\quad n\geq 2, (264)

where Δn=∑μ=1nuxμ​xμ\Delta_{n}=\sum_{\mu=1}^{n}u_{x_{\mu}x_{\mu}} is the Laplace operator on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and x=(x0,x1,…,xn)∈ℝ1,nx=(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{1,n}. The symmetry algebra is (n+2)​(n+3)/2(n+2)(n+3)/2-dimensional conformal algebra of the conformal group Conf⁡(ℝ1,n)\conf(\mathbb{R}^{1,n}) with basis

𝐩μ=∂xμ,𝐝=∑μ=0nxμ∂xμ+1−n2u∂u,μ=0,1,2,…,n,𝐣μ​ν=xμ∂xν−xν∂xμ,𝐣0​ν=x0∂xν+xν∂x0,μ,ν=1,2,…,n𝐜μ=2xμ𝐝−εx2∂xμ+(1−n)xμu∂u,x2=x02−∑μ=1nxμ2,\begin{split}&\mathbf{p}_{\mu}=\partial_{x_{\mu}},\quad\mathbf{d}=\sum_{\mu=0}^{n}x_{\mu}\partial_{x_{\mu}}+\frac{1-n}{2}u\partial_{u},\quad\mu=0,1,2,\ldots,n,\\ &\mathbf{j}_{\mu\nu}=x_{\mu}\partial_{x_{\nu}}-x_{\nu}\partial_{x_{\mu}},\quad\mathbf{j}_{0\nu}=x_{0}\partial_{x_{\nu}}+x_{\nu}\partial_{x_{0}},\quad\mu,\nu=1,2,\ldots,n\\ &\mathbf{c}_{\mu}=2x_{\mu}\mathbf{d}-\varepsilon x^{2}\partial_{x_{\mu}}+(1-n)x_{\mu}u\partial_{u},\quad x^{2}=x_{0}^{2}-\sum_{\mu=1}^{n}x_{\mu}^{2},\end{split} (265)

where ε=1\varepsilon=1 for μ=0\mu=0 and ε=−1\varepsilon=-1 for μ=1,2,…,n\mu=1,2,\ldots,n. The subalgebras spanned by the basis elements {𝐩μ,𝐣μ​ν,𝐣0​ν}\left\{\mathbf{p}_{\mu},\mathbf{j}_{\mu\nu},\mathbf{j}_{0\nu}\right\} and {𝐩μ,𝐣μ​ν,𝐣0​ν,𝐝}\left\{\mathbf{p}_{\mu},\mathbf{j}_{\mu\nu},\mathbf{j}_{0\nu},\mathbf{d}\right\} are called the Poincaré algebra of dimension (n+1)​(n+2)/2(n+1)(n+2)/2 and the similitude algebra of dimension (n2+3​n+4)/2(n^{2}+3n+4)/2, respectively.

5.1 Linearization by symmetry structure

We know that a linear differential equation or one that is linearizable by a point transformation admits an infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra. By checking the existence of such a symmetry structure we can construct linearizing transformations. A well-known example is the potential Burgers’ equation [35]

ut=ux​x+ux2,u_{t}=u_{xx}+u_{x}^{2}, (266)

admitting the infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra generated by the vector fields

𝐯1=∂x,𝐯2=∂t,𝐯3=∂x,𝐯4=2t∂x−x∂u,\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=2t\partial_{x}-x\partial_{u},
𝐯5=2t∂t+x∂x,𝐯6=4t2∂t+xt∂x−(2t+x2)∂u,𝐯ρ=ρ(x,t)e−u∂u,\mathbf{v}_{5}=2t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{6}=4t^{2}\partial_{t}+xt\partial_{x}-(2t+x^{2})\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{\rho}=\rho(x,t)e^{-u}\partial_{u},

where ρ\rho is a solution to the linear heat equation ρt=ρx​x\rho_{t}=\rho_{xx}. It is easy to see that the point transformation u~=eu\tilde{u}=e^{u} maps the basis vector fields to (212) of the linear equation together with 𝐯~ρ=ρ(x,t)∂u~\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{\rho}=\rho(x,t)\partial_{\tilde{u}} and Eq. (266) to the linear heat equation u~t=u~x​x\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xx}. The transformation v=uxv=u_{x} relates (266) to the usual Burgers’ equation

vt=vx​x+2​v​vx.v_{t}=v_{xx}+2vv_{x}. (267)

So we have established the celebrated Cole–Hopf transformation v=(ln⁡u~)x=u~x/u~v=(\ln\tilde{u})_{x}=\tilde{u}_{x}/\tilde{u} taking solutions of (267) to positive solutions of the heat equation.

As well, for higher order PDEs, we can use the same method of looking at the maximal point symmetry algebra (if possible) and constructing a linearizing transformation from its infinite-dimensional symmetry involving an arbitrary function as being solution to a linear PDE. We comment that there might be PDEs with finite symmetry algebra that can be linearized by nonpoint transformations.

Example 5.9.

(Exercise 2.22 of [35]) The nonlinear Thomas equation

𝖤=ut​x+α​ut+β​ux+γ​ux​ut=0,γ≠0\mathsf{E}=u_{tx}+\alpha u_{t}+\beta u_{x}+\gamma u_{x}u_{t}=0,\quad\gamma\neq 0 (268)

can be shown to be linearizable by a point transformation. We first compute its symmetry algebra. A general element of the algebra is written in the form

𝐯=τ(t,x,u)∂t+ξ(t,x,u)∂x+φ(t,x,u)∂u.\mathbf{v}=\tau(t,x,u)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\varphi(t,x,u)\partial_{u}. (269)

We need only the prolongation of 𝐯\mathbf{v} involving coefficients of ut​x,ut,uxu_{tx},u_{t},u_{x}

pr(2)𝐯=𝐯+φt∂ut+φx∂ux+φt​x∂ut​x.{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}+\varphi^{t}\partial_{u_{t}}+\varphi^{x}\partial_{u_{x}}+\varphi^{tx}\partial_{u_{tx}}.

Acting on 𝖤\mathsf{E} by the prolonged vector field provides the linearized equation

φt​x+(α+γ​ux)​φt+(β+γ​ut)​φx=0.\varphi^{tx}+(\alpha+\gamma u_{x})\varphi^{t}+(\beta+\gamma u_{t})\varphi^{x}=0. (270)

Replacing ut​xu_{tx} by −(α​ut+β​ux+γ​ux​ut)-(\alpha u_{t}+\beta u_{x}+\gamma u_{x}u_{t}) and splitting with respect to the derivatives ut​t,ut​t​uxu_{tt},u_{tt}u_{x} and ux​x,ux​x​utu_{xx},u_{xx}u_{t} we find

τx=τu=0,ξt=ξu=0.\tau_{x}=\tau_{u}=0,\qquad\xi_{t}=\xi_{u}=0.

Using the simplification τ=τ⁡(t)\tau=\tau(t) and ξ=ξ⁡(x)\xi=\xi(x) and splitting the remaining determining equations resulting from (270) with respect to the derivatives involving ut​uxu_{t}u_{x}, utu_{t}, uxu_{x} we find

ut​ux:φu​u+γ​φu=0,ut:φx​u+γ​φx+α​ξ′=0,ux:φt​u+γ​φt+β​τ˙=0,u0:φt​x+α​φt+β​φx=0.\begin{split}u_{t}u_{x}:&\quad\varphi_{uu}+\gamma\varphi_{u}=0,\\ u_{t}:&\quad\varphi_{xu}+\gamma\varphi_{x}+\alpha\xi^{\prime}=0,\\ u_{x}:&\quad\varphi_{tu}+\gamma\varphi_{t}+\beta\dot{\tau}=0,\\ u^{0}:&\quad\varphi_{tx}+\alpha\varphi_{t}+\beta\varphi_{x}=0.\end{split} (271)

From the first equation we have φ⁡(t,x,u)=f⁡(t,x)+e−γ​u​g​(t,x)\varphi(t,x,u)=f(t,x)+e^{-\gamma u}g(t,x), γ≠0\gamma\neq 0. Substitution back into (271) determines the form of ff

f⁡(t,x)=−1γ​(α​ξ+β​τ)+c,f(t,x)=-\frac{1}{\gamma}(\alpha\xi+\beta\tau)+c,

where cc is an arbitrary constant. The last equation of (271) gives

e−γ​u​(gt​x+α​gt+β​gx)=α​βγ​(τ˙+ξ′).e^{-\gamma u}(g_{tx}+\alpha g_{t}+\beta g_{x})=\frac{\alpha\beta}{\gamma}(\dot{\tau}+\xi^{\prime}).

This implies that if one of α,β\alpha,\beta is zero then gg has to satisfy a linear PDE and τ\tau, ξ\xi remain arbitrary. The symmetry algebra is then infinite dimensional and is spanned by

𝐯=τ(t)∂t+ξ(x)∂x+[−αγξ(x)+c+g(t,x)e−γ​u]∂u\mathbf{v}=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\left[-\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\xi(x)+c+g(t,x)e^{-\gamma u}\right]\partial_{u}

if β=0\beta=0, and

𝐯=τ(t)∂t+ξ(x)∂x+[−βγτ(t)+c+g(t,x)e−γ​u]∂u\mathbf{v}=\tau(t)\partial_{t}+\xi(x)\partial_{x}+\left[-\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\tau(t)+c+g(t,x)e^{-\gamma u}\right]\partial_{u}

if α=0\alpha=0. The function gg satisfies gt​x+α​gt=0g_{tx}+\alpha g_{t}=0 and gt​x+β​gx=0g_{tx}+\beta g_{x}=0, respectively.

Otherwise, we must have τ˙+ξ′=0\dot{\tau}+\xi^{\prime}=0. This fixes τ\tau and ξ\xi as τ=λ​t+c1\tau=\lambda t+c_{1}, ξ=−λ​x+c2\xi=-\lambda x+c_{2}, where λ,c1,c2\lambda,c_{1},c_{2} are arbitrary constants. Summarizing, we conclude that the general element 𝐯\mathbf{v} depends on four parameters c1,c2,c,λc_{1},c_{2},c,\lambda and an arbitrary solution of a linear PDE. So (268) is invariant under an infinite dimensional symmetry algebra with the basis vector fields

𝐯1=∂t,𝐯2=∂x,𝐯3=∂u,𝐯4=t∂t−x∂x+γ−1(αx−βt)∂u,𝐯(ρ)=e−γ​uρ(t,x)∂u,\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=t\partial_{t}-x\partial_{x}+\gamma^{-1}(\alpha x-\beta t)\partial_{u},\\ &\mathbf{v}(\rho)=e^{-\gamma u}\rho(t,x)\partial_{u},\end{split} (272)

where ρ⁡(t,x)\rho(t,x) solves the linear equation

ρt​x+α​ρt+β​ρx=0.\rho_{tx}+\alpha\rho_{t}+\beta\rho_{x}=0. (273)

The fact that the Lie symmetry algebra depends on solutions of a linear PDE suggests that there must exist a change of dependent variable that will linearize the original equation. Such a transformation is given by u~=F⁡(u)\tilde{u}=F(u) with the property F′=eγ​uF^{\prime}=e^{\gamma u} so that u~=γ−1​eγ​u\tilde{u}=\gamma^{-1}e^{\gamma u} where u~\tilde{u} satisfies

u~t​x+α​u~t+β​u~x=0.\tilde{u}_{tx}+\alpha\tilde{u}_{t}+\beta\tilde{u}_{x}=0.

The linear transformation u~=e−α​x−β​t​v​(t,x)\tilde{u}=e^{-\alpha x-\beta t}v(t,x) removes the parameters α\alpha and β\beta, resulting in

vt​x−α​β​v=0.v_{tx}-\alpha\beta v=0. (274)

This equation inherits the symmetry 𝐯~4=t∂t−x∂x\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{4}=t\partial_{t}-x\partial_{x} from 𝐯4\mathbf{v}_{4}. Its invariants are τ=t​x\tau=tx and vv so we reduce it by the transformation v=G⁡(τ)v=G(\tau) to the ODE

τ​G′′+G′−α​β​G=0.\tau G^{\prime\prime}+G^{\prime}-\alpha\beta G=0.

The general solution of this equation can be written in terms of the modified Bessel functions

G⁡(τ)=c1​I0​(2​α​β​τ)+c2​K0​(2​α​β​τ).G(\tau)=c_{1}I_{0}(2\sqrt{\alpha\beta\tau})+c_{2}K_{0}(2\sqrt{\alpha\beta\tau}).

The choice c1=1c_{1}=1, c2=0c_{2}=0 yields the fundamental solution (or Green’s function) at the origin (0,0)(0,0) (see [2])

G⁡(t,x,0,0)=I0​(2​α​β​t​x).G(t,x;0,0)=I_{0}(2\sqrt{\alpha\beta tx}).

It is sufficient to use the translational invariance to obtain the Green’s function at (t0,x0)(t_{0},x_{0})

G⁡(t,x,t0,x0)=I0​(2​α​β​(t−t0)​(x−x0)).G(t,x;t_{0},x_{0})=I_{0}\left(2\sqrt{\alpha\beta(t-t_{0})(x-x_{0})}\right).

A particular the solution of the given PDE will be in the form

u=1γ​log⁡[γ​G​(t​x)−α​x−β​t].u=\frac{1}{\gamma}\log[\gamma G(tx)-\alpha x-\beta t].
Example 5.10.

We consider a third order KdV-type evolution equation

ut=ux​x​x+6​u−1​ux​ux​x+u−2​ux3.u_{t}=u_{xxx}+6u^{-1}u_{x}u_{xx}+u^{-2}u_{x}^{3}.

The symmetry algebra is infinite-dimensional with basis elements

𝐯1=∂t,𝐯2=∂x,𝐯3=3t∂t+x∂x,𝐯4=u∂u,𝐯ρ=ρ(t,x)u−2∂u,\mathbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=3t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=u\partial_{u},\quad\mathbf{v}_{\rho}=\rho(t,x)u^{-2}\partial_{u},

where ρ\rho is any solution to the linear KdV equation ρt=ρx​x​x\rho_{t}=\rho_{xxx}. The transformation u~=u3\tilde{u}=u^{3} maps the symmetry algebra to that of the linear KdV equation u~t=u~x​x​x\tilde{u}_{t}=\tilde{u}_{xxx}, and hence the original equation to the linear one.

It may not always be practical to calculate the maximal infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra by application of the Lie symmetry algorithm. When this is the case, it is usually useful to give some tests involving only certain finite-dimensional subalgebra of the maximal symmetry algebra. But, in this case, for PDEs the construction of linearizing transformation is a tricky task.

For ODEs, we already encountered such a test (due to Lie) in Example 3.7. See also Remark 4.4. It is sufficient to identify a two-dimensional subalgebra equivalent to the canonical forms A2,2A_{2,2} (abelian) or A2,4A_{2,4} (nonabelian) as the eight-dimensional symmetry algebra of a linearizable second order ODE. Finding linearizing coordinates is immediate. A further example is the following second member of Riccati chain, known to be linearizable to z3=z′′′=0z_{3}=z^{\prime\prime\prime}=0 by the Hopf–Cole transformation y=z′​(x)/z⁡(x)y=z^{\prime}(x)/z(x).

Example 5.11.
𝖤⁡(x,y(2))=y2+3​y​y1+y3=0.\mathsf{E}(x,y^{(2)})=y_{2}+3yy_{1}+y^{3}=0. (275)

This equation admits a linearly connected (rank-one) nonabelian 2-dimensional algebra spanned by

𝐯1=y∂x−y3∂y,𝐯2=λ(x,y)𝐯1,λ(x,y)=xy(1−12xy)\mathbf{v}_{1}=y\partial_{x}-y^{3}\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\lambda(x,y)\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad\lambda(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}\left(1-\frac{1}{2}xy\right)

with commutation relation [𝐯1,𝐯2]=𝐯1[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=\mathbf{v}_{1}. This is verified by noting

pr(2)​𝐯1​(𝖤)=−3​(y2+y1)​𝖤,{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{1}(\mathsf{E})=-3(y^{2}+y_{1})\mathsf{E},

and

pr(2)​𝐯2​(𝖤)=12​[3​x2​(y2+y1)−4]​𝖤,{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}_{2}(\mathsf{E})=\frac{1}{2}[3x^{2}(y^{2}+y_{1})-4]\mathsf{E},

then checking the infinitesimal invariance criterion (24). This knowledge ensures us that Eq. (275) has a eight-dimensional symmetry algebra and thus can be linearized.

A linearizing coordinate transformation r=r⁡(x,y)r=r(x,y), s=s⁡(x,y)s=s(x,y) is found by solving the set of linear first order PDEs 𝐯1​(r)=0\mathbf{v}_{1}(r)=0, 𝐯1​(s)=1\mathbf{v}_{1}(s)=1, 𝐯2​(r)=0\mathbf{v}_{2}(r)=0, 𝐯2​(s)=s\mathbf{v}_{2}(s)=s as

r=x−1y,s=xy−x22.r=x-\frac{1}{y},\quad s=\frac{x}{y}-\frac{x^{2}}{2}.

Note that we simply have chosen rr as a joint invariant and s=λ⁡(x,y)s=\lambda(x,y). The transformed algebra is the canonical form A2,4:{∂s,s∂s}A_{2,4}:\left\{\partial_{s},s\partial_{s}\right\}. This transformation linearizes Eq. (275) to s′′​(r)=0s^{\prime\prime}(r)=0. This is readily seen by calculating the following derivative and using the given equation:

d2​sd​r2=−y3​(y2+3​y​y1+y3)(y2+y1)3=0.\frac{d^{2}s}{dr^{2}}=-\frac{y^{3}(y_{2}+3yy_{1}+y^{3})}{(y^{2}+y_{1})^{3}}=0.

We note that the full eight-dimensional symmetry algebra of the equation is isomorphic to that of the equation s′′=0s^{\prime\prime}=0. This is the sl⁡(3,ℝ)\Sl(3,\mathbb{R}) algebra generated by the vector fields

∂r,r∂r,s∂r,rs∂r+s2∂s,∂s,r∂s,s∂s,r2∂r+rs∂s.\begin{split}&\partial_{r},\quad r\partial_{r},\quad s\partial_{r},\quad rs\partial_{r}+s^{2}\partial_{s},\\ &\partial_{s},\quad r\partial_{s},\quad s\partial_{s},\quad r^{2}\partial_{r}+rs\partial_{s}.\end{split} (276)

The corresponding group is just the projective group SL⁡(3,ℝ)\SL(3,\mathbb{R}) in the (r,s)(r,s) plane

(r~,s~):(r,s)→(a1​r+a2​s+a3a7​r+a8​s+a9,a4​r+a5​s+a6a7​r+a8​s+a9)(\tilde{r},\tilde{s}):\quad(r,s)\to\left(\frac{a_{1}r+a_{2}s+a_{3}}{a_{7}r+a_{8}s+a_{9}},\frac{a_{4}r+a_{5}s+a_{6}}{a_{7}r+a_{8}s+a_{9}}\right)

with the condition

|a1a2a3a4a5a6a7a8a9|≠0.\begin{vmatrix}a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}\\ a_{4}&a_{5}&a_{6}\\ a_{7}&a_{8}&a_{9}\end{vmatrix}\neq 0.

The projective group SL⁡(3,ℝ)\SL(3,\mathbb{R}) maps the family of straight lines onto themselves. Another interesting fact is that this group has the lowest order differential invariant starting at order 7. But obviously there are lower order relative differential invariants such as the second order one I=s′′​(r)I=s^{\prime\prime}(r). This means that, for some differential function μ\mu, s~′′​(r~)=μ​s′′​(r)\tilde{s}^{\prime\prime}(\tilde{r})=\mu s^{\prime\prime}(r) under the projective group. A differential function I:Jn→ℝI:J^{n}\to\mathbb{R} is a relative differential invariant of order nn of a Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} if for some differential function λ⁡(x,u(n))\lambda(x,u^{(n)})

pr(n)​𝐯​(I)=λ⁡(x,u(n))​I{\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}(I)=\lambda(x,u^{(n)})I

for every prolonged vector field pr(n)​𝐯∈𝔤(n){\rm pr}^{(n)}\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{g}^{(n)}. If λ=0\lambda=0, II is a differential invariant of order nn. The seventh order differential invariant can be expressed in terms of relative differential invariants (see [23]).

In the following example we shall make use of the existence of an infinite-dimensional symmetry algebra to find a linearizing transformation.

Remark 5.14.

For an ODE of order n>2n>2, Lie proved that the dimension dnd_{n} of the Lie algebra of its symmetry group is at most n+4n+4. Maximal dimension dn=n+4d_{n}=n+4 is reached for a linear homogeneous ODE, equivalent to the reduced one yn=y(n)=0y_{n}=y^{(n)}=0 by the point transformations in the plane. The corresponding Lie group is the semi-direct sum of GL⁡(n,ℝ)\GL(n,\mathbb{R}) with an nn-dimensional abelian Lie group. A basis for its Lie algebra is given by

𝐯1=y∂y,𝐯2=∂x,𝐯3=x∂x,𝐯4=x2∂x+(n−1)xy∂y,𝐯i+4=yi∂y,i=1,2,⋯,n,\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=y\partial_{y},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{3}=x\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{v}_{4}=x^{2}\partial_{x}+(n-1)xy\partial_{y},\\ &\mathbf{v}_{i+4}=y_{i}\partial_{y},\quad i=1,2,\cdots,n,\end{split} (286)

where yiy_{i}’s form a basis for the solution space to this equation.

The general solution of the equation can be written in the form

y=∑i=1nci​u1n−i​u2i−1,y=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}u^{n-i}_{1}u^{i-1}_{2}, (287)

where u1,u2u_{1},u_{2} are linearly independent solutions to a second order linear, homogeneous ODE. For example, the third order linear ODE (119) has a Lie point symmetry group of dimension seven and admits the general solution

ξ=c1​u12+c2​u1​u2+c3​u22,\xi=c_{1}u_{1}^{2}+c_{2}u_{1}u_{2}+c_{3}u_{2}^{2}, (288)

where u1,u2u_{1},u_{2} are solutions to the second order ODE u′′+I​u=0u^{\prime\prime}+Iu=0.

If we extend (280) to the nonlinear form (a variant of the Ermakov–Pinney equation)

y′′+p⁡(x)​y′+q⁡(x)​y=τ⁡(x)​y−3,τ⁡(x)≠0,y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=\tau(x)y^{-3},\quad\tau(x)\neq 0, (289)

then in terms of (r,s)(r,s) in (283) we have

d2​sd​r2=e2​∫p​𝑑x​τ​(x)​s−3.\frac{d^{2}s}{dr^{2}}=e^{2\int pdx}\tau(x)s^{-3}. (290)

We require that the left hand side of (290) depends only on ss. This implies

τ(x)=Ke−2∫pdx\tau(x)=Ke^{-2\int pdx}

for some nonzero constant KK. Using Abel’s formula for Wronskians we can write τ⁡(x)=K​W0−2​W2​(x)\tau(x)=KW_{0}^{-2}W^{2}(x), where W0≠W_{0}\not= is the value of W⁡(x)W(x) at some point x0x_{0}. With this condition we conclude that a slightly modified form of the standard Ermakov–Pinney equation

y′′+p⁡(x)​y′+q⁡(x)​y=K​W0−2​W2​(x)​y−3y^{\prime\prime}+p(x)y^{\prime}+q(x)y=KW_{0}^{-2}W^{2}(x)y^{-3} (291)

is equivalent to the standard one s′′=K​W0−2​s−3s^{\prime\prime}=KW_{0}^{-2}s^{-3} (see (102)) admitting the general solution

s2=A+2​B​r+C​r2,A​C−B2=K​W0−2.s^{2}=A+2Br+Cr^{2},\quad AC-B^{2}=KW_{0}^{-2}.

Hence, a nonlinear superposition principle for the general solution of (289) is reached in the form

y2=s2​y12=A​y12+2​B​y1​y2+C​y22,(A​C−B2)​W02=Ky^{2}=s^{2}y_{1}^{2}=Ay_{1}^{2}+2By_{1}y_{2}+Cy_{2}^{2},\quad(AC-B^{2})W_{0}^{2}=K (292)

in terms of the linearly independent solutions of the auxiliary linear equation (280). We already encountered this remarkable equation a number of times (see, for example, (112)). An sl⁡(2,ℝ)\Sl(2,\mathbb{R}) algebra as a symmetry algebra of (291) with a basis given by

𝐯1=γ(x)(y12∂x+y1y′1y∂y),𝐯2=γ(x)(y1y2∂x+12(y1y2)′y∂y),𝐯3=γ(x)(y22∂x+y2y′2y∂y),γ(x)=exp[∫p(x)dx].\begin{split}&\mathbf{v}_{1}=\gamma(x)(y_{1}^{2}\partial_{x}+y_{1}y^{\prime}_{1}y\partial_{y}),\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\gamma(x)(y_{1}y_{2}\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(y_{1}y_{2})^{\prime}y\partial_{y}),\\ &\mathbf{v}_{3}=\gamma(x)(y_{2}^{2}\partial_{x}+y_{2}y^{\prime}_{2}y\partial_{y}),\quad\gamma(x)=\exp\left[\int p(x)dx\right].\end{split} (293)

is admitted. Their commutation relations are

[𝐯1,𝐯2]=W0​𝐯1,[𝐯1,𝐯3]=2​W0​𝐯2,[𝐯2,𝐯3]=W0​𝐯3.[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{2}]=W_{0}\mathbf{v}_{1},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=2W_{0}\mathbf{v}_{2},\quad[\mathbf{v}_{2},\mathbf{v}_{3}]=W_{0}\mathbf{v}_{3}. (294)

The nonzero constant W0W_{0} can be put to unity by rescaling the elements of the algebra. For further information on the Ermakov–Pinney equation (291) in the special case p=0p=0, see Refs. [5, 13].

5.2 Lie’s Linearization Theorem

This theorem states that amongst second-order ordinary differential equations, Eq. y2=f⁡(x,y,p)y_{2}=f(x,y,p) with p=y1p=y_{1} is point equivalent to the trivial free-particle equation y2=0y_{2}=0 if and only if the following fourth-order Tresse (absolute) invariants [31]

I1=fp​p​p​p=0,I2=D^x2​fp​p−4​D^x​fy​p−fp​D^x​fp​p+6​fy​y−3​fy​fp​p+4​fp​fy​p=0,I_{1}=f_{pppp}=0,\quad I_{2}=\widehat{D}_{x}^{2}f_{pp}-4\widehat{D}_{x}f_{yp}-f_{p}\widehat{D}_{x}f_{pp}+6f_{yy}-3f_{y}f_{pp}+4f_{p}f_{yp}=0, (295)

are identically zero. Here D^x=∂x+p∂y+f∂p\widehat{D}_{x}=\partial_{x}+p\partial_{y}+f\partial_{p} is the truncation of the usual total derivative operator DxD_{x} restricted to y2=fy_{2}=f. The first condition implies that ff should be at most cubic in p=y1p=y_{1}.

Example 5.15.

Any equation admitting a A2,3A_{2,3}-type symmetry can be linearized if and only if it has the form

x​y2=a​y13+b​y12+(1+b23​a)​y1+b⁡(9​a+b2)27​a2,xy_{2}=ay_{1}^{3}+by_{1}^{2}+\left(1+\frac{b^{2}}{3a}\right)y_{1}+\frac{b(9a+b^{2})}{27a^{2}}, (296)

where a≠0a\neq 0 and bb are arbitrary constants. The necessary and sufficient conditions (295) for linerizability are satisfied. We can simplify (296) using the equivalence group transformation shifting only the parameter bb as b→b+εb\to b+\varepsilon [47]. This means that we can put b=0b=0 by choosing the group parameter ε=−b\varepsilon=-b. This transformation is given by

x~=e−b​(1+x2)−1,y~=e−b/2(y+b3​ax).\tilde{x}=\sqrt{e^{-b}(1+x^{2})-1},\quad\tilde{y}=e^{-b/2}\left(y+\frac{b}{3a}x\right). (297)

x~​y~2=a​y~13+y~1.\tilde{x}\tilde{y}_{2}=a\tilde{y}_{1}^{3}+\tilde{y}_{1}. (298)

Two equivalent equations have isomorphic symmetry groups so that there should be a point transformation mapping the two Lie algebras and Eqs. (298) and y2=0y_{2}=0 into each other. See [47] for the construction of such a map. An easier way of achieving linearization is by using a two-dimensional subalgebra of type A22A_{22} of 4.4 of its entire sl⁡(3,ℝ)\Sl(3,\mathbb{R}) symmetry algebra given by

𝐯1=1x~∂x~,𝐯2=y~x~∂x~.\mathbf{v}_{1}=\frac{1}{\tilde{x}}\partial_{\tilde{x}},\quad\mathbf{v}_{2}=\frac{\tilde{y}}{\tilde{x}}\partial_{\tilde{x}}.

(298) to the linear equation s′′​(r)=y~1−3​(y~1−x~​y~2)=−as^{\prime\prime}(r)=\tilde{y}_{1}^{-3}(\tilde{y}_{1}-\tilde{x}\tilde{y}_{2})=-a. Consequently, the solution in tilde coordinates is

a​y~2+x~2+c1​y~+c2=0.a\tilde{y}^{2}+\tilde{x}^{2}+c_{1}\tilde{y}+c_{2}=0.

Reverting to (x,y)(x,y) coordinates via (297) and redefining arbitrary constants c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} leads to the solution of (296)

a​y2+2​b3​x​y+(1+b29​a)​x2+C1​(y+b3​a​x)+C2=0,ay^{2}+\frac{2b}{3}xy+\left(1+\frac{b^{2}}{9a}\right)x^{2}+C_{1}\left(y+\frac{b}{3a}x\right)+C_{2}=0,

which geometrically describes a family of ellipses or hyperbolas as its discriminant Δ=−4​a\Delta=-4a varies for a<0a<0 or a>0a>0, respectively.

Equation of Example 5.11 with two-dimensional symmetry group generated by {∂x,x∂x−y∂y}\left\{\partial_{x},x\partial_{x}-y\partial_{y}\right\} of the type A23A_{23} of 4.4 (modulo a point transformation (x,y)→(y−1,x+y−1)(x,y)\to(y^{-1},x+y^{-1})) belongs to the class (296) with a=−1a=-1, b=6b=6 or to (298) with a=−1a=-1 and hence once again its linearizability has been established.

In general, if the second order equation y2=f⁡(x,y,p)y_{2}=f(x,y,p) is known to satisfy linearizability conditions (295), it is sufficient to pick a two-dimensional intransitive subalgebra of type A2,2A_{2,2} or A2,4A_{2,4} (up to change of basis) of the sl⁡(3,ℝ)\Sl(3,\mathbb{R}) symmetry algebra to transform to a linear equation.

Linearization criteria (295) for the ODE (279) is fulfilled if g⁡(x,y)g(x,y) satisfies the PDE

For σ=1\sigma=1, we find g⁡(x,y)=h⁡(x)​y​ln⁡yg(x,y)=h(x)y\ln y, y>0y>0, excluding the linear term f⁡(x)​yf(x)y. Then, the vector field 𝐯(ρ)=ρ(x)y∂y\mathbf{v}(\rho)=\rho(x)y\partial_{y}, where ρ\rho solves the linear ODE ρ′′+p​ρ′−h​ρ=0\rho^{\prime\prime}+p\rho^{\prime}-h\rho=0, is a symmetry because pr(2)​𝐯​(𝖤)=ρ⁡(x)​𝖤=0{\rm pr}^{(2)}\mathbf{v}(\mathsf{E})=\rho(x)\mathsf{E}=0 on 𝖤=y2+p​y′+q​y−y−1​y12−h⁡(x)​y​ln⁡y=0\mathsf{E}=y_{2}+py^{\prime}+qy-y^{-1}y_{1}^{2}-h(x)y\ln y=0. We comment that there are also similar tests for second order systems of ODEs based on the structure of symmetry algebras [49]. For systems of PDEs, a general approach to linearizability can be found in the paper [25] (see also the book [4]).

Example 5.16.

Ω(y)=gexp[−A∫g−1dy],Z′=Ω−1.\Omega(y)=g\exp\left[-A\int g^{-1}dy\right],\quad Z^{\prime}=\Omega^{-1}.

5.3 Concluding remarks

So far we restricted our attention to local Lie point transformations that leave the system of differential equations invariant. They are usually called classical symmetries of the system. There are several uses of them in the context of differential equations like group-invariant solutions for PDEs and integration for ODEs among others. One the important generalizations of classical symmetries is the notion of generalized (or Lie–Bäcklund) symmetries. They were originally introduced by E. Noether in her celebrated paper [33] (see [34] for a more recent English translation), which related variational symmetries and (local) conservation laws. They also play a central role in soliton theory of completely integrable nonlinear partial differential equations. Evolution equations like KdV (Korteweg–de Vries) and KP (Kadomtsev–Petviashvili) are known to admit infinite hierarchies of generalized symmetries and conservation laws. An approach to classification of integrable systems is to identify systems admitting generalized symmetries up to differential substitutions preserving the differential structure of the system. The infinitesimal generators of generalized symmetries depend on derivatives of dependent variables. In the special case of one dependent variable, every first order generalized symmetry determines a contact symmetry (local diffeomorphisms of the nn-th order jet space JnJ^{n}, preserving the contact ideal generated by contact forms of the equation) and vice versa.

Over the last few decades, numerous useful extensions of the classical Lie approach to group-invariant solutions have been developed. Among others, they include the method of partially invariant solutions [38], non-classical method, methods of conditional (point or generalized) [37], and of symmetries of potential systems [4].
